questions.q: You're driving along a winding country road. How should you choose your speed?
options: So you can keep up with the vehicle in front
At the maximum speed limit shown for that road
So you can stop within the clear distance ahead
Fast enough to stay well ahead of traffic behind
questions.explain: You should drive at a speed that lets you stop well within the distance you can see to be clear. On country roads, slow down on the approach to bends, which can be sharper than they appear.

questions.q: You're driving along a country road and see this sign. What should you be prepared for?
options: A roundabout just past the bend
The road narrowing on the bend
A double bend, first to the left
A junction on the bend ahead
questions.explain: This sign warns of a junction on a bend ahead. Where there are junctions, be prepared for road users emerging, and adjust your speed as a precaution.

questions.q: You're in a queue of slow-moving traffic. Why should you leave enough space between you and the vehicle in front?
options: So drivers can't pull in front of you
So you can build up speed between stops
So you don't need to use your brakes
So you can get round it if it breaks down
questions.explain: In slow-moving traffic, leave enough space to be able to manoeuvre if the vehicle in front breaks down or an emergency vehicle needs to get past. Never get so close that you can't stop safely.

questions.q: You're approaching a blind bend on a narrow country lane. What should you be prepared for?
options: Oncoming drivers always giving way to you
The road being blocked just beyond the bend
The bend being gentler than it first appears
A clear road, as hazards on bends are signed
questions.explain: Be prepared for unexpected situations, such as the road being blocked beyond a blind bend, and adjust your speed as a precaution. Bends can be sharper than they appear.

questions.q: You're driving through a busy shopping street. A child on the pavement ahead is looking the other way. What should you be ready for?
options: The child waving you on to pass
The child waiting until you've gone by
The child stepping out without seeing you
The child using the nearest crossing
questions.explain: Try to anticipate what pedestrians might do. If pedestrians, particularly children, are looking the other way, they may step out into the road without seeing you.

questions.q: You're parked at the side of the road and about to move off. You've checked all your mirrors. What should you do next?
options: Look round to check your blind spots
Sound your horn to warn other traffic
Switch on your hazard warning lights
Flash your headlights at oncoming traffic
questions.explain: Before moving off, use all your mirrors, then look round to check the blind spots – the areas you can't see in the mirrors. Signal if necessary and take a final look round before you move off.

questions.q: You're about to turn left into a side road. When should you check your mirrors?
options: Once you've started to turn
As you begin to brake for the turn
Only if you hear a horn behind you
In good time before you signal
questions.explain: You should use your mirrors in good time before you signal or change direction or speed, and give a left-turn signal well before you turn.

questions.q: You're about to change direction on a busy road. Which routine does the Highway Code tell you to use?
options: Signal – Mirrors – Manoeuvre
Mirrors – Signal – Manoeuvre
Manoeuvre – Mirrors – Signal
Signal – Manoeuvre – Mirrors
questions.explain: Remember Mirrors – Signal – Manoeuvre. Check your mirrors first so you know what's behind and to each side of you before you signal or change direction.

questions.q: You're waiting to turn right into a side road and a safe gap appears in the oncoming traffic. What should you do before you make the turn?
options: Switch on your hazard warning lights
Sound your horn to warn oncoming traffic
Check your mirrors and blind spot again
Wave to the next oncoming driver to wait
questions.explain: Before turning right, check your mirrors and blind spot again to make sure you aren't being overtaken, then make the turn. Don't cut the corner.

questions.q: You're about to overtake on a motorway. A car you saw in your door mirror a moment ago has disappeared from view. What should you do?
options: Glance sideways to check your blind spot
Assume it has left and move out at once
Speed up so it can't come alongside you
Signal and move straight out into the lane
questions.explain: Before overtaking, take a quick sideways glance into the blind spot area to check the position of a vehicle that may have disappeared from your view in the mirror.

questions.q: You've just hired a car you haven't driven before. Your licence and insurance are in order. What should you do before you set off?
options: Rely on the hire company's checks
Set the mirrors once you're moving
Test the brakes hard on the main road
Find out where all the controls are
questions.explain: Before setting off, you should make sure you know where all the controls are and how to use them, and that your mirrors and seat are adjusted correctly.

questions.q: You've just turned right at a junction and your indicator is still flashing. Why should you make sure it's cancelled?
options: It will flatten the car's battery
It's illegal to signal on a straight road
It will distract your passengers
It could mislead other road users
questions.explain: Signals warn and inform other road users of what you intend to do. Cancel them after use and make sure they won't confuse others, who may think you're about to turn.

questions.q: You're driving along a main road and see this sign. What does it warn you about?
options: The road narrowing on the left
A lane closing on the right
A sharp bend to the left ahead
Traffic merging from the left ahead
questions.explain: This sign warns that traffic will be merging from the left ahead. Where there are junctions, be prepared for road users joining and adjust your speed if necessary.

questions.q: You're signalling to move out past a parked van, but a cyclist is coming up on your right. What should you do?
options: Wait for the cyclist to pass before moving out
Move out, as your signal gives you priority
Sound your horn, then move out
Speed up to get past the van first
questions.explain: Signalling doesn't give you priority. Cyclists are harder to see than larger vehicles and are particularly vulnerable, so give way to them when you change direction – don't cut across them.

questions.q: The driver of the car in front gives this arm signal. What does it mean?
options: I intend to move out to the right
I intend to move in to the left
Please overtake me when it's safe
I intend to slow down or stop
questions.explain: This arm signal means the driver intends to slow down or stop. Watch out for signals given by other road users and only go on when you're satisfied it's safe.
ref: HC Signals to other road users

questions.q: You're waiting to join a roundabout. A car on the roundabout to your right isn't signalling. What should you bear in mind?
options: It must be going straight ahead
It's certain to pass your road
It has to give way to you
It may not be signalling correctly
questions.explain: Watch out for all other road users already on the roundabout, and be aware that they may not be signalling correctly or at all. Wait until you're sure what they're doing.

questions.q: You're waiting at red traffic lights and the phone in your pocket beeps with a message. What should you do?
options: Read it, as the car isn't moving
Read it if the engine has switched itself off
Leave it, as the law still applies at lights
Read it, but put it down before the lights change
questions.explain: It's illegal to hold and use a phone while driving. The law still applies when you're stopped at traffic lights or queuing in traffic – even in a car that turns its engine off when you stop.

questions.q: You're caught holding and using your phone while driving. What penalty can you get?
options: 6 penalty points and a £200 fine
3 penalty points and a £100 fine
6 penalty points and a £100 fine
3 penalty points and a £200 fine
questions.explain: You can get 6 penalty points and a £200 fine if you hold and use a phone, sat nav, tablet or any device that can send and receive data while driving.

questions.q: You passed your driving test 18 months ago. You're caught holding and using your phone while driving. What will happen?
options: You'll get a verbal warning only
You'll get 3 points but keep your licence
You'll have to take extra lessons only
You'll lose your licence
questions.explain: Holding and using a phone can bring 6 penalty points. If you passed your test in the last 2 years, you'll lose your licence and have to pass both the theory and practical tests again.

questions.q: Your car has a hands-free phone system and a call comes in while you're driving. What's the safest thing to do?
options: Answer it, as hands-free calls are safe
Let it go to voicemail and listen later
Pick the phone up to see who's calling
Answer it, but keep the call short
questions.explain: Using hands-free equipment is still likely to distract your attention from the road. It's far safer not to use any phone while driving – find a safe place to stop first, or use voicemail and listen later.

questions.q: You're driving and need to enter a new destination into your sat nav. What should you do?
options: Find a safe place to stop first
Type it in while driving slowly
Do it while you're queuing in traffic
Hold the sat nav low on your lap
questions.explain: Don't be distracted by maps or screen-based information such as navigation systems while driving. If necessary, find a safe place to stop. You MUST keep proper control of your vehicle at all times.

questions.q: You like to listen to loud music while you drive. Why can this be dangerous?
options: It's illegal to play music while driving
It can make your car use more fuel
It may mask other sounds around you
It can affect your car's electrics
questions.explain: Safe driving needs concentration. Loud music is a distraction because it may mask other sounds – you need to be able to look and listen for things like emergency vehicle sirens.

questions.q: You're on a long journey and feel hungry. What should you do?
options: Eat while driving along a quiet road
Eat while you wait at traffic lights
Eat on a straight stretch of motorway
Stop in a safe place to eat
questions.explain: Eating and drinking are distractions you should avoid while driving. Keeping both hands on the wheel where possible helps you stay in full control, so stop somewhere safe to eat.

questions.q: You've recently passed your test. Your friends in the car are being loud and distracting. What should you do?
options: Tell them you need to concentrate
Turn up the music to drown them out
Drive faster to end the journey sooner
Turn round to talk to them at junctions
questions.explain: You're responsible for your passengers' safety. Don't let them distract you or encourage you to take risks – tell them you need to concentrate to get everyone there safely.

questions.q: Your car has driver assistance systems, such as motorway assist and lane departure warning. How should you use them?
options: Rely on them so you can rest your eyes
As an aid, while keeping full concentration
As a way to free up time to check your phone
Let them take responsibility for the car
questions.explain: Driver assistance systems are there to help, but don't rely on them or reduce your concentration. You're still responsible for the vehicle and MUST have full control at all times.

questions.q: You're about to drive home wearing a pair of heavy walking boots. What should you consider first?
options: Whether they'll keep your feet warm enough
Whether they'll leave mud on the floor mats
Whether you'll need them at the other end
Whether you can use the pedals properly
questions.explain: Before setting off, you should make sure your clothing and footwear don't prevent you from using the controls in the correct manner.

questions.q: You're planning a long journey. How often does the Highway Code recommend you take a break?
options: At least 5 minutes every four hours
At least 15 minutes every four hours
At least 30 minutes every hour
At least 15 minutes every two hours
questions.explain: Plan your journey to take enough breaks. A minimum break of at least 15 minutes after every two hours of driving is recommended.

questions.q: You're driving on a motorway and begin to feel sleepy. What should you do?
options: Stop at the next service area to rest
Stop on the hard shoulder for a rest
Open a window and keep on driving
Pull into an emergency area to sleep
questions.explain: If you feel sleepy, stop in a safe place. Don't stop in an emergency area or on the hard shoulder – use a service area, or leave the motorway to find somewhere to rest.

questions.q: You're planning a long drive. Between which times does the Highway Code say natural alertness is at a minimum?
options: 6 am and 9 am
Midnight and 6 am
2 pm and 4 pm
6 pm and midnight
questions.explain: Avoid long journeys between midnight and 6 am, when natural alertness is at a minimum. This is also a time of high risk for new drivers.

questions.q: You've had very little sleep and have a long drive planned for this morning. What should you do?
options: Set off as planned and drink coffee
Drive with the window open all the way
Put off the journey until you've rested
Set off, but drive faster to arrive sooner
questions.explain: Driving when you're tired greatly increases your risk of a collision. Don't begin a journey if you're tired – get enough sleep before setting off on a long journey.

questions.q: Your phone is in a cradle fixed to the dashboard. You want to call a friend while you're driving. What does the law say?
options: You may dial if one hand stays on the wheel
You may dial while stopped in a queue
You may dial if the call will be short
You mustn't pick it up to dial the number
questions.explain: You MUST NOT pick up a phone while driving to dial a number and then put it in the cradle for the conversation. It's far safer not to use any phone while driving: find a safe place to stop first.

questions.q: It's dark and the headlights of an approaching car are dazzling you. What should you do?
options: Flash your headlights back at them
Switch to main beam to see better
Look straight at the oncoming lights
Slow down, and stop if you need to
questions.explain: If you're dazzled by oncoming headlights, slow down and, if necessary, stop. Don't flash your headlights or use main beam, as you MUST NOT use lights in a way that dazzles others.

questions.q: You're about to drive home after dark. You normally wear tinted glasses during the day. What does the Highway Code advise?
options: Wear them to cut down glare from headlights
Don't wear them if they restrict your vision
Wear them, but only on roads with street lights
Wear them only if it starts to rain heavily
questions.explain: At night or in poor visibility, don't use tinted glasses, lenses or visors if they restrict your vision.

questions.q: You see this sign on the approach to a busy junction. What should you be prepared for?
options: A lane for slow vehicles
A closed hard shoulder
Traffic lights out of order
Queuing traffic ahead
questions.explain: This sign warns that traffic queues are likely ahead. Be prepared to slow down or stop, and adjust your speed as a precaution.

questions.q: You're waiting behind another car to join a roundabout. You see a safe gap in the traffic from the right. What should you check before you move off?
options: That your hazard lights are on
That the car behind is well back
That the next exit is clear
That the car in front has moved off
questions.explain: When reaching a roundabout, give priority to traffic approaching from your right, and look forward before moving off to make sure the traffic in front has moved off.

questions.q: You're about to move out to overtake on a motorway. Why should you check your mirrors carefully first?
options: Lorries often change lanes without signalling
You must signal before you use your mirrors
The left-hand lane may be about to end
Traffic may be coming up behind very quickly
questions.explain: Before overtaking on a motorway, remember that traffic may be coming up behind you very quickly. Check all your mirrors carefully, look out for motorcyclists and signal in plenty of time.

questions.q: You need to reverse out of a parking space, but a van parked next to you blocks your view. What should you do?
options: Reverse out quickly before traffic comes
Sound your horn and reverse slowly
Rely on your door mirrors only
Get someone to guide you out
questions.explain: Look carefully before you reverse: use all your mirrors and check all around. If you can't see clearly, get someone to guide you.

questions.q: You're reversing into a parking space. Where should you mainly look while you're moving backwards?
options: In the interior mirror only
At the door mirror on the kerb side
Through the rear window
Forward through the windscreen
questions.explain: Look carefully before you start reversing, then reverse slowly while checking all around and looking mainly through the rear window.

questions.q: You need to turn your car round. Which of these should you avoid?
options: Reversing from a side road into a main road
Driving round a block of nearby side streets
Turning round in a quiet, empty side road
Waiting until you find a safe place to turn
questions.explain: Wait until you find a safe place to turn round, such as a quiet side road, or drive round a block of side streets. Don't reverse from a side road into a main road.

questions.q: You're reversing to the left around a corner. What should you be aware of?
options: The rear of your car will swing out
Your mirrors will show everything
Your brakes will be less effective
The front of your car will swing out
questions.explain: Reverse slowly while checking all around, and be aware that the front of your vehicle will swing out as you turn.

questions.q: You're following a slow van and want to overtake it. You check your mirrors before pulling out. What are you making sure of?
options: The driver behind has flashed you out
The car behind is close enough to follow
Nobody is starting to overtake you
Your indicator is already flashing
questions.explain: Before overtaking, make sure the road is clear enough ahead, that road users aren't beginning to overtake you, and that there's a suitable gap in front of the road user you plan to overtake.

questions.q: You're driving along a busy road. How often should you use your mirrors?
options: Only just before you turn or stop
Whenever you hear another vehicle's horn
Frequently, so you know what's behind you
Once every few miles on a busy road
questions.explain: Use your mirrors frequently so that you always know what's behind and to each side of you. Use them in good time before you signal or change direction or speed.

questions.q: Which of these is an exception to the ban on using a hand-held phone while driving?
options: Answering an urgent call from work
Checking a map in slow-moving traffic
Texting while stopped at traffic lights
Calling 999 when it's unsafe to stop
questions.explain: You MUST NOT use a hand-held phone while driving, even when stationary in traffic. There's an exception to call 999 or 112 in a genuine emergency when it's unsafe or impractical to stop.

questions.q: Your passenger starts a heated argument with you while you're driving. What should you do?
options: Argue back so it's settled quickly
Turn to face them while you talk
Drive faster to end the journey
Avoid arguing so you can concentrate
questions.explain: Safe driving needs concentration. Avoid distractions such as arguing with your passengers or other road users, loud music, eating and drinking, or trying to read maps.

questions.q: The police stop you because you didn't have a full view of the road ahead or proper control of your car. How many penalty points could you get?
questions.explain: You can get 3 penalty points if you don't have a full view of the road and traffic ahead or proper control of the vehicle. The police can stop you if they think you're not in control because you're distracted.

questions.q: The Highway Code describes a 'hierarchy of road users'. Who has the greatest responsibility to reduce the danger they pose to others?
options: Those who are most at risk in a collision
Those driving vehicles that can cause most harm
Those who have held a licence the longest
Those who are travelling at the lowest speed
questions.explain: Those in charge of vehicles that can cause the greatest harm in a collision bear the greatest responsibility to take care and reduce the danger they pose to others. This applies most strongly to drivers of large vehicles, vans, cars and motorcycles.

questions.q: Under the hierarchy of road users, which of these is true about pedestrians?
options: They no longer need to look before crossing
They have priority everywhere on the road
They still need to behave responsibly
They can ignore signals at crossings
questions.explain: The hierarchy doesn't remove the need for everyone to behave responsibly. All road users, including pedestrians, cyclists and horse riders, should have regard for their own and other road users' safety.

questions.q: There's a line of parked cars on your side of the road. An oncoming car is approaching and there isn't room for you both to pass. What should you do?
options: Pull out, as you're already moving
Flash your headlights and carry on
Sound your horn and drive through
Give way to the oncoming car
questions.explain: Give way to oncoming vehicles before passing parked vehicles or other obstructions on your side of the road.

questions.q: You've just passed your driving test. What's one benefit of taking further training such as Pass Plus?
options: It removes any penalty points you have
It lets you drive on motorways sooner
It means the new driver rules don't apply
It could lower your insurance costs
questions.explain: Further training such as Pass Plus could save you money on your insurance, as well as helping you reduce your risk of being involved in a collision.

questions.q: You're visiting a friend outside London and the only space is partly on the pavement. No signs allow pavement parking. Why shouldn't you park there?
options: It could damage your tyres on the kerb
It's only allowed for delivery vans
It can block wheelchairs and prams
It blocks the view of speed cameras
questions.explain: You shouldn't park partially or wholly on the pavement unless signs permit it. It can obstruct and seriously inconvenience pedestrians, people in wheelchairs or with visual impairments, and people with prams or pushchairs.

questions.q: Why does the Highway Code say that driving at an unsafe speed is so dangerous?
options: It's only a risk when you're over the limit
It only matters in bad weather or at night
Collisions become more likely and worse
It mainly increases your fuel costs
questions.explain: Unsafe speed increases the chances of causing a collision, or of being unable to avoid one, as well as its severity. The speed limit is the absolute maximum, not a target.

questions.q: You're waiting to turn right into a side road. A group of cyclists is riding towards you, going straight ahead. What should you do?
options: Wait for a safe gap in the cyclists
Turn between the riders in the group
Flash your headlights to make them stop
Turn quickly before they reach you
questions.explain: Don't cut across cyclists going ahead when you're turning into or out of a junction. Stop and wait for a safe gap in the flow of cyclists if necessary.

questions.q: The driver ahead keeps slowing down and seems unsure where they're going. How should you react?
options: Sound your horn to get them to hurry up
Drive close behind to encourage them on
Be patient – they may not know the area
Overtake them as soon as you possibly can
questions.explain: Try to be understanding if other road users cause problems – they may be inexperienced or not know the area well. Be patient; anyone can make a mistake.

questions.q: A car pulls out of a side road into your path, forcing you to brake. What should you do?
options: Drive close behind to show your anger
Slow down and hold back to let it get clear
Flash your headlights and sound your horn
Overtake it, then brake hard in front
questions.explain: Slow down and hold back if a road user pulls out into your path at a junction. Allow them to get clear, and don't over-react by driving too close behind to intimidate them.

questions.q: Another driver's behaviour has made you very angry and you're struggling to concentrate. What should you do?
options: Follow them to tell them what they did
Drive faster to get away from them
Sound your horn until they pull over
Pull over and calm down before going on
questions.explain: Don't allow yourself to become agitated or involved if someone is behaving badly on the road – this only makes things worse. Pull over, calm down and continue your journey when you feel relaxed.

questions.q: Your passenger has finished a can of drink during the journey. What should happen to the empty can?
options: Keep it until it can be put in a bin
Throw it out onto the grass verge
Throw it out when no one is behind
Throw it out while stopped in traffic
questions.explain: You MUST NOT throw anything out of a vehicle, such as food packaging, cans or paper. It can endanger other road users, particularly motorcyclists and cyclists.

questions.q: A driver is following very close behind the car in front to pressure it into going faster. How does the Highway Code describe this?
options: Acceptable in slow-moving traffic
Allowed if the car ahead is too slow
Dangerous and intimidating
Safe if your car has anti-lock brakes
questions.explain: Tailgating is where the gap to the vehicle in front is too small for you to stop safely if it suddenly brakes. It's dangerous, intimidating and can cause collisions. Don't assume ABS will stop you in a shorter distance.

questions.q: You want to check that you're keeping at least a two-second gap behind the vehicle in front. How can you measure it?
options: Count the car lengths between you
Check your speedometer reading
Watch the other car's brake lights
Use a fixed point, such as a road sign
questions.explain: Allow at least a two-second gap between you and the vehicle in front on high-speed roads. Use a fixed point, such as a sign, to help you measure it.

questions.q: You're about to overtake, but doing so would force an oncoming driver to slow down. What should you do?
options: Overtake, as they'll have time to brake
Flash your headlights and then overtake
Overtake quickly with your hazards on
Stay behind and don't overtake
questions.explain: Don't overtake where you might come into conflict with other road users; for example, when you would force another road user to swerve or slow down.

questions.q: You're keeping a safe gap behind the car in front when another driver overtakes you and pulls into that gap. What should you do?
options: Drop back to restore a safe gap
Close up so no one else can cut in
Flash your headlights at the driver
Sound your horn to show annoyance
questions.explain: If someone overtakes and pulls into the gap in front of you, drop back to maintain a two-second gap.

questions.q: You're driving in fog and the vehicle behind is following far too closely. What should you do?
options: Brake sharply to warn the driver
Speed up to get away from it
Keep going and don't speed up
Switch on your hazard warning lights
questions.explain: In fog, don't accelerate to get away from a vehicle that's too close behind you. Keep a safe distance from the vehicle in front and check your mirrors before you slow down.

questions.q: A driver behind you is trying to overtake. What should you do?
options: Speed up to make it harder for them
Keep a steady course and speed
Move out towards the centre line
Brake hard to let them past quickly
questions.explain: If a driver is trying to overtake you, keep a steady course and speed, slowing down if necessary to let them pass. Never obstruct them – speeding up or driving unpredictably is dangerous.

questions.q: You've recently passed your test. At traffic lights, the driver alongside you revs their engine as if they want to race. What should you do?
options: Pull away quickly to beat them
Rev your engine back at them
Race them to the next set of lights
Ignore them and drive normally
questions.explain: Never show off or try to compete with other drivers, particularly if they're driving badly. Don't let yourself become involved.

questions.q: You're driving along a busy road. When should you flash your headlights at other road users?
options: Only to let them know you're there
To tell them it's safe for them to go
To show them you're annoyed
To thank them for letting you in
questions.explain: Only flash your headlights to let other road users know you're there. Don't flash them to give any other message or to intimidate others.

questions.q: You're waiting to pull out of a side road. A driver on the main road flashes their headlights at you. What should you do?
options: Pull out at once, as they're letting you go
Flash back to accept, then pull out
Use your own judgement before going
Wave to thank them, then pull out
questions.explain: Never assume that flashing headlights is a signal inviting you to go. Use your own judgement and proceed carefully – the driver may only be letting you know they're there.

questions.q: You're driving through a town at midnight. When may you use your horn?
options: To let a friend know that you've arrived
Only if another road user poses a danger
Whenever you're about to overtake someone
To tell off a driver who's parked badly
questions.explain: You MUST NOT use your horn when driving in a built-up area between 11.30 pm and 7.00 am, except when another road user poses a danger.

questions.q: You're waiting in a stationary queue. The driver in front hasn't noticed that the traffic ahead has moved off. What does the Highway Code say about using your horn?
options: Use it to tell them the traffic has moved
Use it, as long as it's before 11.30 pm
Use it, as long as it's only a short beep
Don't use it while you're stationary
questions.explain: You MUST NOT use your horn while stationary on the road, except when another road user poses a danger. Only use it while moving, to warn others of your presence, and never aggressively.

questions.q: A car with flashing green lights is coming up behind you. What should you do?
options: Treat it as an emergency vehicle
Ignore it, as only blue lights matter
Speed up to stay ahead of it
Stop at once, wherever you are
questions.explain: Look and listen for emergency vehicles, including doctors, using flashing blue, red or green lights. Consider the vehicle's route and take appropriate action to let it pass.

questions.q: An ambulance with flashing blue lights is coming up behind you on a country road. Where should you avoid stopping to let it pass?
options: On a straight, wide stretch of road
Where there's room at the side of the road
Just before a bend or the brow of a hill
Where its driver can see you clearly
questions.explain: If necessary, pull to the side of the road and stop to let an emergency vehicle pass, but try to avoid stopping before the brow of a hill, a bend or a narrow section of road.

questions.q: You're waiting at a red traffic light when a fire engine with flashing blue lights comes up behind you. What should you do?
options: Drive through the red light to make room
Stay calm and don't break any traffic rules
Mount the pavement to let it through
Pull forward into the junction to clear a path
questions.explain: When an emergency vehicle approaches, don't panic. Take appropriate action to let it pass while complying with all traffic signs, and avoid mounting the kerb or endangering others.

questions.q: You're approaching a horse rider on a narrow road. The rider signals to you to slow down. What should you do?
options: Sound your horn so the horse hears you
Slow down, as they've asked
Pass quickly to get it over with
Flash your headlights to say thanks
questions.explain: Look out for horse riders' and horse drivers' signals and heed a request to slow down or stop. Treat all horses as a potential hazard, as they can be unpredictable.

questions.q: You've stopped at a zebra crossing and a pedestrian is waiting on the kerb. Why shouldn't you wave them across?
options: Another vehicle may be approaching
It's an offence to signal to pedestrians
They must wait for the road to clear
You'd lose your priority at the crossing
questions.explain: Don't wave, flash your lights or use your horn to invite pedestrians across. This could be dangerous if another vehicle is approaching.

questions.q: You've stopped at a pelican crossing that goes straight across the road with a central island. The amber light is flashing and a pedestrian is crossing from the far side of the island. What must you do?
options: Go, as they're on the other half
Go, as the island splits it in two
Wait, as it's all one crossing
Sound your horn, then move off
questions.explain: Pelican crossings that go straight across the road are one crossing, even when there's a central island. You MUST wait for pedestrians who are crossing from the other side of the island.

questions.q: The vehicle in front of you has stopped at a zebra crossing to let pedestrians cross. What does the law say?
options: You may overtake if the crossing looks clear
You must not overtake it
You may pass if you sound your horn
You may overtake it on the left only
questions.explain: You MUST NOT overtake the moving vehicle nearest the crossing, or the vehicle nearest the crossing that has stopped to give way to pedestrians.

questions.q: You're in a slow-moving queue approaching a pelican crossing. The traffic ahead stops and you wouldn't be able to clear the crossing. What should you do?
options: Stop on the crossing until the queue moves
Edge onto the crossing to keep your place
Drive over and stop on the far zig-zags
Stop before the crossing and keep it clear
questions.explain: In queuing traffic, keep crossings completely clear – blocking them makes it difficult and dangerous for pedestrians to cross. Don't enter a crossing if you can't clear it completely.

questions.q: You're waiting at red traffic lights behind an advanced stop line. Cyclists are waiting in the area ahead of you. What should you do when the lights turn green?
options: Move off quickly to pass them first
Sound your horn so they move aside
Give them time and space to move off
Edge forward into the cyclists' area
questions.explain: At advanced stop lines, allow cyclists, including any moving or waiting alongside you, enough time and space to move off when the green signal shows.

questions.q: A learner driver in front of you stalls as the traffic lights turn green. What should you do?
options: Sound your horn to hurry them
Drive round them through the junction
Be patient and wait for them
Flash your headlights at them
questions.explain: Learners and inexperienced drivers may not be so skilful at anticipating and responding to events. Be particularly patient with learner drivers.

questions.q: You passed your test last month in a small hatchback. A friend offers to lend you their high-powered sports car. What does the Highway Code advise?
options: Drive it on a motorway to get used to it
Drive it only with your friend beside you
Get plenty of experience driving alone first
Take it out late at night when it's quiet
questions.explain: Most new drivers have no experience of driving high-powered or sporty cars. Unless you learnt to drive in one, you need to get plenty of experience driving on your own before driving a more powerful car.

questions.q: You're behind a car displaying a 'new driver' plate. What should you bear in mind?
options: They're likely to drive faster than others
They'll always give way to you at junctions
They're not allowed on dual carriageways
They may not be skilled at anticipating events
questions.explain: Drivers who have recently passed their test may display a 'new driver' plate. Like learners, they may not be so skilful at anticipating and responding to events, so be patient.

questions.q: You're in a slow-moving queue and are about to stop across the end of a side road. What should you do?
options: Sound your horn to warn drivers in it
Stop across it, as you're in a queue
Switch on your hazard warning lights
Leave the side road clear
questions.explain: In slow-moving traffic, allow access into and from side roads, as blocking these will add to congestion.

questions.q: Which of these is true about driving without reasonable consideration for other road users?
options: It's advice only, not an offence
It's allowed if you're running late
It's an offence with penalty points
It's only an offence on motorways
questions.explain: You MUST NOT drive dangerously, without due care and attention, or without reasonable consideration for other road users. Driving without reasonable consideration can bring 3 to 9 penalty points.

questions.q: You're driving past people walking and cycling on a narrow road. Even below the speed limit, why could driving too fast here be a problem?
options: It's always illegal near cyclists
It can be intimidating for them
It wears out your tyres too quickly
It's only a problem after dark
questions.explain: The speed limit is a maximum, not a target. Inappropriate speeds are intimidating and deter people from walking, cycling or riding horses, so reduce your speed when sharing the road with them.

questions.q: You're towing a caravan on a winding road and a long queue of traffic has built up behind you. What should you do?
options: Speed up so you're not holding them up
Wave the drivers past on the bends
Keep going, as they'll pass when they can
Pull in when it's safe and let them pass
questions.explain: Don't hold up a long queue of traffic, especially if you're driving a large or slow-moving vehicle. Check your mirrors frequently and, if necessary, pull in where it's safe and let traffic pass.

questions.q: You're on a single-track road with passing places. The driver behind wants to overtake. What should you do?
options: Pull into a passing place on your left
Speed up to find a wider stretch of road
Stop where you are so they can squeeze by
Wave them past using the grass verge
questions.explain: On single-track roads, if the driver behind wants to overtake, pull into a passing place on your left, or wait opposite a passing place on your right.

questions.q: You're in a queue of slow-moving traffic. What does the Highway Code advise about the gap between you and the vehicle ahead?
options: Close right up so no one can cut in
Keep at least a four-second gap
Reduce it to help keep traffic flowing
Keep the gap you'd leave at 70 mph
questions.explain: In slow-moving traffic, you should reduce the distance between you and the vehicle ahead to maintain traffic flow. But never get so close to the vehicle in front that you can't stop safely.

questions.q: You're approaching road works and the traffic in your lane is queuing. The next lane is moving a little faster. What should you do?
options: Switch lanes to get past the queue
Stay in your lane and wait
Use the hard shoulder to pass the queue
Move over, then cut back in later
questions.explain: At road works, get into the correct lane in good time and as signs direct. Do not switch lanes to overtake queuing traffic.

questions.q: You've just overtaken a slower vehicle on a two-lane dual carriageway. What should you do next?
options: Stay in the right-hand lane until your exit
Slow down while you're in the right-hand lane
Stay right so others can't pass you
Move back to the left lane when it's safe
questions.explain: On a two-lane dual carriageway, stay in the left-hand lane and use the right-hand lane for overtaking or turning right. After overtaking, move back to the left-hand lane when it's safe.

questions.q: You're in slow-moving traffic approaching road works where two lanes become one. What's recommended?
options: Merge in turn, if it's safe
Speed up to the front of the queue
Refuse to let anyone in front
Change lanes as often as you can
questions.explain: Where lanes are restricted at road works, merge in turn. This is recommended when it's safe and traffic is moving at a very low speed. Don't change lanes unnecessarily in congested conditions.

questions.q: Drivers are joining a single lane from two. When is merging in turn NOT recommended?
options: When approaching road works
When traffic is moving very slowly
When traffic is moving at high speed
When approaching a traffic incident
questions.explain: Merging in turn is recommended only when it's safe and vehicles are travelling at a very low speed, such as when approaching road works or an incident. It isn't recommended at high speed.

questions.q: Some Highway Code rules use advisory wording such as 'should' or 'do not'. What could happen if you ignore them?
options: Nothing, as they're only suggestions
You'll automatically get penalty points
They could be used in court to show liability
Your licence will be revoked straight away
questions.explain: Failing to follow advisory rules won't in itself cause you to be prosecuted, but The Highway Code may be used in evidence in court proceedings to establish liability.

questions.q: You're parking on the road behind a car that's displaying a Blue Badge. Why shouldn't you park too close to it?
options: It may need to reverse out in a hurry
Its driver could get a parking fine
It's illegal to park within 10 metres of it
Its occupant may need more room to get out
questions.explain: Don't stop too close to a vehicle displaying a Blue Badge: remember, the occupant may need more room to get in or out.

questions.q: You've just passed a horse and rider on a country road. What should you NOT do?
options: Accelerate rapidly away
Check your mirrors
Keep your speed down
Move gently back to the left
questions.explain: Don't scare animals by sounding your horn, revving your engine or accelerating rapidly once you've passed them. Horses are flight animals and can move very quickly if startled.

questions.q: You're in a queue of slow-moving traffic. A pedestrian is waiting to cross the road between your car and the one in front. What should you do?
options: Let them cross in front of you
Close the gap so they use a crossing
Sound your horn to warn them off
Edge forward so they cross behind you
questions.explain: In slow-moving traffic, you should allow pedestrians and cyclists to cross in front of you.

questions.q: You park your electric car at a roadside charge point. What should you do with the charging cable?
options: Run it across the pavement at full length
Make sure it doesn't create a trip hazard
Leave it on the ground when you've finished
Hang it over a nearby fence or railing
questions.explain: When using an electric vehicle charge point, park close to it and avoid creating a trip hazard for pedestrians from trailing cables. Display a warning sign if you can, and put cables away neatly afterwards.

questions.q: Two cyclists are riding side by side on a narrow road ahead of you. What should you do?
options: Sound your horn so they ride in single file
Drive close behind so they move over
Flash your headlights to get them to move
Wait behind until it's safe to pass
questions.explain: On narrow roads it can be safer for cyclists to ride two abreast or in the centre of the lane, so allow them to do so. Wait behind if you can't overtake safely with enough room.

questions.q: You want to start learning to drive a car. What's the youngest age at which you can apply for a provisional driving licence?
options: 16 years
15 years and 9 months
17 years
16 years and 9 months
questions.explain: You can apply for a provisional driving licence when you're 15 years and 9 months old. You can usually start driving a car when you're 17.

questions.q: A friend has offered to supervise you while you practise driving. What are the minimum requirements they must meet?
options: Aged 18 or over, and held a full licence for 1 year
Aged 21 or over, and held a full licence for 1 year
Aged 21 or over, and held a full licence for 3 years
Aged 18 or over, and held a full licence for 3 years
questions.explain: Learners MUST be supervised by someone at least 21 years old who holds a full licence for that type of car (automatic or manual) and has held one for at least 3 years.

questions.q: Your mother has held a full licence for automatic cars only for 10 years. Can she supervise you while you learn in a manual car?
options: No, she needs a manual car licence
Yes, as long as she's over 21
Yes, as she's held her licence for over 3 years
Yes, if the car has dual controls
questions.explain: Anyone supervising you must be qualified to drive the type of vehicle you're learning in. For example, they must have a manual car licence if they're supervising you in a manual car.

questions.q: You're supervising a learner driver. Which of these would be illegal for you to do?
options: Give the learner directions
Sit in the front passenger seat
Point out hazards ahead
Use a hand-held mobile phone
questions.explain: You MUST NOT use a hand-held mobile phone or similar device when driving or when supervising a learner driver.

questions.q: Your family car has L plates on it for your son, who is learning. You're driving it on your own. What should you do with the plates?
options: Leave them on for safety
Move them to the back only
Remove or cover them
Swap them for P plates
questions.explain: L plates should be removed or covered when the vehicle isn't being driven by a learner (except on driving school vehicles).

questions.q: You're learning to drive in your family's car. Where must the L plates be displayed?
options: On the back only
On the front only
On the front and back
In the rear side windows
questions.explain: You must put an L plate on the front and back of your vehicle so they can be seen easily. L plates must have a red L on a white background and be the right size. In Wales, you can use a D plate instead.

questions.q: A learner driver is caught driving without the right supervision. What's the maximum number of penalty points they could get on their provisional licence?
options: Up to 3
Up to 8
Up to 11
Up to 6
questions.explain: You can be fined up to £1,000 and get up to 6 penalty points on your provisional licence if you drive without the right supervision.

questions.q: What must you have before you can book your car theory test?
options: A provisional driving licence
A minimum of 10 driving lessons
A certificate from your instructor
Your own insured car
questions.explain: You must have a provisional driving licence to book your theory test. There's no minimum number of lessons you must have.

questions.q: You've just passed your theory test. How long is your pass certificate number valid for?
options: 6 months
1 year
2 years
3 years
questions.explain: Your theory test pass certificate number lasts for 2 years. You must pass your driving test in that time, otherwise you'll have to pass the theory test again.

questions.q: What's the minimum type of motor insurance you must have by law?
options: Comprehensive
Third party
Third party, fire and theft
Personal accident cover
questions.explain: Third-party insurance is the minimum cover required by law. It covers anyone you might injure or whose property you might damage.

questions.q: Your car is insured for third party only. You lose control and hit a neighbour's garden wall, damaging both the wall and your car. What will your insurance cover?
options: Damage to your own car only
Damage to both the wall and your car
Nothing, as no other vehicle was involved
Damage to the wall only
questions.explain: Third-party insurance covers anyone you might injure or whose property you might damage. It doesn't cover damage to your own vehicle or injury to yourself.

questions.q: Which type of insurance would cover damage to your own car, up to its market value, after a collision that was your fault?
options: Comprehensive
Third party only
Third party, fire and theft
Breakdown cover
questions.explain: Comprehensive insurance is the most expensive but the best cover. As well as covering other people and property, it covers damage to your own vehicle, up to its market value, and personal injury to yourself.

questions.q: The police catch you driving a car that you're not insured to drive. What fixed penalty could they give you?
options: £100 and 3 penalty points
£200 and 4 penalty points
£300 and 6 penalty points
£1,000 and 11 penalty points
questions.explain: The police could give you a fixed penalty of £300 and 6 penalty points for driving a vehicle you're not insured to drive. If the case goes to court you could get an unlimited fine and be disqualified, and the police can seize the vehicle.

questions.q: A police officer asks to see your driving documents, but you don't have them with you. Within how many days may you be asked to take them to a police station?
options: 3 days
7 days
14 days
28 days
questions.explain: You MUST be able to produce your driving licence, a valid insurance certificate and (if appropriate) a valid MOT certificate when asked by a police officer. If you can't, you may be asked to take them to a police station within 7 days.

questions.q: A police officer stops you and asks to see your documents. Which of these could they ask you to produce?
options: Your vehicle's service history
Your theory test pass certificate
Your vehicle tax reminder letter
Your driving licence
questions.explain: If a police officer asks, you must be able to show your driving licence, a valid insurance certificate and a valid MOT certificate (if your vehicle needs one).

questions.q: You've bought a brand-new car for private use. By when must it have its first MOT?
options: The first anniversary of its registration
The second anniversary of its registration
The third anniversary of its registration
The fifth anniversary of its registration
questions.explain: You must get an MOT for your car by the third anniversary of its registration, and then by the anniversary of its last MOT.

questions.q: Your car is 5 years old. How often must it have an MOT?
options: Every year
Every 2 years
Every 3 years
Every 6 months
questions.explain: Cars must normally pass an MOT test 3 years from the date of first registration and every year after that. An MOT lasts for a year.

questions.q: Your car's MOT certificate has run out. When may you drive it on the road?
options: At any time, as long as it's taxed
To a pre-arranged MOT test appointment
For up to 7 days after it runs out
To work, if you've booked a test
questions.explain: You can't drive your vehicle on the road if the MOT has run out. The only exceptions are driving it to or from somewhere to be repaired, or to a pre-arranged MOT test. You can be fined up to £1,000 for driving without a valid MOT.

questions.q: Your car's MOT has expired and its vehicle tax is due to run out. What does this mean?
options: You can tax it now and book an MOT later
Your tax will be extended automatically
You'll get a 14-day grace period for both
You can't renew the tax until it has a valid MOT
questions.explain: You can't renew your vehicle tax if your MOT has expired. If your tax is due to run out, register the vehicle as off the road (SORN), book an MOT and tax the vehicle once it has passed.

questions.q: Your car is exempt from vehicle tax, so there's nothing to pay. What must you still do?
options: Declare it off the road
Nothing at all
Tax it as normal
Tell your insurer it's exempt
questions.explain: You must tax your vehicle even if you don't have to pay anything because it's exempt from vehicle tax.

questions.q: You're keeping a car in your garage and won't be taxing or insuring it. What must you do?
options: Make a SORN with DVLA
Send the log book back to DVLA
Remove its number plates
Tell your local council
questions.explain: If you're the keeper and want to keep a vehicle untaxed and off the public road, you MUST make a Statutory Off Road Notification (SORN). It's an offence not to, and the vehicle stays SORN until you tax, sell or scrap it.

questions.q: You've made a SORN for your car. When may you drive it on a public road?
options: For short journeys of under 5 miles
Whenever it's insured
At weekends only
To a pre-booked MOT test
questions.explain: You can only drive a vehicle with a SORN on a public road to go to or from a pre-booked MOT or other testing appointment. Using it for any other reason could lead to prosecution and a fine of up to £2,500.

questions.q: You made a SORN for your car last year. You now want to start using it on the road again. What must you do?
options: Renew the SORN
Tax and insure it
Send the V5C to DVLA
Wait for the SORN to expire
questions.explain: A SORN is cancelled automatically when you tax your vehicle again, and you don't need to renew it. You must insure and tax a vehicle that doesn't have a SORN, and it must have a current MOT if it needs one.

questions.q: You've sold your car privately. Who is responsible for sending the completed registration certificate (V5C) to DVLA?
options: The buyer
The buyer's insurer
The seller
The police
questions.explain: You MUST tell DVLA as soon as possible when you buy or sell a vehicle. The buyer and seller complete the registration certificate, and the seller is responsible for sending it to DVLA.

questions.q: What information does a vehicle registration certificate (V5C) give?
options: The registered keeper's details
Proof that the car is roadworthy
Proof that the car is insured
The car's full service history
questions.explain: Registration certificates are issued for all motor vehicles used on the road. They describe the vehicle (make, model, etc) and give details of the registered keeper.

questions.q: You've just moved house. What must you do about your driving licence?
options: Nothing until your licence needs renewing
Tell your local police station
Apply for a new provisional licence
Tell DVLA your new address
questions.explain: You MUST tell DVLA if you change your address. It doesn't cost anything, and you can be fined up to £1,000 if you don't. You must also change the address on your vehicle log book (V5C).

questions.q: You passed your driving test 18 months ago. How many penalty points would lead to your licence being revoked?
options: 3 or more
6 or more
9 or more
12 or more
questions.explain: Under the New Drivers Act, your licence will be revoked if you get 6 or more penalty points within 2 years of passing your first driving test. This applies even if you pay for offences by fixed penalty.

questions.q: A new driver's licence has been revoked under the New Drivers Act. What must they do to get a full licence again?
options: Pass both the theory and practical tests again
Retake only the practical driving test
Wait 12 months and then reapply
Complete a Pass Plus course
questions.explain: If your licence is revoked within 2 years of passing, you'll have to apply and pay for a new provisional licence and pass both the theory and practical tests again to get a full licence.

questions.q: You got 3 penalty points while you were a learner driver. You've now passed your test. What happens to those points?
options: They're wiped when you pass your test
They're doubled on your full licence
They're carried over to your full licence
They only count if you fail a test
questions.explain: Any penalty points on your provisional licence that haven't expired are carried over to your full licence. If further points take you to a total of 6 or more within 2 years of passing, your licence will be revoked.

questions.q: A driver who passed their test many years ago keeps getting penalty points. Under the 'totting-up' rules, how many points within 3 years mean they MUST be disqualified?
options: 6 or more
9 or more
15 or more
12 or more
questions.explain: A driver who builds up 12 or more penalty points within 3 years MUST be disqualified. This will be for a minimum of 6 months, or longer if they've been disqualified before.

questions.q: A driver is convicted of driving with alcohol above the legal limit (code DR10). How long must the endorsement stay on their driving record?
options: 4 years from the date of the offence
11 years from the date of conviction
3 years from the date of conviction
5 years from the date of the offence
questions.explain: Endorsements stay on your driving record for 4 or 11 years, depending on the offence. Drink-driving endorsements (codes DR10 to DR61) must stay on your record for 11 years from the date of conviction.

questions.q: You get penalty points for exceeding the speed limit on a public road (code SP30). How long must the endorsement stay on your driving record?
options: 4 years from the date of the offence
11 years from the date of conviction
2 years from the date of the offence
5 years from the date of conviction
questions.explain: Speed limit endorsements (SP10 to SP50) must stay on your driving record for 4 years from the date of the offence.

questions.q: You've developed a health condition that's likely to affect your driving. What MUST you do?
options: Tell your insurer only
Display a medical notice in your car
Tell DVLA
Only drive during daylight
questions.explain: You MUST report to DVLA any health condition likely to affect your driving.

questions.q: Which of these eyesight problems must you tell DVLA about?
options: Being short-sighted and wearing glasses
Being colour blind
Being long-sighted
A condition affecting both eyes
questions.explain: You must tell DVLA if you've got any problem with your eyesight that affects both of your eyes, or the remaining eye if you only have one eye. This doesn't include being short-sighted, long-sighted or colour blind.

questions.q: You need to wear glasses to read a number plate from 20 metres away. When MUST you wear them?
options: Only when driving at night
Every time you drive
Only on motorways
Only in poor weather
questions.explain: You MUST be able to read a vehicle number plate, in good daylight, from 20 metres. If you need glasses or contact lenses to do this, you MUST wear them every time you drive.

questions.q: You're driving slowly along a residential street. An ice-cream van is parked on the left ahead. What's the main hazard you should be ready for?
options: Children running out into the road
The van sounding its chimes
Traffic lights hidden behind it
The van switching its lights on
questions.explain: Drive carefully and slowly when passing parked vehicles, especially ice-cream vans. Children are more interested in ice cream than traffic and may run into the road unexpectedly.

questions.q: You're driving along a narrow street lined with parked cars. You notice someone sitting in the driver's seat of one of them. What should you be prepared for?
options: Its alarm going off
Its horn being sounded at you
A door opening into your path
Its hazard lights coming on
questions.explain: On streets with parked cars you should drive slowly and carefully. Look out for car doors opening, vehicles moving off and children running out from between parked cars.

questions.q: You're driving through a town and see this sign. What does it warn you of?
options: No cycling allowed ahead
A cycle route ahead
A cycle-only lane ahead
A cycle parking area ahead
questions.explain: This triangular warning sign shows a cycle route ahead. Look out for cyclists, who can be difficult to see, especially at junctions.

questions.q: You're approaching a bus that has stopped at a bus stop on your side of the road. What should you look out for in particular?
options: The bus switching on its hazard lights
Its exhaust fumes blocking your view
The bus driver waving you past
People stepping out in front of it
questions.explain: Drive carefully and slowly past bus stops, as pedestrians may emerge suddenly into the road. Look out for people getting off a bus and crossing the road.

questions.q: You're driving near a school. There's a flashing amber signal below the 'School' warning sign. What should you do?
options: Drive very slowly until you're clear of the area
Stop and wait until the signal stops flashing
Keep to the speed limit and cover your brake
Sound your horn to warn children you're there
questions.explain: A flashing amber signal below the 'School' warning sign tells you there may be children crossing the road ahead. Drive very slowly until you're clear of the area.

questions.q: You're approaching a school crossing patrol waiting at the kerb. A slow-moving van is in front of you. What should you do?
options: Overtake it before you reach the patrol
Stay behind it and don't overtake
Overtake if no children are in view
Sound your horn to warn the patrol
questions.explain: Don't overtake where you might come into conflict with other road users, such as when approaching a school crossing patrol. You MUST stop if the patrol shows a 'Stop for children' sign.

questions.q: You're driving along a street with a tramway. A tram is approaching a stop ahead. What should you look out for?
options: Cars racing the tram from the lights
The tram changing to a different lane
People running to catch the tram
Cyclists riding along the rails
questions.explain: Look out for pedestrians, especially children, running to catch a tram approaching a stop. Also look out for people getting off a tram and crossing the road.

questions.q: You're driving along a country road. Why should you slow down as you approach junctions and turnings?
options: They may be partially hidden
They always have a stop line
Traffic in them must give way to you
They're always on sharp bends
questions.explain: On country roads, reduce your speed at junctions and turnings, which may be partially hidden, and on the approach to bends, which can be sharper than they appear.

questions.q: You're following a powered mobility scooter on the road. Its user wants to turn right, but moving into the middle of the road would be dangerous. What might they do?
options: Stop in the middle of the road and wait
Signal left and then turn right
Speed up to get ahead of the traffic
Stop on the left and wait for a safe gap
questions.explain: If moving into the middle of the road is difficult or dangerous, a mobility scooter user may stop on the left-hand side of the road and wait for a safe gap, or make the turn as a pedestrian. Be patient and give them room.

questions.q: You're waiting to emerge from a side road. A car approaching from the right is signalling left, as if to turn into your road. What should you do?
options: Pull out, as the car is turning in
Wait until you're sure it's turning
Flash your headlights to let it in
Pull out quickly before it reaches you
questions.explain: When waiting at a junction, don't assume that a vehicle coming from the right and signalling left will actually turn. Wait and make sure, as its indicator may not have been cancelled.

questions.q: The car in front has been showing a right-turn signal for some distance but hasn't turned. You want to overtake it. What should you do?
options: Overtake it on the right quickly
Flash your headlights, then overtake
Stay behind until the signal is cancelled
Sound your horn as you overtake
questions.explain: Don't overtake when a road user is indicating right, even if you believe the signal should have been cancelled. Don't take a risk; wait for the signal to be cancelled.

questions.q: You're in slow-moving traffic approaching a pedestrian crossing. Queuing vehicles are blocking your view of the pavement on both sides. Why should you take extra care?
options: People may be crossing between the vehicles
The crossing may be closed to pedestrians
Drivers behind may sound their horns
The road surface may be slippery
questions.explain: Take extra care where the view of either side of a crossing is blocked by queuing traffic or incorrectly parked vehicles. Pedestrians may be crossing between stationary vehicles.

questions.q: You're following a large lorry on a single carriageway road. How can you improve your view of the road ahead?
options: Drop back to increase the gap
Move closer so you can see past it
Switch your headlights to main beam
Drive with your wheels on the centre line
questions.explain: Large vehicles can block your view. Your ability to see and to plan ahead will be improved if you pull back to increase your separation distance.

questions.q: You're following an articulated lorry along a busy road. Why should you keep well back?
options: So you can read its number plate
So you're clear of its exhaust fumes
So it can't reverse into you
So the driver can see you in the mirrors
questions.explain: If you're following a large vehicle, be aware that the driver may not be able to see you in the mirrors. Dropping back should allow the driver to see you, and it also improves your view ahead.

questions.q: You're driving through a hilly area and see this sign. What should you be prepared for?
options: Rocks on the road ahead
A steep drop at the roadside
Loose chippings from road works
Low-flying aircraft overhead
questions.explain: This sign warns of falling or fallen rocks. Be prepared for rocks on the road and drive at a speed that lets you stop well within the distance you can see to be clear.

questions.q: You're driving along a country road and see this sign. What does it warn you of?
options: Road humps
Uneven road
Hump bridge
Steep hill upwards
questions.explain: This sign warns of a hump bridge. You can't see far enough ahead as you approach a hump bridge to be sure it's safe, so don't overtake there.

questions.q: You're driving along a country road and see this sign. What does it warn you of?
options: A zebra crossing ahead
Pedestrians in the road ahead
A school entrance ahead
A footbridge over the road
questions.explain: This sign warns of pedestrians in the road ahead, for example where there's no pavement. Slow down, be prepared to stop and give them plenty of room as you pass.

questions.q: You've been driving in thick fog, which now seems to be clearing. What should you be aware of?
options: You can speed up to make up lost time
You may suddenly find yourself in thick fog
You can close up to the vehicle ahead
You can ignore any further 'Fog' signs
questions.explain: Even if fog seems to be clearing, you can suddenly find yourself in thick fog. Keep a safe distance and make sure you can pull up well within the distance you can see clearly.

questions.q: You're driving on a country road and see this sign. What should you do?
options: Keep to the right on the bend
Reduce your speed before the bend
Brake firmly while on the bend
Overtake before you reach the bend
questions.explain: This sign warns of a bend to the right. On country roads, reduce your speed on the approach to bends, which can be sharper than they appear. Keep well to the left on right-hand bends to improve your view.

questions.q: You see this sign. What should you do?
options: Keep your speed and brake hard if needed
Speed up to get through it quickly
Slow down and avoid harsh braking
Steer sharply round the slippery parts
questions.explain: This sign warns of a slippery road. Skidding is usually caused by braking, accelerating or steering too harshly, or by driving too fast for the road conditions.

questions.q: You're driving on a motorway and the vehicle in front switches on its hazard warning lights, as shown. What does this tell you?
options: The driver is about to change lanes
There's a hazard or obstruction ahead
The driver is leaving at the next exit
The vehicle is towing a trailer
questions.explain: On a motorway or unrestricted dual carriageway, drivers may briefly use hazard warning lights to warn drivers behind of a hazard or obstruction ahead. Be ready to slow down.
ref: HC Signals to other road users

questions.q: You're driving through road works. Part of the road has been marked off by traffic cones, but nobody seems to be working there. What should you do?
options: Drive through it to pass the queue
Use it if the lane beside it is busy
Drive through it slowly and carefully
Keep out of the coned-off area
questions.explain: Do not drive through an area marked off by traffic cones. Areas marked off by cones can contain significant hazards.

questions.q: Farm animals are often herded along the country roads where you live. What may the herders do to warn traffic, especially near a bend?
options: Send someone ahead along the road
Set up temporary traffic lights
Park a tractor across the road
Put warning triangles on the verge
questions.explain: People herding animals should, if possible, send another person along the road in front to warn other road users, especially at a bend or the brow of a hill. Look out for animals being driven on the road and be ready to stop.

questions.q: You're driving at night on a road with no pavement. Ahead, a red light is being carried by someone walking in the road on your side. What could it be?
options: The front of an organised group of walkers
The rear of an organised group of walkers
A person directing traffic at an incident
A broken-down car's hazard light
questions.explain: Organised walks on a road without a pavement should keep to the left. At night, the look-out in front should show a white light and the one at the back a red light. Slow down and give them plenty of room.

questions.q: You're driving across open moorland on an unfenced road and see this sign. What should you be prepared for?
options: Animals being herded along the road
A riding school entrance ahead
Wild animals on the road
A cattle grid across the road
questions.explain: This sign warns of wild animals. Watch out for animals on unfenced roads: drive slowly, give them plenty of room and be ready to stop.

questions.q: You see this sign. What does it warn you about?
options: Wild horses or ponies
A horse racing course ahead
A stables entrance ahead
Accompanied horses or ponies
questions.explain: This sign warns of accompanied horses or ponies on the road. When you see a horse, slow down and, when it's safe, pass wide and slowly.

questions.q: You're driving along a winding country lane. Which of these should you be prepared to find on the road?
options: Trams crossing the road
Vehicles using a hard shoulder
Zig-zag lines on the bends
Mud on the road surface
questions.explain: Take extra care on country roads. Be prepared for pedestrians, horse riders, cyclists, slow-moving farm vehicles or mud on the road surface, and make sure you can stop within the distance you can see to be clear.

questions.q: You're driving along a country lane with no pavement. Where are pedestrians advised to walk?
options: On the right, facing oncoming traffic
On the left, with their backs to traffic
In the middle of the lane
On whichever side has more room
questions.explain: If there's no pavement, pedestrians are advised to keep to the right-hand side of the road so they can see oncoming traffic. Expect walkers coming towards you on your side of the road.

questions.q: You're driving at night on an unlit road. Why should you drive more slowly than you would in daylight?
options: Speed limits are lower at night
Your brakes work less well in the dark
Other drivers must dip their headlights
It's harder to see other road users
questions.explain: You should reduce your speed when driving at night, as it's more difficult to see other road users. Drive at a speed that will allow you to stop well within the distance you can see to be clear.

questions.q: You're thinking about overtaking a slow-moving van at night. Why do you need to take extra care?
options: It's harder to judge speed and distance
Overtaking isn't allowed after dark
You must use main beam as you pass
The van driver can't see your lights
questions.explain: Take extra care when overtaking at night and in poor visibility, when it's harder to judge speed and distance. Keep your headlights dipped until you're level with the other vehicle.

questions.q: You're driving towards a low, bright sun and it's dazzling you. What should you do?
options: Slow down, and stop if necessary
Speed up to get out of the glare
Switch on your rear fog lights
Look at the kerb and keep going
questions.explain: If you're dazzled by bright sunlight, slow down and, if necessary, stop.

questions.q: It's been raining heavily. How will your stopping distance compare with the distance on a dry road?
options: It'll be about the same
It'll be up to half as much again
It'll be at least double
It'll be ten times greater
questions.explain: In wet weather, stopping distances will be at least double those required for stopping on dry roads, because your tyres have less grip on the road. They can be ten times greater on icy roads.

questions.q: You're driving along a town street. The pavement ahead is closed for street repairs. What should you be prepared for?
options: Traffic lights that aren't working
Pedestrians walking in the road
Cyclists riding on the closed pavement
Buses stopping in the middle of the road
questions.explain: Drive carefully and slowly when the pavement is closed due to street repairs, as pedestrians may be directed to use the road.

questions.q: You're driving on a cold winter's day. The roads have been gritted, but there are icy patches about. What should you be prepared for?
options: Normal grip, as the road has been treated
Shorter stopping distances than usual
Conditions changing over short distances
Ice only on the busiest stretches of road
questions.explain: In icy or snowy weather, drive with care even if the roads have been treated, and be prepared for the road conditions to change over relatively short distances.

questions.q: There's snow and ice on the roads and you want to check how much grip your tyres have. What should you do?
options: Accelerate hard on a straight stretch
Brake gently in a safe place
Steer sharply from side to side
Brake hard at a moderate speed
questions.explain: When there's snow or ice, check your grip on the road surface by choosing a safe place to brake gently. If the steering feels unresponsive, this may indicate ice and that your vehicle is losing its grip.

questions.q: A recovery vehicle is helping a broken-down car at the side of the road ahead. Why should you drive carefully and slowly as you pass?
options: Recovery vehicles always have priority
People may be working in or beside the road
The law sets a 10 mph limit when passing
You MUST stop until it has moved off
questions.explain: Drive carefully and slowly when passing roadside rescue and recovery vehicles or going through road works, as there may be people working in or at the side of the road.

questions.q: You're driving in thick fog, closely following the rear lights of the car in front. Why could this be dangerous?
options: They give a false sense of security
They'll stop you seeing road signs
They'll make the fog seem thicker
They mean you can't use your headlights
questions.explain: When driving in fog, keep a safe distance behind the vehicle in front, as rear lights can give a false sense of security. Make sure you can pull up well within the distance you can see clearly.

questions.q: You're driving through road works with a temporary 40 mph speed limit. The road looks clear and nobody seems to be working. What MUST you do?
options: Return to the road's normal speed limit
Keep to the temporary speed limit
Exceed it, as no workers are present
Treat the limit as advice only
questions.explain: At road works, take extra care and observe all signs; they're there for your safety and the safety of road workers. You MUST NOT exceed any temporary maximum speed limit.

questions.q: You're driving through road works and there's a lot of activity in the works area beside you. Where should your attention be?
options: On the machinery in the works area
On the road ahead
On your mirrors the whole time
On your satnav for a quicker route
questions.explain: At road works, concentrate on the road ahead, not the road works. Bear in mind the road ahead may be obstructed by the works or by slow-moving or stationary traffic.

questions.q: You're approaching road works on a dual carriageway and see this sign. What does it show?
options: The hard shoulder is closed for road works
One lane crossover at contraflow road works
Two lanes merge into one at road works
The end of the road works and restrictions
questions.explain: This sign shows a one-lane crossover at contraflow road works. In a contraflow you may be in a narrower lane than normal, with no permanent barrier between you and oncoming traffic.

questions.q: You're driving past road works. A works vehicle showing flashing amber lights is travelling in the road ahead of you. What should you do?
options: Overtake it as soon as you can
Follow it closely through the works
Flash your lights so it pulls in
Leave extra space behind it
questions.explain: Where vehicles are travelling in the road at road works and displaying amber warning lights, leave extra space and expect them to slow or turn into a works area.

questions.q: You're driving along a busy street and see this sign. What should you be ready to do?
options: Give way to traffic at a roundabout
Stop at a school crossing patrol
Stop for people at a zebra crossing
Give way to cyclists on a cycle route
questions.explain: This sign warns of a zebra crossing ahead. Look out for pedestrians waiting to cross and be ready to slow down or stop to let them cross.

questions.q: You see this sign on a country road. What does it tell you?
options: You're entering a one-way street
Overtaking is allowed ahead
There's a lay-by on the left
The road bends sharply ahead
questions.explain: Chevron signs like this show a sharp deviation of route. Reduce your speed on the approach, as bends can be sharper than they appear.

questions.q: You're waiting to turn at a junction and a horse rider is approaching. What should you be aware of?
options: They may take an unexpected line
They must keep close to the kerb
They'll always signal before turning
They have to give way to you
questions.explain: Take extra care at junctions. Watch out for horse riders, who may take a different line on the road from the one you'd expect.

questions.q: You're following a slow van and see this sign. Why shouldn't you overtake here?
options: There's a bend ahead
The road narrows ahead
There's a junction ahead
It's a one-way street
questions.explain: This sign warns that the road narrows on both sides. Don't overtake where you might come into conflict with other road users, such as where the road narrows.

questions.q: You're driving in England. What's the legal limit for alcohol in your breath?
options: 22 microgrammes per 100 ml of breath
35 microgrammes per 100 ml of breath
50 microgrammes per 100 ml of breath
80 microgrammes per 100 ml of breath
questions.explain: In England and Wales you MUST NOT drive with a breath alcohol level higher than 35 microgrammes per 100 millilitres of breath. The limit is lower in Scotland.

questions.q: You're driving in Scotland. What's the legal limit for alcohol in your breath?
options: 35 microgrammes per 100 ml of breath
50 microgrammes per 100 ml of breath
80 microgrammes per 100 ml of breath
22 microgrammes per 100 ml of breath
questions.explain: In Scotland the legal limits are lower than in the rest of the UK. You MUST NOT drive with a breath alcohol level higher than 22 microgrammes per 100 millilitres of breath.
