questions.q: In England and Wales, what's the legal limit for alcohol in your blood when driving?
options: 35 milligrammes per 100 ml of blood
50 milligrammes per 100 ml of blood
80 milligrammes per 100 ml of blood
107 milligrammes per 100 ml of blood
questions.explain: In England and Wales you MUST NOT drive with a blood alcohol level of more than 80 milligrammes per 100 millilitres of blood. In Scotland the blood limit is 50 milligrammes.

questions.q: You've had a couple of alcoholic drinks and feel fine. How could the alcohol affect your driving?
options: It'll speed up your reactions
It'll improve your judgement of distance
It won't affect you below the limit
It can give you false confidence
questions.explain: Alcohol gives a false sense of confidence, reduces co-ordination, slows down reactions and affects judgement of speed, distance and risk. It reduces your driving ability even if you're below the legal limit.

questions.q: You drank a lot of alcohol at a party last night. You need to drive to work early this morning. What should you bear in mind?
options: A cold shower will sober you up
You may still be unfit to drive
Strong coffee removes the alcohol
A night's sleep clears all the alcohol
questions.explain: Alcohol takes time to leave your body. You may be unfit to drive in the morning after drinking the previous evening, or in the evening after drinking at lunchtime.

questions.q: Which of these can make a difference to how alcohol affects you?
options: The size of your car's engine
How far you're planning to drive
Your stress levels at the time
Whether it's daytime or night-time
questions.explain: The way alcohol affects you depends on your weight, age, sex and metabolism, the type and amount of alcohol, what you've eaten recently and your stress levels at the time. It's impossible to say exactly how many drinks will take you over the limit.

questions.q: Your pharmacist tells you that a medicine you've been given may impair your driving. What should you do?
options: Don't drive while you're taking it
Drive only on quiet country roads
Drive, but take some extra breaks
Drive only during daylight hours
questions.explain: You MUST NOT drive under the influence of drugs or medicine. Check with your doctor or pharmacist, and don't drive if you're advised that you may be impaired.

questions.q: Why is it so dangerous to drive after taking illegal drugs?
options: They only affect your eyesight
They make you drive too slowly
They're only risky mixed with alcohol
Their effects are unpredictable
questions.explain: Never take illegal drugs if you intend to drive. The effects are unpredictable, but can be even more severe than alcohol and result in fatal or serious road crashes.

questions.q: A driver is convicted of driving with alcohol above the legal limit. What's the minimum period they MUST be disqualified for?
options: 6 months
3 months
12 months
2 years
questions.explain: For serious offences such as drink-driving, the court MUST order disqualification. The minimum period is 12 months, and it may be longer for repeat offenders or where the alcohol level is high.

questions.q: Why could even a small amount of an illegal drug put you over the legal limit for driving?
options: The limits are the same as for alcohol
Drug tests can't measure small amounts
The limits only apply to large doses
The limits are set at very low levels
questions.explain: You MUST NOT drive with illegal drugs in your blood above specified limits. These have been set at very low levels, so even small amounts of use could put you over the limit.

questions.q: You've bought some cold medicine from a shop without a prescription. How can you find out whether it may affect your driving?
options: Read the label
Assume it's safe as it wasn't prescribed
Take a dose and see how you feel
Check how much alcohol it contains
questions.explain: Even over-the-counter medicines can affect your ability to drive safely. Read the label to see if they may affect your driving, and check with your doctor or pharmacist if you're unsure.

questions.q: A police officer suspects that your eyesight may not meet the standard for driving. What can they do?
options: Let you drive on if you're wearing glasses
Require you to take an eyesight test
Only issue you with a warning letter
Ban you from driving on the spot
questions.explain: You MUST be able to read a vehicle number plate, in good daylight, from 20 metres. The police have the power to require a driver to undertake an eyesight test.

questions.q: You see this sign. What does it warn you of?
options: A ford across the road
A risk of flooding
A quayside or river bank
An opening bridge ahead
questions.explain: This warning sign shows that there's a quayside or river bank ahead.

questions.q: You're driving near an airfield and see this sign. What does it warn you of?
options: An airport car park ahead
The route to an airport
A helicopter landing pad
Low-flying aircraft
questions.explain: This warning sign means low-flying aircraft or sudden aircraft noise, which could startle you. On direction signs, an aircraft symbol shows the route to an airport.

questions.q: Which of these eyesight conditions do you NOT need to tell the DVLA about?
options: A problem affecting both eyes
A problem with your only working eye
Double vision in both eyes
Being short-sighted
questions.explain: You must tell DVLA about any eyesight problem that affects both eyes, or the remaining eye if you only have one. This doesn't include being short-sighted, long-sighted or colour blind.

questions.q: You're approaching road works on a busy road. What should you bear in mind about the road ahead?
options: It may be blocked by queuing traffic
It will be clear once you pass the sign
The speed limit no longer applies
Workers will always wave you through
questions.explain: At road works, take extra care and look for signs giving more instructions. Bear in mind that the road ahead may be obstructed by the works or by slow-moving or stationary traffic.

questions.q: You're driving along a one-way street and see this sign. What does it tell you?
options: The road ahead is closed to traffic
Two-way traffic straight ahead
You must turn left at the junction
Traffic merges from the left ahead
questions.explain: This sign warns of two-way traffic straight ahead. Be prepared for oncoming vehicles and keep to the left.

questions.q: You see this sign. What does it warn you of?
options: A hump bridge on a narrow road
A level crossing with barriers
An opening or swing bridge
A low bridge with little headroom
questions.explain: This sign warns of an opening or swing bridge ahead. Alternately flashing red lights at lifting bridges mean you MUST stop.

questions.q: You're about to overtake a cyclist who's riding past a row of parked cars. Why might they be further out from the cars than you'd expect?
options: Because they must ride in mid-lane
Because they want you to wait behind
To ride over the drain covers
To keep clear of doors being opened
questions.explain: Cyclists are advised to ride at least a door's width or 1 metre from parked cars for their own safety. Give them plenty of room when you overtake.

questions.q: You've stopped at red traffic lights in slow traffic. Why should you check your mirrors and blind spots before moving off when they change?
options: A motorcyclist may be waiting alongside you
The driver behind may want to overtake you
Your brake lights might not be working
The lights might be about to change back
questions.explain: It's often difficult to see motorcyclists and cyclists, especially when they're waiting alongside you, coming up from behind or filtering through traffic. Check your mirrors and blind spots carefully before moving off.

questions.q: Your car has broken down on a busy main road and you have a warning triangle. How far behind your car should you put it?
options: At least 25 metres
At least 45 metres
At least 15 metres
At least 100 metres
questions.explain: You should put a warning triangle on the road at least 45 metres (147 feet) behind your broken-down vehicle, on the same side of the road. Take great care when placing or retrieving it.

questions.q: You've broken down on the hard shoulder of a motorway. You have a warning triangle in your boot. What should you do with it?
options: Place it 45 metres behind your car
Place it 100 metres behind your car
Don't use it on the motorway
Place it on the roof of your car
questions.explain: You should never use a warning triangle on a motorway, and DO NOT place one on the carriageway. Instead, get well away from your vehicle and moving traffic and call for help.

questions.q: Your car has broken down on a narrow road and is partly blocking the carriageway. How should you warn other traffic?
options: Switch on your hazard warning lights
Leave your headlights on main beam
Sound your horn at approaching vehicles
Stand in the road and wave traffic past
questions.explain: If your broken-down vehicle is causing an obstruction, warn other traffic by using your hazard warning lights. Don't stand, or let anyone else stand, between your vehicle and oncoming traffic.

questions.q: You've broken down on a country road at night and need to get out of your car. What should you wear to help other road users see you?
options: Reflective clothing
Dark, warm clothing
Clothing the same colour as your car
Anything, if your hazard lights are on
questions.explain: Help other road users see you by wearing light-coloured or fluorescent clothing in daylight and reflective clothing at night or in poor visibility.

questions.q: Your car has broken down on a main road at night and you're waiting for help. Why shouldn't you stand at the back of your car?
options: You might stop other drivers seeing your lights
Your exhaust fumes could make you dizzy
Recovery drivers will find the car harder to spot
Your hazard lights could dazzle you
questions.explain: Don't stand, or let anybody else stand, between your vehicle and oncoming traffic. At night or in poor visibility, don't stand where you'll prevent other road users seeing your lights.

questions.q: You're driving on a motorway when a warning light comes on and you need to stop. Where is the safest place to stop?
options: On the hard shoulder
In an emergency area
At a service area
On the verge of a slip road
questions.explain: On motorways and other high-speed roads, the safest place to stop is a service area. Emergency areas and hard shoulders are places of relative safety, but hard shoulders give less protection because they're so close to high-speed traffic.

questions.q: You've stopped in a lay-by on a busy dual carriageway after a breakdown. Why should you and your passengers keep well away from your car and the moving traffic?
options: Your car could be hit and pushed into you
So recovery drivers can see the car clearly
So the engine can cool down more safely
So you don't breathe in exhaust fumes
questions.explain: You and your passengers should, where possible, keep well away from your vehicle and moving traffic. Otherwise moving traffic could collide with your vehicle, forcing it into you.

questions.q: You stop to help at the scene of a collision on a busy road. How should you warn other traffic?
options: Leave your headlights on main beam
Sound your horn repeatedly
Switch on your hazard warning lights
Park across the road to block it
questions.explain: If you're involved in a collision or stop to give assistance, use your hazard warning lights to warn other traffic, and put on high-visibility clothing if you have it.

questions.q: You arrive at a crash scene where several cars are damaged. Why should you ask the drivers to switch off their engines?
options: To save fuel while they wait
To reduce the risk of fire
To stop the batteries going flat
So the police can check the engines
questions.explain: Further collisions and fire are the main dangers following a crash. You should ask drivers to switch off their engines and ask everyone to stop smoking.

questions.q: You're at the scene of a collision where people are injured. You call the emergency services. What should you tell them?
options: Only the registration numbers of the vehicles
Only your own name and address
Which driver you think caused it
The location and details of any casualties
questions.explain: Contact the emergency services on 999 and provide full details of the incident location and any casualties. You can use an emergency telephone, a mobile phone, or your vehicle's SOS button if it has one.

questions.q: You're calling the emergency services from the scene of a crash on a dual carriageway. Which extra detail will help them reach it quickly?
options: The make and model of your car
The direction of traffic involved
The time you set off on your journey
The weather forecast for the area
questions.explain: The emergency services need the exact location of the incident, including the direction of traffic (for example, northbound), and the number of vehicles involved. Also tell them about the condition of any casualties.

questions.q: You arrive at a crash. A driver is still in their car and seems to be injured, but there's no threat of fire or further danger. What should you do?
options: Pull them out of the car straight away
Help them walk to the side of the road
Lay them down on the road surface
Leave them in the car unless in danger
questions.explain: DO NOT move injured people from their vehicles unless they're in immediate danger. Keep them warm and reassure them until the emergency services arrive.

questions.q: A motorcyclist has been injured in a collision and is lying in the road, still wearing their helmet. What should you do about the helmet?
options: Take it off to make them comfortable
Only remove it if it's essential
Take it off so you can check for injuries
Lift their head and loosen it
questions.explain: DO NOT remove a motorcyclist's helmet unless it's essential and you're trained to do so. Keep the casualty warm and reassure them while you wait for the emergency services.

questions.q: You've been involved in a collision on a busy road. Your passengers aren't hurt. What should you do with them?
options: Keep them in the car with seat belts on
Ask them to direct the traffic around you
Ask them to stand behind the car as a warning
Move them to a place of relative safety
questions.explain: You should move uninjured people away from the vehicles to a place of relative safety, where they're less likely to be at risk from moving traffic.

questions.q: You've been involved in a collision in which someone was hurt. You've called 999. What should you do next?
options: Stay until the emergency services arrive
Drive home and phone the police later
Leave once another driver stops to help
Leave a note on the other car and go
questions.explain: You should stay at the scene until the emergency services arrive. Be prepared to give first aid and to exchange details.

questions.q: An injured person at a crash scene asks you for a drink of water. What should you do?
options: Give them small sips of water
Give them a hot, sweet drink
Don't give them anything to drink
Give them a drink if they seem thirsty
questions.explain: DO NOT give casualties anything to eat or drink. Keep them warm, dry and as comfortable as you can, and reassure them until help arrives.

questions.q: You're looking after a casualty at a crash scene while waiting for an ambulance. They're conscious but upset. How can you help them?
options: Encourage them to walk about to stay alert
Leave them alone so they can rest
Keep them warm and reassure them
Ask them who caused the crash
questions.explain: Try to keep casualties warm, dry and as comfortable as you can. Give reassurance confidently and try not to leave them alone or let them wander into the path of other traffic.

questions.q: You're giving first aid at the scene of a crash and remember the letters DR ABC. What does the D stand for?
options: Danger
Doctor
Distance
Dial
questions.explain: D stands for Danger: check that it's safe to approach. The letters stand for Danger, Response, Airway, Breathing and Circulation.

questions.q: You reach a casualty who's lying still after a collision. It's safe to approach. How should you check whether they respond?
options: Splash some cold water onto their face
Sit them up and loudly call their name
Shake their head gently from side to side
Gently shake their shoulders and ask loudly
questions.explain: Try to get a response by gently shaking the casualty's shoulders and asking loudly 'Are you all right?' If they respond, check for injuries.

questions.q: A casualty at a crash scene doesn't respond when you speak to them. How should you open their airway?
options: Lift their chin forward with your fingers
Tilt their head down onto their chest
Turn their head sharply to one side
Sit them upright, leaning against the car
questions.explain: If there's no response, open the casualty's airway by placing your fingers under their chin and lifting it forward. Then check that they're breathing normally.

questions.q: A pedestrian injured in a collision is lying on the pavement. They're unconscious but breathing normally. What should you do until medical help arrives?
options: Start chest compressions straight away
Place them in the recovery position
Sit them up against a wall
Leave them alone to look for help
questions.explain: If the casualty is unconscious and breathing, place them in the recovery position until medical help arrives. Only start CPR if there are no signs of breathing.

questions.q: An adult casualty isn't breathing and you start CPR. How far should you press down on the centre of their chest?
options: About 1 to 2 centimetres
About 3 to 4 centimetres
About 5 to 6 centimetres
About 10 to 12 centimetres
questions.explain: Interlock your fingers, place them in the centre of the casualty's chest and press down hard and fast, around 5 to 6 centimetres.

questions.q: You're giving CPR to an adult at the scene of a crash. How fast should you press on their chest?
options: About twice a second
About once a second
About once every two seconds
About five times a second
questions.explain: When giving CPR to an adult, press down hard and fast in the centre of the chest, about twice a second.

questions.q: A baby involved in a crash isn't breathing. How should you give chest compressions?
options: Both hands, 5 to 6 centimetres deep
One hand, pressing as hard as possible
Heel of one hand, on the stomach
Two fingers, a third of the chest depth
questions.explain: For infants, use two fingers in the middle of the chest and press down about a third of the chest depth. For a child you may only need one hand, and shouldn't press down as far as for an adult.

questions.q: You've started CPR on a casualty who wasn't breathing. When should you stop?
options: After about two minutes of compressions
When they breathe or a medic takes over
As soon as you've done 30 compressions
When a police officer arrives at the scene
questions.explain: Don't stop CPR until the casualty starts breathing again or a medical professional takes over.

questions.q: A casualty at a crash scene is bleeding heavily from a leg wound. There's nothing in the wound. What should you do?
options: Wash the wound with clean water first
Leave it uncovered to let it clot
Apply firm pressure over the wound
Keep the leg moving so it doesn't stiffen
questions.explain: If nothing is embedded, apply firm pressure over the wound to stem the flow of blood. As soon as practical, fasten a pad to the wound with a bandage or length of cloth, using the cleanest material available.

questions.q: A casualty has a piece of glass stuck in a bleeding wound on their arm. What should you do?
options: Pull the glass out, then press on the wound
Press firmly on the glass to stop the bleeding
Leave it in and build up padding either side
Wash the glass out with water
questions.explain: Don't remove anything that's stuck in a wound. Taking care not to press on the object, build up padding on either side of it.

questions.q: A driver has been burned in a vehicle fire. The flames are out. How long should you cool the burn with clean, cool water?
options: For about 1 minute
For at least 5 minutes
For no more than 10 minutes
For at least 20 minutes
questions.explain: Cool the burn for at least 20 minutes with plenty of clean, cool water. Cover the burn with cling film if available.

questions.q: You're helping someone who has a burn on their arm. Some of their clothing is stuck to it. What should you do?
options: Pull the clothing off gently
Peel it away after cooling the burn
Leave it there and cool the burn
Soak it, then pull it off quickly
questions.explain: Don't try to remove anything that's sticking to a burn. Cool the burn with plenty of clean, cool water and cover it with cling film if available.

questions.q: You've stopped to help at a crash. What are the main dangers at the scene?
options: Theft from the vehicles
Further collisions and fire
Traffic jams and delays
Flat batteries in the cars
questions.explain: Further collisions and fire are the main dangers following a crash. Approach any vehicle involved with care, watching out for spilt oil or broken glass, switch off all engines and warn other traffic if possible.

questions.q: You've stopped to help at a crash. Why should you take care as you approach the damaged vehicles?
options: There may be spilt oil or broken glass
You could disturb evidence for the police
The drivers may not want your help
You might be blamed for the damage
questions.explain: Further collisions and fire are the main dangers following a crash. Approach any vehicle involved with care, watching out for spilt oil or broken glass.

questions.q: You arrive at a collision involving a tanker carrying dangerous goods. People appear to be trapped in a car beside it. What should you do?
options: Try to rescue them as quickly as you can
Move closer so that you can reassure them
Ask a passer-by to help you pull them free
Keep well away and call the emergency services
questions.explain: If an incident involves a vehicle carrying dangerous goods, keep well away and don't be tempted to try to rescue casualties, as you could become one yourself. Switch off engines, DO NOT smoke, and call the emergency services.

questions.q: A lorry carrying a flammable load has been involved in a crash. You need to call the emergency services. What should you do?
options: Use your mobile phone right beside the lorry
Give details of its labels from a safe distance
Wait until the fire service has arrived
Only report the number of people hurt
questions.explain: Call the emergency services and give as much information as possible about the labels and markings on the vehicle. DO NOT use a mobile phone close to a vehicle carrying flammable loads.

questions.q: You see this symbol on a hazard warning plate. Which kind of vehicle displays plates like this?
options: A vehicle carrying livestock
A tanker carrying dangerous goods
A vehicle with an overhanging load
A lorry weighing over 7.5 tonnes
questions.explain: Road tankers and vehicles carrying tank containers of dangerous goods display hazard warning plates; this symbol shows a toxic substance. If such a vehicle is involved in an incident, keep well away and give the emergency services details of its markings.

questions.q: You've hit a parked car while manoeuvring, causing damage. The owner comes out to speak to you. What MUST you give them?
options: Only your mobile phone number and email
Only the name of your insurance company
Your driving licence for them to keep
Your name, address and vehicle registration
questions.explain: If you're involved in a collision that causes damage or injury, you MUST stop and give your own and the vehicle owner's name and address, and the vehicle's registration number, to anyone with reasonable grounds for requiring them.

questions.q: You've damaged a parked car and can't find the owner to give them your details. What MUST you do?
options: Report it to the police within 24 hours
Report it to the police within 7 days
Report it to your insurer within a month
Nothing, if the damage is minor
questions.explain: If you don't give your name and address at the time of the collision, you MUST report it to the police as soon as reasonably practicable, and in any case within 24 hours.

questions.q: You're involved in a crash in which someone is injured, and you can't produce your insurance certificate at the time. Within what time MUST you produce it for the police?
options: 24 hours
48 hours
7 days
14 days
questions.explain: If another person is injured and you don't produce your insurance certificate at the time, you MUST report the crash to the police as soon as possible and within 24 hours, and produce your certificate for the police within seven days.

questions.q: You've had a minor collision and exchanged details with the other driver. You don't intend to make a claim. Should you tell your insurance company?
options: Yes, even though you're not claiming
No, only if you decide to claim
No, only if the police were involved
Only if the other driver asks you to
questions.explain: You must report an accident to your insurance company, even if you're not planning to make a claim.

questions.q: Your car breaks down on a level crossing. What should you do first?
options: Try to restart the engine several times
Get everyone out and clear of the crossing
Phone your breakdown recovery service
Stay in the car with your hazard lights on
questions.explain: If your vehicle breaks down on a level crossing, get everyone out of the vehicle and clear of the crossing immediately. Then use a railway telephone, if available, to tell the signal operator.

questions.q: You've broken down on a level crossing and everyone is safely clear. There's a railway telephone nearby. What should you do?
options: Call a breakdown service on your mobile
Wait for the barriers to come down
Walk along the line to warn the driver
Use it to tell the signal operator
questions.explain: Use the railway telephone to tell the signal operator, and follow the instructions you're given. Only move the vehicle clear of the crossing if there's time before a train arrives.

questions.q: Your car has stalled on a level crossing and you're trying to push it clear. The alarm sounds and the amber light comes on. What should you do?
options: Leave the car and get clear immediately
Keep pushing, as there's still time
Get back in and try to restart it
Stand by the car and wave to warn the train
questions.explain: Only try to move the vehicle clear if there's time before a train arrives. If the alarm sounds or the amber light comes on, leave the vehicle and get clear of the crossing immediately.

questions.q: You're driving when you see flames coming from under your car's bonnet. You stop safely. What should you do?
options: Open the bonnet to put the fire out
Pour water into the engine compartment
Get everyone out and call the fire brigade
Drive on quickly to the nearest garage
questions.explain: If your vehicle catches fire, get the occupants out quickly and to a safe place, then call the fire brigade. Don't try to put out a fire in the engine compartment, as opening the bonnet will make the fire flare.

questions.q: You hit a dog that ran into the road, and it's injured. What MUST you do?
options: Carry on if your car isn't damaged
Stop at the scene
Report it only if the dog dies
Drive on and phone the police later
questions.explain: If you're involved in a collision that causes damage or injury to any other person, vehicle, animal or property, you MUST stop. You must also give your details to anyone with reasonable grounds for requiring them.

questions.q: You're deaf and are planning a long car journey. What does The Highway Code recommend you do before you set off?
options: Register for the 999 text service
Fit a flashing amber beacon to your car
Plan a route that avoids all motorways
Display a sign saying you're deaf
questions.explain: If you're deaf, hard of hearing or speech impaired, it's recommended that you register for the 999 text service (emergencySMS.net) before making a journey.

questions.q: You're approaching an incident on a dual carriageway. A traffic officer is directing traffic past the scene. What MUST you do?
options: Follow the traffic officer's directions
Pass on whichever side looks clearest
Stop and wait for the police to arrive
Only follow directions from the police
questions.explain: The emergency services, traffic officers and recovery workers may need to work in the carriageway at an incident. You MUST follow any directions given by police or traffic officers as to whether you can safely pass the incident or obstruction.

questions.q: Part of your load falls from your trailer onto a quiet road in a village. What should you do?
options: Leave it there; the council will clear it
Phone 999 and wait in your car
Remove it, but only if it's safe to do so
Drive on and report it next week
questions.explain: On roads other than motorways and high-speed roads, you should only remove an obstruction if it's safe to do so. On a motorway or other high-speed road, DO NOT remove it yourself; stop in a place of relative safety and call 999.

questions.q: You're driving on a dual carriageway and see emergency vehicles with flashing lights a long way ahead. What should you do?
options: Speed up to get past before it's blocked
Slow down and be ready to change lane or stop
Keep your speed and watch the incident closely
Flash your headlights to warn the drivers ahead
questions.explain: If you see emergency or incident support vehicles with flashing lights in the distance, there may be an incident ahead. Slow down and be prepared to move safely into another lane or stop. You MUST follow any directions from police or traffic officers.

questions.q: You're driving on a dual carriageway. There's been a crash on the other side of the central reservation and the emergency services are already there. What should you do?
options: Slow down so you can get a better look
Stop on the verge to see if you can help
Use your phone to film the scene as you pass
Keep going and concentrate on the road ahead
questions.explain: When passing the scene of an incident, remain alert for hazards but don't slow down unnecessarily, for example if it's on the other side of a dual carriageway. Focus on the road ahead, as a lack of attention could cause another collision or congestion.

questions.q: You have a disability that prevents you from getting out of your car. Your car breaks down on a motorway. What should you do?
options: Switch on hazard lights, stay in and call 999
Try to get out and wait on the hard shoulder
Flash your headlights at passing drivers
Open the door and wave to passing drivers
questions.explain: If a disability prevents you following the usual breakdown advice, switch on your hazard warning lights, stay in your vehicle with your seat belt on, and call 999 immediately and ask for the police. Alternatively, press your SOS button if your vehicle has one.

questions.q: You're filling up at a petrol station and accidentally spill some diesel on the forecourt. What should you do?
options: Ignore it, as it'll evaporate quickly
Report it to the attendant straight away
Wipe it with a cloth and drive off
Drive off before it spreads further
questions.explain: Any spilled fuel should be reported to the petrol station attendant immediately. Diesel spillage is dangerous to other road users, particularly motorcyclists, as it greatly reduces the grip between tyres and the road surface.

questions.q: You're about to join a motorway. Which of these road users MUST NOT use it?
options: A van driver
A cyclist
A car towing a caravan
A coach driver
questions.explain: Motorways MUST NOT be used by pedestrians, cyclists, horse riders, riders of motorcycles under 50 cc, certain slow-moving vehicles and agricultural vehicles. Vans, coaches and cars towing caravans may use them.

questions.q: You're a learner driver in England and want some motorway experience before your test. When are you allowed to drive on a motorway?
options: With any supervisor who has held a licence for three years
Only outside rush hours when traffic is light
With an approved driving instructor in a dual-controlled car
Only on motorways that have two lanes
questions.explain: Learner car drivers MUST NOT drive on a motorway unless they're with a DVSA approved driving instructor in a car with dual controls that's displaying L plates (D plates in Wales). It's illegal to practise on the motorway with family or friends.

questions.q: You're driving on a motorway for the first time. Why is it especially important to use your mirrors earlier and look further ahead than on other roads?
options: Motorways have more junctions than other roads
Lane markings are harder to see on motorways
There are more speed cameras on motorways
Traffic is faster, so you have less time to react
questions.explain: Traffic on motorways usually travels faster than on other roads, so you have less time to react. You should use your mirrors earlier and look much further ahead than you would elsewhere.

questions.q: You're on a slip road, about to join a motorway. There's traffic in the left-hand lane. Who has priority?
options: You, as the joining vehicle
Traffic already on the motorway
Whoever is travelling faster
Whichever driver signals first
questions.explain: When you join a motorway you should give priority to traffic already on it. Check the traffic and match your speed so you can fit safely into the flow in the left-hand lane.

questions.q: You're accelerating along a slip road to join a busy motorway. How should you join the traffic in the left-hand lane?
options: Match your speed to fit safely into the flow
Join slowly and expect traffic to move over
Use the hard shoulder until a gap appears
Cross the solid white line as soon as you can
questions.explain: You should check the traffic on the motorway and match your speed to fit safely into the traffic flow in the left-hand lane. Don't cross solid white lines that separate lanes or use the hard shoulder.

questions.q: You're joining a motorway. The slip road doesn't end but carries on as an extra lane on the motorway. What should you do?
options: Move straight into the next lane on your right
Build up speed on the hard shoulder
Cross the solid white line when it's clear
Stay in the lane the slip road becomes
questions.explain: If the slip road continues as an extra lane on the motorway, you should stay in it. Remain in the left-hand lane long enough to adjust to the speed of the traffic before you consider overtaking.

questions.q: You're driving a car on a motorway. There are no signs showing a lower limit. What's the national speed limit for your car?
options: 60 mph
50 mph
70 mph
80 mph
questions.explain: The national speed limit for cars on a motorway is 70 mph (112 km/h). You MUST NOT exceed it, and signs may show a lower limit.

questions.q: You're towing a caravan on a motorway. No other speed limit is shown. What's the maximum speed you're allowed to drive at?
options: 60 mph
50 mph
70 mph
40 mph
questions.explain: Cars towing caravans or trailers have a speed limit of 60 mph (96 km/h) on motorways and dual carriageways. The 70 mph motorway limit applies to cars that aren't towing.

questions.q: You're towing a trailer on a three-lane motorway. What does the law say about using the right-hand lane?
options: You may use it only to overtake
You may use it when traffic is light
You MUST NOT drive in it
You may use it if you keep below 50 mph
questions.explain: On a motorway with three or more lanes, you MUST NOT use the right-hand lane if you're drawing a trailer, except in prescribed circumstances.

questions.q: You've just joined a motorway from a slip road. When should you consider overtaking?
options: Straight away, while still accelerating
As soon as you reach the left-hand lane
Only after you pass the next junction
After adjusting to the speed of traffic
questions.explain: When joining a motorway, remain in the left-hand lane long enough to adjust to the speed of traffic before considering overtaking.

questions.q: You're driving on a motorway and see this sign above the carriageway. What does it mean?
options: Don't use the left lane; 40 mph limit applies
Left lane for slow vehicles; 40 mph advised
Lanes ahead narrow; 40 mph minimum speed
Obstruction ahead; leave at the next exit
questions.explain: The red X means you MUST NOT enter or carry on in the left lane, and a speed shown in a red circle is a mandatory limit. You should move safely to an open lane and keep to the temporary limit.

questions.q: You see this signal at the side of a motorway. What does it show?
options: Minimum speed you must keep to
Number of the next junction
Temporary maximum speed advised
Distance to a hazard in yards
questions.explain: This signal shows a temporary maximum speed advised. A speed limit shown inside a red circle is mandatory, and you MUST NOT exceed it.

questions.q: You're joining a motorway and see this sign. What does it tell you?
options: Speed limits here are only advisory
End of the variable speed limit section
Cameras check for drivers using phones
Variable speed limits enforced by cameras
questions.explain: This sign shows that a variable speed limit is in use and is enforced by cameras. Variable speed limit signs change the maximum speed limit on some motorways, and you MUST NOT exceed a limit shown in a red circle.

questions.q: You're driving on a motorway and the signals ahead are showing flashing amber lights. What should you do?
options: Reduce speed and be ready for a hazard
Move into the right-hand lane straight away
Leave the motorway at the next exit
Stop on the hard shoulder and wait
questions.explain: Flashing amber lights warn of a hazard ahead. You should reduce your speed and be prepared for the hazard.

questions.q: You've slowed down on a motorway because the signals were showing flashing amber lights. When can you increase your speed again?
options: As soon as traffic around you speeds up
After one mile if you've seen no hazard
Once you can't see any hazard ahead
After passing a signal that isn't flashing
questions.explain: You should only increase your speed when you pass a signal that isn't flashing, or a sign showing a national speed limit or the word 'END', and you're sure it's safe to do so.

questions.q: You're on a motorway and pass this signal. What does it mean?
options: End of the motorway
Exit lane ends ahead
End of restriction
End of the hard shoulder
questions.explain: This signal means the end of a restriction. You should only increase your speed when you're sure it's safe to do so.

questions.q: You're driving on a motorway and this signal appears above your lane. What MUST you do?
options: Stay in the lane but slow down
Move safely to an open lane
Stop in the lane and wait
Switch on your hazard warning lights
questions.explain: A red X above a lane means you MUST NOT carry on in that lane. You MUST follow the signs to move safely to an open lane. Lane closures shown by red lights are enforced by the police.

questions.q: A lane on the motorway ahead is closed by a red X, but it looks clear. Why is it important not to drive in it?
options: There may be people or stopped vehicles in it
It's being kept free for faster traffic
It's reserved for vehicles leaving the motorway
The road surface has just been painted
questions.explain: A red X identifies a closed lane where people, stopped vehicles or other hazards are present, and there can be several hazards in it. Emergency services and traffic authorities also use closed lanes to reach incidents.

questions.q: You plan to leave the motorway at the next junction, but the left-hand lane is closed by a red X at the exit slip road. What does this mean?
options: You can use the hard shoulder to reach the exit
You can enter the lane just before the exit
You can use the exit if you slow right down
The exit can't be used
questions.explain: Where the left lane is closed at an exit slip road, the exit can't be used. You MUST NOT drive in a closed lane, so carry on to the next exit.

questions.q: On a motorway, the signals ahead show red flashing lights and every lane is shown as closed. What MUST you do?
options: Use the hard shoulder to pass the closure
Drive slowly past in the left-hand lane
Stop and not go beyond the signal
Reverse back to the last exit
questions.explain: When red flashing lights show all lanes closed, the road is closed. You MUST NOT go beyond the sign in any lane or use the hard shoulder to avoid the closure unless a police or traffic officer directs you to. You MUST NOT reverse on a motorway.

questions.q: You see this signal above your lane on a motorway. What does it mean?
options: Change lane
Leave the motorway here
Hard shoulder now open
Slow vehicles keep left
questions.explain: This signal tells you to change lane in the direction the arrow shows. Use your mirrors and move over when it's safe.

questions.q: You're driving on a motorway and see this signal. What does it mean?
options: Two-way traffic ahead
Hard shoulder open as a lane
Slip road joins from the right
Lane ahead closed
questions.explain: This signal warns that a lane ahead is closed. You MUST follow the signs in advance of a closed lane to move safely to an open lane.

questions.q: A motorway signal shows the word 'Fog', but the road ahead looks clear. What should you do?
options: Ignore it, as the fog has probably cleared
Be prepared for a bank of fog ahead
Switch on your rear fog lights now
Speed up to get past before the fog
questions.explain: If 'Fog' is shown on a sign but the road is clear, be prepared for a bank of fog or drifting patchy fog ahead. You MUST NOT use fog lights unless visibility is seriously reduced.

questions.q: You're driving on a clear three-lane motorway with no slower traffic ahead. Which lane should you use?
options: The middle lane
The right-hand lane
Any lane, if you keep to the limit
The left-hand lane
questions.explain: You should keep in the left lane unless you're overtaking. If you've overtaken, return to the left lane when it's safe to do so.

questions.q: You're overtaking a lorry on a motorway and plan to move back into the left lane. What should you make sure of?
options: That you've reached at least 70 mph
That you don't cut in on the lorry
That the lorry driver flashes you in
That you keep signalling right
questions.explain: When you've overtaken, return to the left lane when it's safe, making sure you don't cut in on the vehicle you've just overtaken.

questions.q: You're in the left-hand lane of a motorway. Ahead, a recovery vehicle is helping a broken-down car on the hard shoulder. What should you do if it's safe?
options: Sound your horn to warn them you're passing
Slow right down to see what's happening
Move into the next lane to give them space
Flash your headlights at the recovery driver
questions.explain: Be aware of recovery workers and stopped vehicles on the hard shoulder or in an emergency area. If you're in the left lane and it's safe, move into the adjacent lane to create more space between you and them.

questions.q: You're in the middle lane of a motorway, behind a slower car that's also in the middle lane. The left-hand lane is clear. What should you do?
options: Move into the left lane to pass it
Overtake on the right when it's safe
Flash your headlights so it moves over
Stay close behind until it moves left
questions.explain: You should overtake only on the right. Don't overtake on the left or move to a lane on your left to overtake.

questions.q: You're in slow, congested motorway traffic. The lanes are moving at similar speeds, but your lane on the left is moving slightly faster than the lane to your right. What should you do?
options: Keep up with the traffic in your lane
Change to the lane on your right
Weave between lanes to make progress
Use the hard shoulder to get ahead
questions.explain: In congested conditions, traffic in left-hand lanes may sometimes move faster than traffic to the right. You may keep up with the traffic in your lane, even if this means passing traffic on your right, but don't change lanes unnecessarily or weave in and out.

questions.q: You're approaching a motorway junction. Signs show that the left-hand lane leads directly off the motorway. When should you get into that lane?
options: Whenever it has less traffic than the others
When you need to overtake slower vehicles
As soon as you see the first sign
Only if you want to go the way it leads
questions.explain: At some junctions a lane may lead directly off the motorway. Only get into that lane if you wish to go in the direction shown by the signs or road markings.

questions.q: Traffic on the motorway is moving very slowly and the hard shoulder beside you is empty. It isn't being used as an extra lane. When may you drive on it?
options: When the left lane is at a standstill
To reach your exit more quickly
Only in an emergency or if directed to
When there are no vehicles on it
questions.explain: You MUST NOT use a hard shoulder except in an emergency, or if you're directed to by the police, traffic officers or a traffic sign.

questions.q: You're on a motorway where the hard shoulder can be used as an extra lane at busy times. When can you drive in it?
options: When a red X is displayed above it
When a speed limit is shown above it
When the sign above it is left blank
Whenever the traffic becomes heavy
questions.explain: You can only use the hard shoulder as an extra lane when a speed limit is shown above it. A red X or a blank sign above the hard shoulder means you MUST NOT use it except in an emergency.

questions.q: You're driving on a motorway with no hard shoulder. How will you recognise an emergency area?
options: Green signs showing a white letter P
Blue signs with an orange SOS telephone
Yellow signs showing a breakdown truck
Red signs with a white warning triangle
questions.explain: Emergency areas are marked by blue signs with an orange SOS telephone symbol and may have orange surfacing. They MUST only be used in an emergency.

questions.q: You're stuck in a stationary queue on a motorway. You want to see what's causing the delay. What does the law say?
options: You MUST NOT walk on the motorway
You may walk along the hard shoulder
You may walk if your hazards are on
You may walk on the verge only
questions.explain: You MUST NOT pick up or set down anyone, or walk on a motorway, except in an emergency.

questions.q: You stopped in an emergency area after your car developed a fault. It's now been fixed. How should you rejoin the motorway?
options: Build up speed and pull out into a gap
Phone the operator and follow their advice
Use hazard lights and pull out slowly
Wait until the lane beside you is empty
questions.explain: To rejoin the carriageway from an emergency area, you MUST use the emergency telephone provided and follow the operator's advice. A lane may need to be closed so that you can rejoin safely.

questions.q: You're ready to rejoin the motorway from the hard shoulder after a breakdown. What should you do?
options: Build up speed, signal and watch for a safe gap
Pull straight into the left lane at low speed
Switch on your hazard lights and pull out
Wait for a driver to flash you out
questions.explain: To rejoin from a hard shoulder, build up speed, indicate and watch for a safe gap in the traffic. Be aware that vehicles, obstructions or debris may be on the hard shoulder.

questions.q: You realise you've just missed your exit on the motorway. What should you do?
options: Reverse along the hard shoulder
Stop on the hard shoulder to check a map
Carry on to the next exit
Cross the central reservation
questions.explain: If you've missed your exit or taken the wrong route, carry on to the next exit. You MUST NOT reverse, cross the central reservation or drive against the traffic flow.

questions.q: You're driving on a motorway when your mobile phone rings. It's an important call you've been expecting. What should you do?
options: Stop on the hard shoulder to answer it
Pull into an emergency area to answer it
Answer it quickly while holding the phone
Call back when parked at a service area
questions.explain: Don't stop on any part of a motorway, including the hard shoulder or an emergency area, to make or receive phone calls, except in an emergency. You MUST NOT use a hand-held phone while driving.

questions.q: You're driving along a motorway slip road and see someone hitchhiking at the side of the road. What does the law say?
options: You MUST NOT stop to pick them up
You may pick them up if you use hazard lights
You may stop on the hard shoulder for them
You may stop briefly at the end of the slip road
questions.explain: You MUST NOT pick up or set down anyone on a motorway, except in an emergency. Pedestrians MUST NOT be on motorways or slip roads except in an emergency.

questions.q: You're in the middle lane of a motorway and want to leave at the next junction. What should you do?
options: Stay in the middle lane until the last marker
Move into the left-hand lane well before your exit
Cut across to the slip road at the last moment
Slow down in the middle lane before the exit
questions.explain: Watch for the signs telling you you're getting near your exit and move into the left-hand lane well before you reach it. Signal left in good time and reduce your speed on the slip road as necessary.

questions.q: You're driving on your own when your car breaks down on a motorway. When you call for help, what should you tell them?
options: Your car's MOT expiry date
That you're travelling alone
The name of your insurer
How fast you were driving
questions.explain: When you get help, tell them if you're a vulnerable motorist, such as disabled, older or travelling alone. Wait well away from your vehicle and moving traffic, behind the safety barrier if there is one.

questions.q: You've just left a motorway after driving at 70 mph for a long time. Why should you check your speedometer?
options: Your speedometer may read high after a long run
Slip roads have a higher limit than motorways
Your tyres will be hotter than usual
You may be going faster than you realise
questions.explain: On leaving a motorway your speed may be higher than you realise; 50 mph may feel like 30 mph. Check your speedometer and adjust your speed, as some slip roads and link roads have sharp bends.

questions.q: You're driving on a motorway at night. What colour are the reflective studs between the carriageway and the central reservation?
options: Amber
Red
Green
White
questions.explain: Amber studs mark the central reservation of a dual carriageway or motorway. Red studs mark the left edge of the road and white studs mark the lanes.

questions.q: You're driving at night on a motorway. Which colour reflective studs mark the left-hand edge of the carriageway?
options: White
Green
Amber
Red
questions.explain: Red studs mark the left edge of the road. Amber studs mark the central reservation, and green studs mark the edge of the main carriageway at slip roads and lay-bys.

questions.q: You're driving on a motorway at night and see green reflective studs on your left. What do they mark?
options: The edge of the central reservation
The lines between the motorway lanes
Where a slip road joins or leaves
Temporary lane layouts at road works
questions.explain: Green studs mark the edge of the main carriageway at lay-bys and slip roads.

questions.q: You're driving through road works on a motorway at night and see green/yellow reflective studs. What do they show?
options: The edge of a slip road or lay-by
Temporary changes to the lane layout
The edge of the central reservation
A lane for works vehicles only
questions.explain: Green/yellow studs indicate temporary adjustments to lane layouts, for example where road works are taking place. Lanes at road works may be narrower than normal, so keep a safe distance from the vehicle in front.

questions.q: Your car develops a problem on a motorway and you can't reach an exit or a service area. Where should you try to stop?
options: In an emergency area or on the hard shoulder
In the right-hand lane by the central reservation
In the lane you're in, with hazard lights on
On the verge of the central reservation
questions.explain: If you can't leave at the next exit or reach a service area, move into the left lane and pull into an emergency area or onto a hard shoulder if you can. Stop as far to the left as possible, with your wheels turned to the left.

questions.q: You're pulling onto the hard shoulder because your car has developed a fault. If you can, where should you stop?
options: Just before an exit slip road
Under a bridge for shelter
Just beyond an emergency telephone
Halfway between two emergency telephones
questions.explain: If you can, stop just beyond an emergency telephone, as far to the left as possible and leaving space to get out. Switch on your hazard warning lights.

questions.q: You've stopped on the hard shoulder after a breakdown. How should you and your passengers get out of the car?
options: Through the driver's door, facing the traffic
Through whichever door is nearest to you
Through the rear door on the traffic side
Through the doors on the side away from traffic
questions.explain: Leave your vehicle by the side furthest from traffic, if it's safe and possible to do so, and make sure your passengers do the same. Then get well away from the vehicle and moving traffic.

questions.q: Your car has broken down on the hard shoulder and you're waiting for help behind the safety barrier. It starts to rain heavily. What should you do?
options: Get back into your car to keep dry
Stay where you are, away from the car
Shelter behind the open boot of the car
Stand in front of the car, out of the wind
questions.explain: Wait well away from your vehicle and moving traffic, behind the safety barrier where there is one. DO NOT return to your vehicle, even if it's raining, cold or dark.

questions.q: Your car breaks down in a live lane of a motorway. You can't get it to the left lane and it isn't safe to get out. What should you do?
options: Stay in the car, keep your belt on and call 999
Get out and push the car onto the hard shoulder
Put a warning triangle behind the car
Stand behind the car to wave traffic past
questions.explain: If you can't get your vehicle to the left lane or a place of relative safety and can't get out safely, stay in it with your seat belt and hazard warning lights on. Call 999 immediately and ask for the police, or press your SOS button if your vehicle has one.

questions.q: You've broken down on a motorway and are calling for help on your mobile phone. How can you give your exact location?
options: Describe the nearest bridge or building
Quote the details on a nearby marker post
Tell them how many lanes the motorway has
Read out your car's registration number
questions.explain: Quote the numbers and letters on the marker posts or driver location signs along the edge of the road. You can also use a mobile phone mapping app, or press your vehicle's SOS button if it has one.

questions.q: You've stopped on the hard shoulder with a puncture in a tyre on the traffic side of your car. What should you do?
options: Change the wheel yourself as quickly as you can
Change it if you wear high-visibility clothing
Change it with your hazard lights switched on
Leave it and call for help from a safe place
questions.explain: You should not attempt repairs on your vehicle on a motorway. Get well away from it and moving traffic, then use the emergency telephone or contact a breakdown recovery service.

questions.q: You're driving on a motorway when a box falls off your roof rack onto the carriageway. What should you do?
options: Stop somewhere relatively safe and call 999
Stop on the hard shoulder and walk back for it
Reverse along the hard shoulder to collect it
Drive on, as someone else will move it
questions.explain: If anything falls from your vehicle onto a motorway, DO NOT try to remove it yourself. Stop in a place of relative safety and call the emergency services on 999.

questions.q: You're driving on a motorway when the traffic ahead slows suddenly because of a queue. Why might you briefly switch on your hazard warning lights?
options: To show you're about to change lanes
To warn drivers behind you of the hazard
To thank a driver who let you in
To tell the driver ahead to move over
questions.explain: You MUST NOT use hazard warning lights while driving unless you're on a motorway or unrestricted dual carriageway and need to warn drivers behind you of a hazard or obstruction ahead. Only use them long enough for your warning to be seen.

questions.q: You're on a motorway in good conditions and can see well ahead. How should you drive?
options: Varying your speed to stay alert
As close to 70 mph as you can
At a steady speed within the limit
At 50 mph to stay in the left lane
questions.explain: When you can see well ahead and road conditions are good, drive at a steady cruising speed which you and your vehicle can handle safely and is within the speed limit.

questions.q: On a motorway you come up behind a slow-moving works vehicle showing this sign on its back. What MUST you do?
options: Stop behind it until it moves off
Pass on whichever side is clearer
Pass it on the side the arrow shows
Follow it until the next junction
questions.explain: Where a 'Keep Left' or 'Keep Right' sign is shown on the back of a works vehicle, you MUST move over and pass it on the side indicated. Don't return to the closed lane until you can see it's safe.

questions.q: You've broken down on a motorway with your dog in the car. You and your passengers are going to wait behind the safety barrier. What should you do with the dog?
options: Let it off the lead on the verge
Tie it to the safety barrier
Walk it along the hard shoulder
Keep it in the car
questions.explain: Animals MUST be kept in the vehicle or, in an emergency, under control on the verge.

questions.q: You're about to enter a contraflow system at motorway road works. What should you do?
options: Speed up to clear it quickly
Slow down and leave a bigger gap
Close up on the vehicle in front
Move nearer the oncoming traffic
questions.explain: In a contraflow you may be in a narrower lane than normal, with no permanent barrier between you and oncoming traffic. At the start and finish, slow down and increase your distance from the vehicle in front, as changes in the camber of the road may affect your vehicle's stability.

questions.q: Your car breaks down while you're driving through road works on a motorway. If one is available, where should you move it?
options: Into a signed road works refuge
Into the area coned off for the works
Onto the central reservation
Into the nearest closed lane
questions.explain: If you break down in road works, follow the usual breakdown advice, but remember that areas marked off by cones contain significant hazards. Where available, move your vehicle into a signed road works refuge location.

questions.q: You're driving along a main road and see this sign. What does it mean?
options: Motorway services on the M62 ahead
End of motorway regulations on the M62
Start of motorway; motorway rules apply
Diversion route for traffic on the M62
questions.explain: This sign shows the start of a motorway and the point from which motorway regulations apply. For example, from here you MUST NOT stop except in an emergency.

questions.q: You're following a long lorry. As it approaches a junction on the left, it moves out towards the centre of the road. What should you do?
options: Pass it on the left while there's room
Stay back, as it may be turning left
Overtake it quickly on the right
Sound your horn to warn the driver
questions.explain: Long vehicles may need extra road space to turn, and may move over to the right before turning left. Stay back and be prepared to stop and wait if it needs room or time to turn.

questions.q: You're approaching a roundabout behind a long vehicle that is straddling both lanes. What should you do?
options: Stay back and watch for its signals
Pass it on the left as you enter
Sound your horn so it picks a lane
Overtake it before the roundabout
questions.explain: Because of their length, long vehicles (including those towing trailers) might have to take a different course or straddle lanes, either approaching or on the roundabout. Give them plenty of room and watch out for their signals.

questions.q: At a mini-roundabout, which vehicles may drive over the central markings?
options: Cars that are turning right at them
Any vehicle that's making a U-turn
Large vehicles unable to get round them
Cars that are towing small trailers
questions.explain: All vehicles MUST pass round the central markings at a mini-roundabout, except large vehicles which are physically incapable of doing so. Avoid making U-turns at mini-roundabouts.

questions.q: You're thinking of overtaking a long lorry on a single carriageway road. What should you bear in mind?
options: Its driver must slow down for you
You can cut in sharply once past
Lorries must pull over to let you by
It'll take longer to pass than a car
questions.explain: Overtaking large vehicles is more difficult. It takes longer to pass a large vehicle, so make sure you have enough room to complete the manoeuvre before committing yourself. If in doubt, don't overtake.

questions.q: The car in front of you pulls out to overtake a long lorry. You also want to overtake. What should you do?
options: Follow the car closely past the lorry
Flash the car ahead to make it hurry
Wait until you can see it's safe yourself
Pull out alongside the car
questions.explain: Don't assume you can follow a vehicle ahead which is overtaking a long vehicle. If a problem develops, the driver may abort overtaking and pull back in.

questions.q: You're following a tractor towing a trailer along a country road. Why should you stay well back?
options: Tractors aren't fitted with brake lights
There may be another slow vehicle ahead
Its driver will wave you past soon
Tractors can't use indicators
questions.explain: Getting too close to large vehicles, including agricultural vehicles such as a tractor with a trailer, will obscure your view of the road ahead, and there may be another slow-moving vehicle in front. Dropping back also helps the driver see you in their mirrors.

questions.q: You're driving on a wet dual carriageway behind a lorry that's throwing up a lot of spray. What should you do?
options: Move closer to get out of the spray
Switch to main beam to see through it
Drop back to improve your view
Overtake it on the left
questions.explain: Rain and spray from vehicles can make it difficult to see and be seen. In wet weather keep well back from the vehicle in front; pulling back from a large vehicle improves your ability to see and plan ahead.

questions.q: Many large vehicles are fitted with speed limiting devices. What speed do these restrict them to, even on a motorway?
options: 50 mph
56 mph
60 mph
70 mph
questions.explain: Many large vehicles may be fitted with speed limiters which restrict their speed to 56 mph (90 km/h), even on a motorway. Be patient, as larger vehicles are subject to lower speed limits than cars.

questions.q: It's a very windy day. Which of these vehicles is most likely to be affected by the wind?
options: A small hatchback
A low sports car
A high-sided lorry
A family saloon
questions.explain: High-sided vehicles are most affected by windy weather, but strong gusts can also blow a car, cyclist, motorcyclist or horse rider off course.

questions.q: You're following a goods vehicle of more than 7.5 tonnes on a dual carriageway in England. The national speed limit applies. What's the lorry's speed limit?
options: 40 mph
50 mph
60 mph
70 mph
questions.explain: On a dual carriageway in England and Wales, the national speed limit for goods vehicles of more than 7.5 tonnes maximum laden weight is 60 mph. Be patient, as larger vehicles are subject to lower speed limits than cars.

questions.q: You're driving along a town road. A bus ahead at a bus stop signals to pull out. What should you do?
options: Speed up to pass before it moves
Sound your horn to warn the driver
Flash your lights to keep it waiting
Give way to it if it's safe to do so
questions.explain: Give priority to buses, coaches and trams when you can do so safely, especially when they signal to pull away from stops.

questions.q: You're driving in a city where trams run along the road. Why do you need to take extra care near them?
options: They're quiet and can't steer around you
They must always give way to cars
They only ever travel very slowly
They can swerve to avoid other traffic
questions.explain: Be careful of electric vehicles such as trams and milk floats. Trams move quickly but silently and cannot steer to avoid you.

questions.q: You're driving along a street where trams share the road with other traffic. Which of these should you do?
options: Race trams away from traffic lights
Pass moving trams on the inside
Always give way to trams
Drive along on top of the rails
questions.explain: Always give way to trams. Don't try to race or overtake them, or pass them on the inside, unless they're at tram stops or stopped by tram signals and there's a designated tram lane for you to pass. Avoid driving directly on top of the rails.

questions.q: A tram has stopped at a stop with no platform to pick up passengers. No other route is signed. What should you do?
options: Pass between it and the left kerb
Wait until the tram moves off
Overtake it on the right
Sound your horn and pass slowly
questions.explain: At stops without platforms you MUST NOT drive between a tram and the left-hand kerb when it has stopped to pick up passengers. If there's no alternative route signed, don't overtake the tram – wait until it moves off.

questions.q: A tram is signalling to pull away from a stop. Why should you give it priority if it's safe to do so?
options: Trams aren't fitted with brakes
Tram drivers can't see other traffic
It's an offence to follow a tram
Standing passengers could be injured
questions.explain: Always give priority to trams, especially when they signal to pull away from stops, unless it would be unsafe. They may be carrying large numbers of standing passengers who could be injured if the tram had to make an emergency stop.

questions.q: You see this symbol on a hazard warning plate on a tanker. What does it mean?
options: Corrosive substance
Toxic substance
Radioactive substance
Compressed gas
questions.explain: Certain tank vehicles carrying dangerous goods must display hazard information panels. This diamond symbol shows a corrosive substance. If such a vehicle is involved in an incident, keep well away.

questions.q: You're following a motorcyclist on a wet road where there are tram rails. Why should you take extra care?
options: They may need more space to cross
They must ride between the rails
Motorcycles must stop when trams pass
They're not allowed to cross the rails
questions.explain: Cyclists and motorcyclists should take extra care near tram tracks, especially when the rails are wet, and it's safest to cross them at right angles. Be aware that they may need more space to cross the tracks safely.

questions.q: A bus has stopped at a bus stop on your left, leaving a gap between it and the kerb. What should you do?
options: Pass it on the right when it's safe
Drive through the gap on its left
Sound your horn and pass either side
Flash your lights so it pulls in
questions.explain: Don't overtake between the kerb and a bus or tram when it's at a stop. Look out for people getting off the bus and crossing the road, and give priority to the bus if it signals to pull away.

questions.q: You're in a queue of slow-moving traffic on a town road. What should you be especially aware of?
options: Traffic lights changing more slowly
Motorcyclists passing on either side
Cars being allowed to use bus lanes
Oncoming traffic having to stop
questions.explain: In slow-moving traffic, be aware of cyclists and motorcyclists who may be passing on either side. They're more difficult to see than larger vehicles and their riders are particularly vulnerable.

questions.q: You're approaching a roundabout when an ambulance with flashing blue lights comes up behind you. Why shouldn't you brake harshly?
options: A vehicle behind may not have the same view
Ambulances must give way at roundabouts
The ambulance will always go round you
It's an offence to stop near a roundabout
questions.explain: When an emergency vehicle approaches, don't panic: consider its route and take appropriate action to let it pass. Don't brake harshly on approach to a junction or roundabout, as a following vehicle may not have the same view as you.

questions.q: You're waiting at a red traffic light beside a tramway. The tram next to you moves off while your light is still red. What's the most likely reason?
options: Trams usually have their own signals
Trams can ignore all traffic signals
Your traffic light has stopped working
The tram is answering an emergency call
questions.explain: Tram drivers usually have their own traffic signals and may be permitted to move when you're not. Always give way to trams, and don't try to race them.

questions.q: A powered mobility scooter is being used on the pavement beside the road. What's the maximum speed it may travel at on the pavement?
options: 4 mph
6 mph
8 mph
12 mph
questions.explain: Powered wheelchairs and mobility scooters MUST NOT travel faster than 4 mph (6 km/h) on pavements or in pedestrian areas. Class 3 vehicles, which can also be used on the road, are restricted to 8 mph (12 km/h).

questions.q: Powered wheelchairs and mobility scooters can be used on some roads. Where MUST they NOT be used?
options: On motorways
On dual carriageways
On roads without a pavement
On roads with a 40 mph limit
questions.explain: Powered wheelchairs and mobility scooters MUST NOT be used on motorways. They shouldn't be used on unrestricted dual carriageways where the speed limit exceeds 50 mph, but if they are, they MUST have a flashing amber beacon.

questions.q: You're driving along a main road and see a vehicle ahead showing a flashing amber beacon. What does this usually warn you of?
options: An ambulance on an emergency call
A police car about to stop you
A slow-moving or stationary vehicle
A doctor on an emergency call
questions.explain: Flashing amber beacons warn of a slow-moving or stationary vehicle, such as a traffic officer vehicle, salt spreader, snow plough or recovery vehicle, or an abnormal load. Approach with caution.

questions.q: On an unrestricted dual carriageway, which of these vehicles MUST use a flashing amber beacon?
options: Tractors limited to 25 mph or less
Cars towing caravans or trailers
Vans carrying heavy loads
Lorries over 7.5 tonnes
questions.explain: On unrestricted dual carriageways, motor vehicles first used on or after 1 January 1947 with a maximum speed of 25 mph or less, such as tractors, MUST use a flashing amber beacon.

questions.q: You're driving behind a snowplough on a dual carriageway. When may you overtake it?
options: As soon as there's a gap
Once your intended lane is cleared
Whenever it drops below 20 mph
When it flashes its headlights
questions.explain: Watch out for snowploughs, which may throw out snow on either side. Don't overtake them unless the lane you intend to use has been cleared.

questions.q: Which of these is true about mini motos and motorised 'go ped' scooters?
options: They may be used in cycle lanes
They MUST NOT be used on roads
They may be used on pavements
They're legal on quiet roads
questions.explain: Most mini motos (miniature motorcycles) and motorised scooters (go peds) don't meet the requirements for road vehicles. They MUST NOT be used on roads, pavements, footpaths or bridleways.

questions.q: You're on a motorway behind a works vehicle displaying the sign 'CONVOY VEHICLE NO OVERTAKING'. What MUST you do?
options: Stay behind it and don't pass
Overtake it on the right
Pass it only if it's slowing
Use the hard shoulder to get by
questions.explain: Where a vehicle displays the sign 'CONVOY VEHICLE NO OVERTAKING', you MUST NOT pass it.

questions.q: You're driving along a narrow road. An ambulance using flashing blue lights and its siren comes up behind you. What should you do?
options: Brake hard and stop at once
Mount the pavement to let it pass
Find a safe place to let it pass
Speed up to stay ahead of it
questions.explain: Consider the route of the emergency vehicle and take appropriate action to let it pass, while complying with traffic signs. If necessary pull to the side and stop, but avoid stopping before the brow of a hill, a bend or a narrow section of road, and avoid mounting the kerb.

questions.q: What colour flashing lights are used by traffic officer and incident support vehicles?
options: Blue
Green
Amber
Red
questions.explain: Traffic officer and incident support vehicles use flashing amber lights. Ambulances, fire engines, police, doctors and other emergency vehicles may use flashing blue, red or green lights.

questions.q: You see this sign. What does it warn you of?
options: A bus lane ahead
A level crossing ahead
Trams crossing ahead
A tram stop ahead
questions.explain: This sign warns of trams crossing ahead. Take extra care: trams move quickly but silently and can't steer to avoid you.

questions.q: Rear marking boards are required on large goods vehicles over 7,500 kg. Where else are the vertical versions of these markings required?
options: On taxis and private hire cars
On powered mobility scooters
On all horse-drawn vehicles
On builders' skips in the road
questions.explain: Large goods vehicle rear markings are fitted to motor vehicles over 7,500 kg and trailers over 3,500 kg. The vertical markings are also required on builders' skips placed in the road and on commercial vehicles or combinations longer than 13 metres.

questions.q: You see this marker on a lorry's load. What does it tell you?
options: Its load overhangs by over 2 metres
The lorry is carrying dangerous goods
The lorry weighs more than 7,500 kg
The lorry is towing a long trailer
questions.explain: Side and end projection markers are required when a load or equipment, such as a crane jib, overhangs the front or rear of a vehicle by more than two metres.

questions.q: You see a plain orange reflective plate like this on the back of a lorry. What does it mean?
options: It's an abnormal load
It's carrying livestock
It's a slow-moving vehicle
It's carrying dangerous goods
questions.explain: Vehicles carrying dangerous goods in packages are marked with plain orange reflective plates. Road tankers and vehicles carrying tank containers of dangerous goods have hazard warning plates.

questions.q: You're driving on a motorway and see this sign on the back of a works vehicle. What does it mean?
options: A works vehicle has closed a lane ahead
The road works end in 800 yards
A contraflow system starts in 800 yards
All lanes are closed for 800 yards
questions.explain: This sign on the back of a works vehicle warns that a lane ahead has been closed by a works vehicle, without cones. Works vehicles may be used to close lanes for repairs on motorways and other high-speed roads, so take special care.

questions.q: You're driving along a road and see this sign. What does it tell you?
options: No stopping for the next 100 yards
A 'Stop' line is 100 yards ahead
A level crossing is 100 yards ahead
Give way to traffic for 100 yards
questions.explain: This sign warns of the distance to a 'Stop' line ahead. When you reach it, you MUST stop behind the line and wait for a safe gap in the traffic before you move off.

questions.q: You're about to emerge from a side road at a junction with this sign. Who MUST you give way to?
options: Only vehicles that are signalling
Only traffic coming from your left
Traffic on the main road
Nobody, if you're turning left
questions.explain: This is a 'Give Way' sign. You MUST give way to traffic on the main road when emerging from a junction with broken white lines across the road.

questions.q: You're driving along a road and pass this sign. What does it mean?
options: There's no speed limit here
60 mph limit for all vehicles
End of minimum speed
National speed limit applies
questions.explain: This sign means the national speed limit applies. It doesn't mean there's no limit – the maximum depends on the type of road and your vehicle, for example 60 mph for cars on a single carriageway but 50 mph if you're towing.

questions.q: You see this sign at the side of the road. What does it tell you?
options: The maximum speed you may drive at
The minimum speed you must keep to
The speed advised for the bend ahead
The average speed of traffic here
questions.explain: Signs with red circles are mostly prohibitive. This sign shows the maximum speed, and you MUST NOT exceed it. A minimum speed is shown in a blue circle.

questions.q: You drive past this sign. When do the waiting restrictions within the zone apply?
options: At all times, every day
Only on Sundays and bank holidays
At the times shown on the sign
Only during school term times
questions.explain: This sign marks the entrance to a controlled parking zone. The zone entry signs show the times when the waiting restrictions within the zone are in force. Parking may be allowed in some places at other times.

questions.q: You drive past this sign into a residential area. How far does the 20 mph limit apply?
options: Only for the first mile after the sign
Until you pass a sign showing the zone ends
Only during school opening and closing times
Until you reach the next junction
questions.explain: This sign marks the entry to a 20 mph zone. The limit applies throughout the zone until you pass the 'End of 20 mph zone' sign. Look out for pedestrians, children, cyclists and vehicles emerging from junctions or driveways.

questions.q: You're driving along a road with this sign. What does the blue circle tell you about the speed shown?
options: It's the maximum speed allowed
It's an advised speed for the bends ahead
It applies to lorries and buses only
It's a minimum speed
questions.explain: Blue circles give positive instructions, and this sign shows a minimum speed. A speed limit shown in a red circle is a maximum that you MUST NOT exceed.

questions.q: You're driving on a motorway and see this sign. What does the 40 in a red circle mean?
options: It's an advised maximum speed
It's the minimum speed allowed
It's a mandatory speed limit
It's the distance to the obstruction
questions.explain: A speed limit shown in a red circle is mandatory, and you MUST NOT exceed it. This sign also shows that the left lane is closed, so you MUST NOT enter or carry on in it.

questions.q: You're following a slow-moving tractor and see this sign. What MUST you do?
options: Stay behind it while the restriction applies
Overtake it only if it's doing under 10 mph
Overtake it on the left if there's room
Overtake it if the road ahead looks clear
questions.explain: This sign means no overtaking. You MUST obey traffic signs giving orders, so stay behind the tractor while the restriction applies.

questions.q: You're approaching a narrow bridge where this sign is shown. A car is coming towards you from the other side. What should you do?
options: Drive on, as you have priority
Give way to the oncoming car
Flash your headlights and drive on
Speed up to get across first
