questions.explain: This sign means give priority to vehicles from the opposite direction. Wait and let the oncoming car come through first.

questions.q: You're driving along a road with this sign. Which vehicles may stop there?
options: Any car picking up passengers
Vans loading or unloading goods
Buses, but no other vehicles
Any vehicle for up to 2 minutes
questions.explain: This Red Route sign means no stopping during the period shown – here, at any time – except for buses. You MUST NOT stop on a Red Route unless signs show that you may.

questions.q: This sign is a blue circle with no red border. What does that tell you about its message?
options: It's warning you of a hazard
It's telling you what's prohibited
It's giving tourist information
It's giving a positive instruction
questions.explain: Signs with blue circles but no red border mostly give positive instructions – this one means ahead only. Red circles are mostly prohibitive, and triangles mostly warn.

questions.q: You see a circular sign with a red border. What type of message do these signs mostly give?
options: Prohibitions
Warnings
Directions
Positive instructions
questions.explain: Signs with red circles are mostly prohibitive – they tell you what you mustn't do. Plates below signs qualify their message.

questions.q: What shape are most warning signs?
options: Triangular
Circular
Rectangular
Octagonal
questions.explain: Warning signs are mostly triangular. Signs giving orders are mostly circular, and direction and information signs are mostly rectangular.

questions.q: You're following direction signs with a white background and a black border. What type of road are you on?
options: A motorway
A primary route
A non-primary or local route
A route to a tourist attraction
questions.explain: Direction signs on non-primary and local routes have black borders. Motorway signs have blue backgrounds, primary route signs have green backgrounds, and brown signs show routes to tourist attractions.

questions.q: You're planning to follow a primary route. What colour background will its direction signs have?
options: Green
Blue
White
Brown
questions.explain: Signs on primary routes have green backgrounds. Motorway direction signs are blue, and brown signs show the way to tourist attractions.

questions.q: You see this brown sign by the road. What does the brown background tell you?
options: It's showing a route for heavy lorries
It's directing you to a tourist attraction
It's showing a diversion route
It's warning of farm animals on the road ahead
questions.explain: Brown signs direct you to tourist attractions, such as the zoo shown here.

questions.q: You're approaching a junction on a primary route. The green direction sign has a blue panel on it. What does the blue panel show?
options: A tourist attraction is that way
A local route leads from the junction
A motorway starts at the junction ahead
The road leads to an airport
questions.explain: On primary route signs, blue panels show that the motorway starts at the junction ahead. White panels show local or non-primary routes, and brown panels show routes to tourist attractions.

questions.q: You're driving on a motorway and pass these markers on the left. What does each bar represent?
options: About 1 mile to the exit
About 300 yards to the exit
About 50 yards to the exit
About 100 yards to the exit
questions.explain: These are countdown markers to an exit from the motorway. Each bar represents about 100 yards to the exit, so move into the left-hand lane in good time.

questions.q: You're a learner driver practising in your family's car with a relative. You see this sign ahead. What should you do?
options: Join it, but stay in the left-hand lane
Take another route before the motorway
Join it, but keep below 50 mph
Join it if your relative is over 21
questions.explain: This sign marks the start of a motorway. Learner car drivers MUST NOT drive on a motorway unless they're accompanied by an approved driving instructor in a car with dual controls.

questions.q: You're driving alone in your car at 8 am on a Tuesday. You see this sign at the start of a lane. What should you do?
options: Use the lane, as cars are allowed in it
Use the lane only to overtake
Use the lane if you're turning off soon
Keep out of the lane at these times
questions.explain: This lane is for high-occupancy vehicles carrying at least the number of people shown (here, 2 or more) during the times shown. You MUST NOT drive in it during those times unless the signs show your vehicle is permitted.

questions.q: You're approaching a bus lane with this marking. How will you know whether any other vehicles may use it?
options: Signs will show which vehicles may use it
Any vehicle may use it when it's empty
Only taxis are ever allowed to use it
Cars may use it if carrying passengers
questions.explain: Bus lanes are shown by road markings and signs that indicate which (if any) other vehicles are permitted to use them. Unless signs show otherwise, you shouldn't drive in a bus lane during its period of operation.

questions.q: You're driving through a city where trams run along the road. You notice a diamond-shaped sign. Who is it giving instructions to?
options: Cyclists
Tram drivers
Bus drivers
Pedestrians
questions.explain: Diamond-shaped signs and white light signals give instructions to tram drivers only. You MUST NOT enter a road, lane or other route reserved for trams.

questions.q: A school crossing patrol steps out ahead holding up this sign. What MUST you do?
options: Slow down and pass behind them
Stop before you reach the patrol
Give way only if children are crossing
Drive on if the children are on the far side
questions.explain: You MUST stop when a school crossing patrol shows a 'Stop for children' sign. You MUST obey signs used by school crossing patrols.

questions.q: You're driving near a school and see amber lights flashing below a 'School' warning sign. What does this tell you?
options: The school car park is full
A 20 mph limit starts in 1 mile
Children may be crossing the road ahead
Parking is allowed outside the school
questions.explain: A flashing amber signal below the 'School' warning sign tells you there may be children crossing the road ahead. Drive very slowly until you're clear of the area.

questions.q: You're approaching a level crossing when these lights start to flash. What MUST you do?
options: Cross quickly before the barriers come down
Slow down and look for a train
Stop only if you can see a train
Stop behind the white line
questions.explain: Alternately flashing red lights mean you MUST stop. At a level crossing, you MUST stop behind the white line across the road.

questions.q: You're approaching a level crossing that has no barriers. The red lights start to flash. What does this mean?
options: A train is approaching
A train has just gone past
The lights are being tested
You may cross if you look first
questions.explain: At level crossings where there are no barriers, a train is approaching when the lights show. You MUST always obey the flashing red stop lights and stop behind the white line.

questions.q: You're approaching a junction and see this sign. What does it mean?
options: Traffic signals ahead
Traffic signals not in use
Level crossing lights ahead
No stopping at the lights
questions.explain: This sign warns that traffic signals aren't in use. If traffic lights aren't working, treat the situation as you would an unmarked junction and proceed with great care.

questions.q: You see this warning sign for a staggered junction. What does the broader line in the symbol show?
options: The road with the most traffic
The road with a lower speed limit
The road that has priority
The road that's a dead end
questions.explain: On junction warning signs, the priority through route is indicated by the broader line.

questions.q: You see this sign showing a 20% gradient. How could the same gradient be shown as a ratio?
questions.explain: Gradients on steep hill signs may be shown as a percentage or as a ratio – a 20% gradient is the same as 1:5.

questions.q: You're on a road with these lines, and the broken line is on your side. You want to overtake. When may you cross the lines?
options: Only to pass a cyclist doing 10 mph or less
Never, as these lines ban overtaking
Only if the vehicle ahead waves you on
If you can get back before a solid line
questions.explain: Where the line nearer to you is broken, you may cross the lines to overtake if it's safe, provided you can complete the manoeuvre before reaching a solid white line on your side. White arrows on the road tell you to get back to your side.

questions.q: You see this warning sign with a plate below it. What's the plate for?
options: To tell you what the danger is
To give the distance to the next town
To show a temporary speed limit
To show the times the sign applies
questions.explain: This is the 'other danger' sign. The plate below it tells you the nature of the danger – here, a hidden dip. Plates below signs qualify their message.

questions.q: You drive past this sign. What should you be prepared for?
options: A 50 mph limit on the road ahead
Children playing in the road
A road with no parking at any time
Queues for a car park
questions.explain: This sign marks the entry to a Home Zone, where people could be using the whole of the road – for example, children playing. Drive slowly and carefully, and be prepared to stop.

questions.q: You see this sign. What should you do?
options: Speed up to get through the works quickly
Change lanes to pass queuing traffic
Take extra care and look for further signs
Watch the road workers instead of the road
questions.explain: This sign warns of road works. Take extra care and look for additional signs giving more specific instructions. Concentrate on the road ahead, not the road works.

questions.q: You see this sign on the approach to road works. What does it tell you about the speed limit ahead?
options: You MUST NOT exceed it
It's only advice and can be ignored
It applies only when workers are present
It applies only to large goods vehicles
questions.explain: This sign warns of a mandatory speed limit ahead. At road works you MUST NOT exceed any temporary maximum speed limit.

questions.q: You've moved over to pass a works vehicle showing this sign. When should you move back into the lane it's closing?
options: As soon as you draw level with it
When traffic behind starts to pass
Only when you can see it's safe
After you pass the next junction
questions.explain: Where a works vehicle shows a 'Keep Left' or 'Keep Right' sign on the back, you MUST pass it on the side indicated. Don't return to the closed lane until you can see it's safe to do so.

questions.q: At road works, a worker is holding this sign facing you. What MUST you do?
options: Drive on slowly past the worker
Stop only if traffic is coming towards you
Give way to oncoming traffic, then go
Stop and wait until you're shown 'GO'
questions.explain: This is a manually operated temporary 'STOP' sign. You MUST obey temporary signs, so stop and wait. When the 'GO' sign is shown, proceed with care.

questions.q: The broken white line along the centre of the road changes to this pattern, with longer lines and shorter gaps. What does this tell you?
options: There's a hazard ahead
You're entering a 30 mph area
You're now allowed to overtake
The road ahead is one-way
questions.explain: When a centre line lengthens and the gaps shorten, it's a hazard warning line. Don't cross it unless you can see the road is clear and you want to overtake or turn off.

questions.q: You're driving on a road with these lines, and the solid line is nearest to you. When may you cross it to overtake?
options: To pass a car travelling below 30 mph
To pass a cyclist going at 10 mph or less
Whenever you can see the road ahead is clear
To pass any vehicle that's signalling left
questions.explain: You MUST NOT cross or straddle a solid line nearest you. But you may cross it, if the road is clear, to pass a stationary vehicle or to overtake a pedal cycle, horse or road maintenance vehicle travelling at 10 mph or less.

questions.q: You're on a road with these markings, and the broken line is on your side. You want to park. What does the Highway Code say?
options: You may park, as your line is broken
You MUST NOT park where these lines are
You may park for up to 20 minutes
You may park, but only at night
questions.explain: You MUST NOT stop or park on a road marked with double white lines, even when a broken white line is on your side, except to pick up or set down passengers, or to load or unload goods.

questions.q: You're driving along a road with this area of white diagonal stripes, bordered by broken white lines. What should you do?
options: Drive in it to pass slow traffic
Use it to park if you need to
Use it as an extra lane at busy times
Keep out unless it's necessary and safe
questions.explain: Hatch markings separate traffic lanes or protect traffic turning right. If the area is bordered by a broken white line, you shouldn't enter it unless it's necessary and you can see it's safe to do so.

questions.q: There's an area of white chevrons painted on the road, bordered by a solid white line. When may you drive into it?
options: Only in an emergency
To overtake a slow vehicle
When you're turning right
When traffic is queuing
questions.explain: If an area is marked with chevrons and bordered by solid white lines, you MUST NOT enter it except in an emergency.

questions.q: You're driving at night on a road with reflective studs. What do white studs mark?
options: The left-hand edge of the road
The edge of the central reservation
The lanes or the middle of the road
The edge at lay-bys and slip roads
questions.explain: White studs mark the lanes or the middle of the road. Red studs mark the left edge, amber studs mark the central reservation and green studs mark the edge of the main carriageway at lay-bys and slip roads.

questions.q: You want to drop off a passenger on a road with these lines. There are no loading restrictions. What are you allowed to do?
options: Park for up to 20 minutes
Stop while your passenger gets out
Wait as long as you stay in the car
Park with your hazard lights on
questions.explain: Double yellow lines mean no waiting at any time. You may stop while passengers board or alight, and to load or unload unless there are also loading restrictions.

questions.q: The plate next to this yellow line shows times but no days. When does the waiting restriction apply?
options: Monday to Friday only, except Bank Holidays
Monday to Saturday only
Every day except Sundays and Bank Holidays
Every day, including Sundays and Bank Holidays
questions.explain: If no days are shown on the signs, the restrictions are in force every day, including Sundays and Bank Holidays. Always check the times shown on the plates.

questions.q: You're driving along a Red Route marked with these lines. You aren't a taxi driver and don't hold a Blue Badge. When may you stop to let a passenger out?
options: Not at any time
Only outside peak hours
For up to two minutes
Only on Sundays
questions.explain: On Red Routes, double red lines ALWAYS mean no stopping at any time. This includes stopping to let passengers board or alight, unless you're driving a licensed taxi or hold a Blue Badge.

questions.q: You see this bay marked in red on a Red Route. What does the red marking tell you?
options: It's available all day for the purpose shown
It's reserved for Blue Badge holders only
It may only be available for part of the day
It's a taxi rank at all times
questions.explain: On Red Routes, a box marked in red may only be available for the purpose specified for part of the day, such as between busy peak periods. A box marked in white is available throughout the day.

questions.q: You see these yellow marks on the kerb. Which of these is still allowed?
options: Loading goods for up to 20 minutes
Stopping to let a passenger get out
Unloading heavy shopping
Parking for up to an hour
questions.explain: Double kerb marks mean no loading or unloading at any time. You may still stop while passengers board or alight.

questions.q: You're collecting a child from school and see these markings outside the entrance. What should you do?
options: Stop on them briefly to pick up your child
Wait on them with your engine running
Keep them clear and stop somewhere else
Park on them if there are no other spaces
questions.explain: These markings mean keep the school entrance clear of stationary vehicles, even if picking up or setting down children. Where upright signs show a ban on stopping, you MUST NOT stop on them.

questions.q: You want to park in this marked area for a few minutes while you visit a shop. What should you do?
options: Park, as long as no bus is in sight
Park for no more than five minutes
Park with your hazard lights on
Find somewhere else to park
questions.explain: This marking shows a bus stop. Don't stop or park at or near a bus or tram stop.

questions.q: You're approaching a box junction like this at a signalled roundabout. When may you enter the box?
options: Only if you can cross it without stopping
Whenever the traffic lights are green
When you're waiting to turn right
When the traffic ahead is moving
questions.explain: At signalled roundabouts you MUST NOT enter a box junction unless you can cross over it completely without stopping. At other box junctions, you may wait in the box to turn right if you're only stopped by oncoming traffic or other vehicles waiting to turn right.

questions.q: You want to turn right at a box junction. Your exit road is clear, but oncoming traffic is stopping you from turning. May you enter the box and wait?
options: No, never enter until you can clear it
Only if the traffic lights are red
Yes, you may wait in the box to turn
Only if you're driving a large vehicle
questions.explain: You MUST NOT enter a box junction until your exit road or lane is clear. But you may enter the box and wait when you want to turn right and are only stopped by oncoming traffic or other vehicles waiting to turn right.

questions.q: Traffic ahead is queuing, and the only space left for you is on these markings. What should you do?
options: Stop on them, as the queue will soon move
Stop on them with your hazard lights on
Stop on them if no one is waiting to pull out
Wait before them until there's space beyond
questions.explain: These markings mean don't block that part of the carriageway. Wait before them until there's room for you beyond, so the area stays clear.

questions.q: A car ahead of you is showing this signal. What does it mean?
options: The driver intends to reverse
The driver is braking
The driver intends to turn left
The car has broken down
questions.explain: Reversing lights mean 'I intend to reverse'. This signal shouldn't be used except for the purpose described.
ref: HC Signals to other road users

questions.q: You're driving along a one-way street and see this sign. What does it mean?
options: Buses must use the left lane
There's a contraflow bus lane
There's a bus stop ahead
Buses have priority at the junction
questions.explain: This sign shows a contraflow bus lane, where buses travel in the opposite direction to other traffic. In one-way streets, buses and cycles may have a contraflow lane.

questions.q: You're waiting at traffic lights that change to show this. What MUST you do?
options: Move off if the way is clear
Stop and wait until green shows
Go, but give way to pedestrians
Go if you're turning left
questions.explain: Red and amber together also mean 'Stop'. Don't pass through or start until green shows.

questions.q: The traffic lights show this and you want to turn left. Pedestrians are crossing the road you're turning into. What should you do?
options: Go, as you have priority on green
Sound your horn to warn them
Edge forward to hurry them across
Give way to the pedestrians
questions.explain: Green means you may go on if the way is clear. Take special care when turning, and give way to pedestrians who are crossing.

questions.q: You're waiting at traffic lights showing red, with this green filter arrow lit. You want to go straight ahead. What should you do?
options: Wait for the full green light
Go, as the arrow lets all lanes move
Move into the filter lane and go
Go if no traffic is coming
questions.explain: A green filter arrow means you may go only in the direction shown by the arrow. Don't enter the filter lane unless you want to go that way – wait for the full green light to go straight ahead.

questions.q: You see this sign. What does it warn you of?
options: A level crossing with barriers ahead
Trams crossing the road ahead
A level crossing without barriers ahead
A railway bridge over the road
questions.explain: This sign warns of a level crossing without a barrier or gate ahead. At crossings with no barriers, a train is approaching when the lights show.

questions.q: You've moved out of a motorway lane closed by this signal. How will you know when the lane is open again?
options: The lane will look clear of hazards
You'll have passed the next junction
A sign will show a speed limit or 'END'
Traffic around you will start using it
questions.explain: A red X identifies a closed lane, and you MUST NOT drive in it. A sign will tell you when the lane is no longer closed by showing a speed limit or the word 'END'.

questions.q: You see this signal on a motorway with its amber lights flashing, but you can't see any problem ahead. Why might it be on?
options: It's being tested by the operator
It applies to large vehicles only
It's left on from an earlier incident
There may be a hazard you can't see yet
questions.explain: Motorway signals warn you of hazards ahead, such as an incident, fog, a spillage or road workers, which you may not immediately be able to see. Reduce your speed and be prepared for the hazard.

questions.q: You're approaching a narrow section of road and see this sign. What does it mean?
options: You must give way to oncoming traffic
The road ahead is one-way
Two-way traffic crosses ahead
You have priority over oncoming traffic
questions.explain: This rectangular information sign means traffic has priority over oncoming vehicles. A circular sign with a red border is used where you must give priority to vehicles from the opposite direction.

questions.q: You're on a motorway where the hard shoulder is sometimes used as an extra lane. The sign above it is blank. What does this mean?
options: Use it at up to 50 mph
Use it only if traffic is heavy
Use it only to reach the next exit
Don't use it except in an emergency
questions.explain: A red X or a blank sign above the hard shoulder means you MUST NOT use it except in an emergency. You can only use it as an extra lane when a speed limit is shown above it.

questions.q: You're driving under lane control signals. What does a green arrow above your lane mean?
options: The lane ahead is about to close
You should change to the left lane
The lane is for buses and taxis only
The lane is available to you
questions.explain: On lane control signals, a green arrow means the lane is available to traffic facing the sign. Red crosses mean the lane is closed, and a white diagonal arrow means change lanes in the direction shown.

questions.q: You're approaching a junction where a police officer is controlling traffic. The officer faces you and gives this signal. What MUST you do?
options: Drive on slowly past them
Stop before reaching the officer
Turn left at the junction
Flash your headlights and drive on
questions.explain: This is a police officer signalling 'Stop' to traffic approaching from the front. You MUST obey signals given by police officers.

questions.q: A police car wants you to stop. How will it try to attract your attention?
options: Flashing amber lights from in front
Flashing green lights from the side
Flashing blue lights, usually from behind
Waving a red flag from the roadside
questions.explain: Where possible, the police will attract your attention by flashing blue lights or headlights, or sounding their siren or horn, usually from behind. You MUST then pull over and stop as soon as it's safe.

questions.q: You see this vehicle. On which roads do its officers have the power to stop vehicles?
options: Only on motorways and trunk roads
On all roads, including motorways
Only at roadside check sites
Only on roads in towns and cities
questions.explain: This is a DVSA officer vehicle. DVSA officers have the power to stop vehicles on all roads, including motorways and trunk roads, and you MUST obey any signals they give.

questions.q: You want to turn left at a junction controlled by a police officer. Which hand may you use to give this arm signal?
options: Your right hand only
Your left hand only
Either hand
Neither – use your indicators only
questions.explain: This arm signal tells a person controlling traffic that you want to turn left. You can give it with either hand.

questions.q: When should a driver use arm signals?
options: Only when turning right in the dark
Instead of brake lights in daylight
Only when a police officer asks you to
To reinforce your indicators if needed
questions.explain: Arm signals are for use when direction indicator signals are not used, or when necessary to reinforce your indicators and brake lights.
ref: HC Signals to other road users

questions.q: A vehicle ahead of you is showing this signal. What could its driver or rider intend to do?
options: Stop on the left
Move out to the right
Overtake on the right
Reverse into a gap
questions.explain: This signal means the driver or rider intends to move in to the left, turn left or stop on the left. Proceed only when you're sure it's safe, as an indicator may not have been cancelled.
ref: HC Signals to other road users

questions.q: You're driving a car on a single carriageway road and pass this sign. What's the maximum speed you can now drive at?
options: 50 mph
60 mph
70 mph
40 mph
questions.explain: This sign means the national speed limit applies. For cars on a single carriageway that's 60 mph, but you should still drive at a speed that suits the conditions.

questions.q: You're driving a car on a dual carriageway where the national speed limit applies. What's the maximum speed limit?
options: 60 mph
50 mph
80 mph
70 mph
questions.explain: The national speed limit for cars on a dual carriageway is 70 mph. It's the absolute maximum, not a target.

questions.q: Some rules in the Highway Code use the words 'MUST' or 'MUST NOT'. What does this tell you?
options: They're only good advice
They apply only to learners
They apply only on motorways
They're legal requirements
questions.explain: Rules that use 'MUST' or 'MUST NOT' are legal requirements. If you disobey them you're committing a criminal offence, and you may be fined, get penalty points, be disqualified or, in the most serious cases, be sent to prison.

questions.q: You're turning right at a crossroads. An oncoming vehicle is also turning right. Which way of turning is generally safer?
options: Right side to right side
Left side to left side
Whichever lets you go first
Cutting the corner to turn sooner
questions.explain: Turning right side to right side, keeping the other vehicle on your right and turning behind it, is generally safer as you have a clear view of approaching traffic. Turning left side to left side can block your view of oncoming vehicles.

questions.q: You're driving in England on a road with street lights. There are no signs showing a different speed limit. What limit generally applies?
options: 20 mph
40 mph
50 mph
30 mph
questions.explain: In England and Scotland a 30 mph limit generally applies to roads with street lights (excluding motorways) unless signs show otherwise.

questions.q: You're driving in Wales along a road with street lights. No signs show a different speed limit. What's the speed limit?
options: 30 mph
20 mph
40 mph
50 mph
questions.explain: In Wales a 20 mph limit generally applies to roads with street lights unless signs show otherwise. In England and Scotland it's generally 30 mph.

questions.q: You're following a coach along a single carriageway road where the national speed limit applies. What's the coach's maximum speed limit?
options: 40 mph
60 mph
50 mph
70 mph
questions.explain: Buses, coaches and minibuses are limited to 50 mph on single carriageways, lower than the 60 mph limit for cars. Be patient, as larger vehicles are subject to lower speed limits.

questions.q: You're driving on a country road where the national speed limit applies. It's raining and there are sharp bends ahead. What should you remember about the speed limit?
options: It's the absolute maximum, not a target
It's the speed you should aim to keep to
It only applies when the road is dry
It may be exceeded briefly to overtake
questions.explain: The speed limit is the absolute maximum and doesn't mean it's safe to drive at that speed. You should reduce your speed where there are hazards such as bends, and when the weather makes it safer to do so.

questions.q: You're driving along a two-lane dual carriageway. Which lane should you normally use?
options: The right-hand lane
Whichever lane is less busy
The left-hand lane
The lane with faster traffic
questions.explain: On a two-lane dual carriageway you should stay in the left-hand lane. Use the right-hand lane for overtaking or turning right, then move back to the left when it's safe.

questions.q: You're on a single carriageway road with three lanes. No signs or markings give priority to either direction. What should you use the middle lane for?
options: Driving at a steady speed
Pulling in to let others pass
Turning left into side roads
Overtaking or turning right
questions.explain: Use the middle lane only for overtaking or turning right. You have no more right to use it than a driver coming from the opposite direction, and you shouldn't use the right-hand lane.

questions.q: You're driving in the left-hand lane of a busy multi-lane road and need to move into the right-hand lane. What should you do first?
options: Signal and move across straight away
Check your mirrors and blind spot
Sound your horn to warn other drivers
Brake so that traffic behind can pass
questions.explain: Before changing lane, use your mirrors and, if necessary, take a quick sideways glance to make sure you won't force anyone to change course or speed. Then signal and move over when it's clear.

questions.q: You're driving along a one-way street with two lanes. You want to turn right at the end. Unless signs or markings show otherwise, which lane should you use?
options: The left-hand lane
Either lane
The right-hand lane
The lane with less traffic
questions.explain: In a one-way street you should use the right-hand lane when going right and the left-hand lane when going left, unless signs or markings show otherwise. Choose the correct lane as soon as you can.

questions.q: You're going straight ahead along a busy one-way street with several lanes. What should you be aware of?
options: Traffic could pass you on both sides
Overtaking isn't allowed in one-way streets
You must stay in the left-hand lane
Cyclists aren't allowed to use the street
questions.explain: When going straight ahead in a one-way street, use the most appropriate lane and remember that traffic could be passing on both sides. Don't change lanes suddenly.

questions.q: You're driving along a town road with a bus lane on your left. Signs show it's in operation and don't allow other vehicles. When may you enter it?
options: To get past slow-moving traffic
To stop, load or unload if allowed
When no buses can be seen behind you
To overtake a cyclist in your lane
questions.explain: Unless signs show otherwise, you shouldn't drive in a bus lane during its period of operation. You may enter it to stop, load or unload where this isn't prohibited.

questions.q: You're driving on a road with a cycle lane marked by a solid white line. It's during the lane's times of operation. What must you do?
options: Drive in it only if it's empty
Park in it for no more than 20 minutes
Use it to pass queuing traffic
Not drive or park in it
questions.explain: You MUST NOT drive or park in a cycle lane marked by a solid white line during its times of operation. If it's marked by a broken line, don't drive or park in it unless it's unavoidable.

questions.q: You're approaching a lane shown by this sign. It's within the times shown. Which vehicles may use the lane?
options: Any car that isn't towing a trailer or caravan
Only vehicles with just one person inside
Vehicles carrying the minimum number shown
Only lorries and other large goods vehicles
questions.explain: When a high-occupancy vehicle (HOV) lane is in operation it MUST only be used by vehicles carrying at least the minimum number of people shown on the signs, and by other vehicles, such as buses, that the signs allow.

questions.q: You're driving in a city where trams run along some streets. A lane ahead is reserved for trams. What does the Highway Code say about entering it?
options: You must not enter it
You may use it to overtake
You may use it outside peak hours
You may use it if no tram is coming
questions.explain: You MUST NOT enter a road, lane or other route reserved for trams. Take extra care where trams run along the road, and don't follow them when they leave the main carriageway.

questions.q: You're approaching a roundabout. There are no signs, road markings or traffic lights telling you otherwise. Which traffic should you give priority to?
options: Traffic approaching from your left
Traffic waiting to join behind you
Traffic heading for your exit
Traffic approaching from your right
questions.explain: When you reach a roundabout you should give priority to traffic approaching from your right, unless signs, road markings or traffic lights direct otherwise.

questions.q: You're going to take the first exit to the left at a roundabout. Unless signs or markings show otherwise, how should you approach?
options: Signal right and use the right-hand lane
Signal left and use the left-hand lane
Give no signal and use either lane
Signal left and use the right-hand lane
questions.explain: For the first exit, signal left and approach in the left-hand lane. Keep to the left on the roundabout and continue signalling left to leave.

questions.q: You're going to take an exit to the right at a roundabout. There are no signs or markings telling you otherwise. What should you do?
options: Signal left and approach in the left-hand lane
Approach in the left-hand lane with no signal
Signal right and approach in the right-hand lane
Signal right and approach in the left-hand lane
questions.explain: When taking an exit to the right, signal right and approach in the right-hand lane. Keep to the right on the roundabout until you need to change lanes to exit, and signal left after you've passed the exit before the one you want.

questions.q: You're going straight ahead at a roundabout, using an exit between the first and the last. When should you signal left?
options: As you approach the roundabout
As soon as you join the roundabout
You don't need to signal at all
After passing the exit before yours
questions.explain: For an intermediate exit you won't normally need to signal on approach. Stay in your lane and signal left after you've passed the exit before the one you want.

questions.q: You're driving a car and approaching a mini-roundabout. The road is quiet. What must you do?
options: Pass round the central markings
Drive over the central markings
Give way to traffic from your left
Signal right whichever exit you take
questions.explain: All vehicles MUST pass round the central markings at a mini-roundabout, except large vehicles that are physically unable to. Approach it in the same way as a normal roundabout.

questions.q: You're approaching a double mini-roundabout. How should you deal with it?
options: Treat it as one large roundabout
Give way only at the first one
Treat each roundabout separately
Give way to traffic from the left
questions.explain: At double mini-roundabouts you should treat each roundabout separately and give way to traffic from the right.

questions.q: You're approaching a roundabout in an unfamiliar town. When should you decide which exit you need?
options: When you reach the give way line
As early as possible
Once you're on the roundabout
As you pass the exit before it
questions.explain: On the approach to a roundabout, decide as early as possible which exit you need, give an appropriate signal and get into the correct lane.

questions.q: You're approaching a junction with this sign and a solid white line across the road. You can see that the main road is clear. What must you do?
options: Slow down and drive on if it's clear
Stop only if traffic is coming
Stop behind the line, then go when safe
Stop with your front wheels on the line
questions.explain: At a 'Stop' sign with a solid white line across the road you MUST stop behind the line, even if the road looks clear. Wait for a safe gap in the traffic before you move off.

questions.q: You're about to emerge from a side road. There are broken white lines like these across the end of it. What must you do?
options: Give way to traffic on the main road
Stop, even if the road is clear
Expect main-road traffic to let you out
Give way only to traffic from the left
questions.explain: You MUST give way to traffic on the main road when emerging from a junction with broken white lines across the road. Only pull out when there's a safe gap.

questions.q: You're turning left into a side road. There's a bus lane on your left, and a bus is coming up in it from behind. What should you do?
options: Turn across the lane quickly
Stop in the bus lane and wait
Give way to the bus
Signal and expect the bus to stop
questions.explain: When turning, keep as close to the left as is safe and give way to any vehicles using a bus lane, cycle lane, cycle track or tramway from either direction.

questions.q: You're on a main road and want to turn right into a side road. There's no space marked for traffic turning right. Where should you position your car?
options: Just left of the middle of the road
Close to the left-hand kerb
On the right-hand side of the road
Straddling the centre line
questions.explain: Well before you turn right, check your mirrors, give a right-turn signal and take up a position just left of the middle of the road. Leave room for other vehicles to pass on the left if possible.

questions.q: You're waiting at traffic lights to go straight ahead across a box junction like this. The lights are green but your exit road is blocked. What should you do?
options: Enter the box and wait there
Sound your horn at the traffic ahead
Wait until your exit road is clear
Enter if the traffic ahead is moving
questions.explain: You MUST NOT enter a box junction until your exit road or lane is clear. The only exception is when you're turning right and are stopped only by oncoming traffic or other vehicles waiting to turn right.

questions.q: You're driving through a housing estate and approach crossroads with no signs or road markings. Who has priority?
options: Traffic coming from the right
Traffic on the wider road
Vehicles going straight ahead
Nobody has priority
questions.explain: At unmarked junctions nobody has priority. Look all around before emerging, and only cross when there's a gap large enough to do so safely.

questions.q: You're approaching a mini-roundabout. Compared with a normal roundabout, what should you remember?
options: You don't need to signal at all
Traffic from the left has priority
Cars may drive over the centre
There's less space and time to signal
questions.explain: Approach a mini-roundabout in the same way as a normal roundabout, but remember there's less space to manoeuvre and less time to signal. All vehicles MUST pass round the central markings, except large vehicles that can't.

questions.q: You're towing a trailer and want to turn right across a dual carriageway. The central reservation isn't deep enough for the length of your car and trailer. What should you do?
options: Wait in the central gap, partly blocking a lane
Wait until you can cross both halves in one go
Cross the first half, then stop in the right lane
Switch on your hazard lights and edge out
questions.explain: Before crossing or turning right onto a dual carriageway, check whether the central reservation is deep enough to protect the full length of your vehicle. If it's too shallow, wait until you can cross both carriageways in one go.

questions.q: You're crossing a dual carriageway from a side road. The central reservation is deep enough to protect your whole car. Where should you wait for a gap in the traffic on the second half?
options: In the right-hand lane of the first half
Just over the give way line of the second half
On the grass verge beside the main road
In the central reservation
questions.explain: If the central reservation is deep enough to protect the full length of your vehicle, treat each half of the dual carriageway as a separate road. Wait in the central reservation until there's a safe gap on the second half.

questions.q: You're approaching traffic lights that have been green for some time. They change to amber. When may you carry on?
options: If you can get through before red
If no pedestrians are waiting
If stopping might cause a collision
If the road beyond is clear
questions.explain: Amber means stop at the stop line. You may go on only if you've already crossed the stop line or are so close to it that stopping might cause a collision.

questions.q: You're waiting at a red traffic light. A green arrow pointing right lights up alongside it, as shown. You want to turn right. What does the green arrow mean?
options: You must wait for the full green light
You may go right if the way is clear
You may go in any direction if clear
You must wait until the red goes out
questions.explain: A green arrow means you may go in the direction it shows, if the way is clear, whatever other lights are showing. Give other traffic, especially cyclists, time and room to move into the correct lane.

questions.q: You're approaching traffic lights and want to go straight ahead. The left-hand lane is a filter lane with a green arrow pointing left. What should you do?
options: Keep out of the filter lane
Use the filter lane to pass the queue
Use it, then move right at the junction
Wait in the filter lane for full green
questions.explain: A green filter arrow indicates a filter lane only. Don't enter that lane unless you want to go in the direction of the arrow.

questions.q: You're approaching a junction with an advanced stop line for cyclists. The lights turn red before you reach the first white line. Where must you stop?
options: At the second white line
At the first white line
In the cyclists' waiting area
As close to the lights as possible
questions.explain: You MUST stop at the first white line if the lights are amber or red, and avoid encroaching on the area marked for cyclists. You only stop at the second line if you'd already crossed the first when the lights turned red.

questions.q: You're approaching a junction where the traffic lights aren't working. What should you do?
options: Assume you have priority if going straight
Wait until the lights are working again
Sound your horn and drive straight on
Treat it as an unmarked junction
questions.explain: If the traffic lights aren't working, treat the situation as you would an unmarked junction, where nobody has priority, and proceed with great care.

questions.q: You're behind a slow-moving car on a road with double white lines like these. The line nearest to you is solid. What should you do?
options: Overtake if the road ahead is clear
Overtake if it's doing under 30 mph
Stay behind the car
Straddle the lines to see ahead
questions.explain: You MUST NOT overtake if you'd have to cross or straddle double white lines with a solid line nearest to you. The exceptions are passing a stationary vehicle, or overtaking a cycle, horse or road maintenance vehicle travelling at 10 mph or less.

questions.q: You're following a slow tractor along a country road. Where should you NOT overtake it?
options: On a straight road with a clear view
Where the road ahead is wide and empty
Where you can see a long way ahead
Approaching the brow of a hill
questions.explain: Don't overtake if there's any doubt, or where you can't see far enough ahead to be sure it's safe, such as when approaching a bend, a hump bridge or the brow of a hill.

questions.q: You're driving along a single carriageway road. When may you overtake the vehicle in front on the left?
options: When it's signalling right and there's room
When it's travelling below the speed limit
When its driver waves you through
When it's slowing for a hazard ahead
questions.explain: You should only overtake on the left if the vehicle in front is signalling to turn right and there's room to do so.

questions.q: You need to stop briefly to let a passenger out. The only space is a taxi bay shown by signs and road markings. What does the law say?
options: You MUST NOT stop or park in it
You may stop to set down a passenger
You may stop there for up to 2 minutes
You may stop there outside rush hour
questions.explain: You MUST NOT stop or park in taxi bays, as indicated by upright signs and markings. Find a safe, legal place to stop instead.

questions.q: You want to overtake a slow vehicle, but you'd have to drive in a bus lane during its hours of operation. What does the law say?
options: You may if no buses are coming
You MUST NOT overtake
You may if it's only for a short way
You may if you signal first
questions.explain: You MUST NOT overtake if you would have to enter a lane reserved for buses, trams or cycles during its hours of operation.

questions.q: You're parking in a residential street near a junction. There are no marked parking spaces. You shouldn't park within what distance of the junction?
options: 5 metres (16 feet)
15 metres (49 feet)
10 metres (32 feet)
20 metres (66 feet)
questions.explain: Don't stop or park opposite or within 10 metres (32 feet) of a junction, except in an authorised parking space.

questions.q: You want to drop off a passenger close to a zebra crossing. There are white zig-zag lines on the approach to it. What's the rule?
options: You must not stop or park on them
You may stop briefly to let them out
You may park there for up to 2 minutes
You may stop if you switch on hazard lights
questions.explain: You MUST NOT stop or park on a pedestrian crossing or in the area marked by the zig-zag lines. Find a safe and legal place further away.

questions.q: You've found a parking space on the road, but it's directly opposite a traffic island. What should you do?
options: Park there with your hazard lights on
Park there, as it isn't a junction
Find somewhere else to park
Park partly on the pavement instead
questions.explain: Don't stop or park opposite a traffic island. Other places to avoid include bends, near the brow of a hill and within 10 metres of a junction, except in an authorised parking space.

questions.q: You're collecting a friend in town and need to stop for a few minutes. Which of these places should you avoid?
options: A marked parking bay
An off-street car park
Near a bus stop
A lay-by
questions.explain: Don't stop or park at or near a bus or tram stop or taxi rank. Use off-street parking areas or marked parking bays wherever possible.

questions.q: You've found a space to park, but the kerb there has been lowered to help wheelchair users. What should you do?
options: Park there, as it's easy to get out
Find somewhere else to park
Park there for a few minutes only
Park there if you're not blocking traffic
questions.explain: Don't stop or park where the kerb has been lowered to help wheelchair users and powered mobility vehicles. In Scotland you MUST NOT park where the kerb has been lowered to help pedestrians or cyclists.

questions.q: You're driving in London and the only space you can find is partly on the pavement. What's the rule?
options: You must not park partly or wholly on it
You may park with two wheels on it
You may park there for up to 30 minutes
You may park there with hazards on
questions.explain: You MUST NOT park partially or wholly on the pavement in London or Scotland, except in limited circumstances. Pavement parking can seriously inconvenience pedestrians, wheelchair users and people with prams or pushchairs.

questions.q: You're parking on a road at night. You're not in a recognised parking space. What must you NOT do?
options: Park close to the kerb on your side
Park facing against the traffic flow
Park under or near a street light
Switch off your headlights and engine
questions.explain: You MUST NOT park on a road at night facing against the direction of the traffic flow unless you're in a recognised parking space.

questions.q: You park your car at night in a lay-by on a road with a 50 mph speed limit. What must you do?
options: Leave your parking lights on
Switch off all your lights
Leave your dipped headlights on
Leave your hazard lights flashing
questions.explain: All vehicles MUST display parking lights when parked on a road, or in a lay-by on a road, with a speed limit greater than 30 mph.

questions.q: You're leaving your car overnight on a road with a 30 mph limit. It isn't in a parking place or lay-by. Where may you leave it without lights?
options: Within 10 metres of a junction, close to the kerb
At least 10 metres from a junction, facing against the traffic
At least 10 metres from a junction, facing with the traffic
Anywhere under a street light, facing either way
questions.explain: On a road with a speed limit of 30 mph or less, a car may be parked without lights if it's at least 10 metres (32 feet) from any junction, close to the kerb and facing in the direction of the traffic flow.

questions.q: You're driving along a main road and pass this sign. What does it tell you that you must NOT do?
options: Stop on the road
Overtake other vehicles
Drive faster than 30 mph
Turn into side roads
questions.explain: This sign means no stopping (clearway). You MUST NOT stop or park on a clearway.

questions.q: You're driving through a town centre and see this sign. During the times shown, when may you stop on this road?
options: To load or unload goods from a van
For up to 20 minutes if you stay with it
Whenever you can find a free space
Only to set down or pick up passengers
questions.explain: On an urban clearway you MUST NOT stop within its hours of operation, except for as long as necessary to pick up or set down passengers.

questions.q: You see this sign by some parking bays. You don't have a permit. What should you do?
options: Park for up to 20 minutes
Park if you're only loading
Park if the bays are empty
Park somewhere else
questions.explain: You MUST NOT park in parking spaces reserved for specific users, such as permit holders, residents, Blue Badge holders or motorcycles, unless you're entitled to do so.

questions.q: You realise you're going the wrong way along a busy main road. What's the safest way to turn round?
options: Make a U-turn across the main road
Do a three-point turn in the main road
Reverse back along the main road
Drive round a block of side streets
questions.explain: If you need to turn your vehicle round, wait until you find a safe place. Try not to reverse or turn round in a busy road; find a quiet side road or drive round a block of side streets.

questions.q: You're about to park on your driveway, which opens onto a busy road. What does the Highway Code advise?
options: Drive in and reverse out later
Reverse in so you can drive out
Drive in and turn round in the road
Whichever way is quickest for you
questions.explain: When using a driveway, reverse in and drive out if you can. You also shouldn't reverse from a side road into a main road.

questions.q: You're reversing your car into a quiet side road. How far are you allowed to reverse?
options: No further than necessary
No more than 10 metres
As far as you like if it's clear
No more than two car lengths
questions.explain: You MUST NOT reverse your vehicle further than necessary. Look all around before and while reversing, and give way to any pedestrians who may be crossing.

questions.q: You've missed your turning and are approaching a mini-roundabout. You're thinking of making a U-turn there. What does the Highway Code advise?
options: U-turns are best made at mini-roundabouts
Only make a U-turn if you signal right
Avoid making U-turns at mini-roundabouts
U-turns are fine if you drive over the centre
questions.explain: Avoid making U-turns at mini-roundabouts, where there's less space to manoeuvre and less time to signal. Beware of other drivers doing this.

questions.q: You're waiting at a level crossing. A train passes, but the red lights keep flashing. What must you do?
options: Cross, as the train has passed
Keep waiting, as another train is coming
Zig-zag round the barriers if it's clear
Phone the signal operator, then cross
questions.explain: You MUST wait if a train goes by and the red lights continue to flash. This means another train will be passing soon. Only cross when the lights go off and the barriers open.

questions.q: You're driving over a level crossing. You've just crossed the white line when the amber light comes on. What should you do?
options: Stop on the crossing and wait
Reverse back behind the white line
Keep going and clear the crossing
Stop and switch on hazard lights
questions.explain: Keep going if you've already crossed the white line when the amber light comes on. Don't reverse onto or over a controlled crossing.

questions.q: You're driving on a single carriageway road that has four lanes. Which lanes should you use?
options: Only those signs or markings show
Any lane that's clear of traffic
The two lanes nearest the kerb
Whichever lane is moving fastest
questions.explain: Where a single carriageway has four or more lanes, use only the lanes that signs or markings indicate.

questions.q: You come to a level crossing with user-operated gates and small red and green lights. When may you cross?
options: When the red light is showing
When you can't see a train coming
After sounding your horn twice
Only when the green light is on
questions.explain: You MUST NOT cross when the red light is showing; only cross if the green light is on. Open the gates on both sides, check the green light is still on, cross quickly and close the gates when you're clear.

questions.q: Traffic is moving slowly over a level crossing ahead of you. The road on the far side is congested. What should you do?
options: Follow the car in front closely
Wait until it's clear on the other side
Stop on the crossing if the lights are off
Drive onto the crossing and wait there
questions.explain: Never drive onto a level crossing until the road is clear on the other side, and don't get too close to the car in front. Never stop or park on, or near, a crossing.

questions.q: You're approaching a zebra crossing. A pedestrian is waiting on the pavement to cross. What should you do?
options: Wave them across in front of you
Flash your headlights at them
Sound your horn to warn them
Slow down and give way to them
questions.explain: Be ready to slow down or stop, and give way to pedestrians waiting to cross. Don't wave, flash your lights or use your horn to invite them across, as this could be dangerous if another vehicle is approaching.

questions.q: You've stopped at a pelican crossing. The red light changes to flashing amber. What does this mean?
options: You must wait for the green light
It's about to change back to red
You may go if the crossing is clear
Pedestrians must now give way to you
questions.explain: At a pelican crossing, flashing amber follows the red light. You MUST give way to any pedestrians on the crossing, but if there's no one on it you may proceed with caution.

questions.q: You've overtaken using the right-hand lane of a three-lane dual carriageway. What should you do next?
options: Stay in the right-hand lane
Return to the middle, then the left lane
Cut straight across to the left lane
Stay in the middle lane from now on
questions.explain: On a dual carriageway with three or more lanes, you may use the middle lanes or the right-hand lane to overtake, but you should return to the middle lanes and then the left-hand lane when it's safe.

questions.q: When are you allowed to drive on or over a pavement?
options: To get past a queue of traffic
To let a bus pass on a narrow road
To reach a property or in an emergency
To park there for a short time
questions.explain: You MUST NOT drive on or over a pavement, footpath or bridleway except to gain lawful access to property, or in the case of an emergency.

questions.q: You're approaching a puffin crossing, but its lights aren't working. What should you do?
options: Drive through, as it's out of use
Expect pedestrians to wait for you
Stop and wait until it's repaired
Proceed with extreme caution
questions.explain: If a signal-controlled crossing isn't working, proceed with extreme caution. Don't enter the crossing if you can't completely clear it.

questions.q: You want to pull up on the left just after a side road. When should you signal left?
options: As you're passing the side road
Before you reach the side road
Only after you've stopped
There's no need to signal
questions.explain: Make sure your signals won't confuse others. If you want to stop after a side road, don't signal until you're passing it; signalling earlier may make others think you're turning into it.

questions.q: You're on a busy road and have signalled to move into the next lane. What should you remember?
options: Other drivers must now let you in
You needn't check your mirrors again
You should leave your signal on afterwards
Your signal doesn't give you priority
questions.explain: Signalling doesn't give you priority. Only move over when it's safe, and cancel your signal after use.

questions.q: Road markings show that you can join a roundabout without giving way. What should you still do?
options: Look to the right before joining
Stop at the line before joining
Sound your horn as you join
Signal left as you join
questions.explain: Check whether road markings allow you to enter the roundabout without giving way. If so, proceed, but still look to the right before joining.

questions.q: A police car behind you is flashing its blue lights, and the officer points for you to pull over. What must you do?
options: Stop straight away, wherever you are
Stop when safe and turn off the engine
Speed up so the police car can pass
Keep going until you find a car park
questions.explain: If the police want to stop your vehicle, you MUST pull over and stop as soon as it's safe to do so. Then switch off your engine.

questions.q: A vehicle in front of you is flashing amber lights. A Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) officer in it is signalling for you to follow. What should you do?
options: Overtake it as soon as it's safe
Ignore it, as only police can stop you
Follow it to a safe place to stop
Stop immediately in the road
questions.explain: DVSA officers have the power to stop vehicles on all roads. Flashing amber lights from the front mean they want you to follow them to a safe place to stop, and it's an offence not to comply.

questions.q: You're driving on a motorway in England. Uniformed traffic officers want to stop you because your roof load looks insecure. How will they usually attract your attention?
options: Flashing blue lights and sounding a siren
Flashing amber lights, usually from behind
Flashing green lights from in front of you
A red flag waved from the hard shoulder
questions.explain: Traffic officers can stop vehicles on most motorways and some 'A' class roads in England and Wales. They'll usually flash amber lights from behind and direct you to pull over; you MUST then stop when it's safe and switch off your engine.

questions.q: You're driving on a motorway at 70 mph in good, dry conditions. What is the typical overall stopping distance?
options: 53 metres (175 feet)
73 metres (240 feet)
96 metres (315 feet)
36 metres (118 feet)
questions.explain: At 70 mph on a dry road the typical overall stopping distance is 96 metres (315 feet): 21 metres thinking distance plus 75 metres braking distance. That's about twenty-four car lengths.

questions.q: You're driving along a dry street with a 30 mph speed limit. What is the typical overall stopping distance at 30 mph?
options: 12 metres
36 metres
9 metres
23 metres
questions.explain: At 30 mph the typical overall stopping distance is 23 metres (75 feet): 9 metres thinking distance plus 14 metres braking distance, or about six car lengths.

questions.q: You're driving at 50 mph on a dry road when a hazard appears ahead. What is the typical thinking distance at this speed?
options: 15 metres
12 metres
38 metres
18 metres
questions.explain: At 50 mph the typical thinking distance is 15 metres. The braking distance adds a further 38 metres, giving a typical overall stopping distance of 53 metres (175 feet).

questions.q: You're travelling at 60 mph on a dry single carriageway. What is the typical braking distance at this speed, not counting thinking distance?
options: 73 metres
55 metres
38 metres
18 metres
questions.explain: At 60 mph the typical braking distance is 55 metres. Add the 18 metres thinking distance and the typical overall stopping distance is 73 metres (240 feet).

questions.q: You're driving at 40 mph on a dry road. What is the typical overall stopping distance?
options: 23 metres
24 metres
36 metres
53 metres
questions.explain: At 40 mph the typical overall stopping distance is 36 metres (118 feet): 12 metres thinking distance plus 24 metres braking distance, or about nine car lengths.

questions.q: You're on a dry dual carriageway at 60 mph. Taking an average car length as 4 metres, about how many car lengths is your typical overall stopping distance?
options: Nine
Thirteen
Twenty-four
Eighteen
questions.explain: At 60 mph the typical overall stopping distance is 73 metres (240 feet), or about eighteen car lengths. The safe rule is never to get closer than the overall stopping distance to the vehicle in front.

questions.q: The Highway Code's typical stopping distances are only a general guide. Which factor does it say your thinking distance depends on?
options: The condition of your brakes
The road surface
Your attention
The type of tyres fitted
questions.explain: The stopping distances diagram says the distance will depend on your attention (thinking distance), the road surface, the weather conditions and the condition of your vehicle at the time.

questions.q: You're following another car on a fast road. What does the Highway Code give as the safe rule for how close you should get?
options: Never closer than the typical braking distance
Never closer than the overall stopping distance
Never closer than the typical thinking distance
Never closer than three car lengths away
questions.explain: Leave enough space to pull up safely if the vehicle in front suddenly slows down or stops. The safe rule is never to get closer than the overall stopping distance.

questions.q: You're driving on a dry, high-speed road. What is the minimum time gap you should leave between you and the vehicle in front?
options: One second
Half a second
Four seconds
Two seconds
questions.explain: You should allow at least a two-second gap on high-speed roads and in tunnels where visibility is reduced. Use a fixed point, such as a sign, to help you measure it.

questions.q: It's raining and you're driving on a dual carriageway. In the dry you'd leave a two-second gap. What gap should you now leave?
options: At least four seconds
About three seconds
Two seconds is still enough
About one second
questions.explain: The two-second gap should be at least doubled on wet roads. In wet weather stopping distances will be at least double those on dry roads, because your tyres have less grip.

questions.q: You're driving on an icy road. Compared with a dry road, how much greater might your gap from the vehicle in front need to be?
options: Up to twice as great
Up to ten times greater
Up to four times greater
About the same
questions.explain: The gap should be up to ten times greater on icy roads. Stopping distances can be ten times greater than on dry roads, so keep well back from the road user in front.

questions.q: You're driving through a tunnel and the traffic ahead comes to a stop. What is the minimum gap you should leave between you and the vehicle in front?
options: 2 metres
10 metres
5 metres
20 metres
questions.explain: If you have to stop in a tunnel, leave at least a 5-metre gap between you and the vehicle in front. While moving, allow at least a two-second gap, as visibility in tunnels is reduced.

questions.q: Your passenger says the driver behind you is tailgating. What does tailgating mean?
options: Driving with the rear fog lights on
Overtaking a vehicle on its left
Towing a trailer that sways
Following too closely to stop safely
questions.explain: Tailgating is where the gap between you and the vehicle in front is too small for you to stop safely if it suddenly brakes. It's dangerous, intimidating and can cause collisions, especially at speed.

questions.q: You're driving at 20 mph on a dry road. What's the typical overall stopping distance?
options: 6 metres
12 metres
23 metres
9 metres
questions.explain: At 20 mph the typical overall stopping distance is 12 metres (40 feet): 6 metres thinking distance plus 6 metres braking distance, or about three car lengths.

questions.q: Which of these does the Highway Code say need a greater distance to stop than a car?
options: Cars with no passengers
Cars with automatic gearboxes
Large vehicles and motorcycles
Cars that have ABS fitted
questions.explain: Remember, large vehicles and motorcycles need a greater distance to stop. Leave enough space so that you can pull up safely if the vehicle in front suddenly slows down or stops.

questions.q: You're driving through heavy rain when the steering suddenly feels unresponsive. What should you do?
options: Ease off and slow down gradually
Brake hard to slow down quickly
Steer sharply to regain grip
Accelerate to get through the water
questions.explain: If the steering becomes unresponsive in wet weather, it probably means that water is preventing the tyres from gripping the road. Ease off the accelerator and slow down gradually.

questions.q: You're driving on a wet road and pass a fuel station. Why should you be aware of spilt diesel on the road?
options: It makes your brakes overheat
It damages your tyre sidewalls
It causes your engine to stall
It makes the road very slippery
questions.explain: Spilt diesel makes the road surface very slippery, as it significantly reduces the grip between tyres and the road. It's especially dangerous for motorcyclists.

questions.q: The local forecast warns of snow and ice overnight. You'd planned to drive somewhere the next morning. What should you do?
options: Drive as normal once the roads are gritted
Drive only if your journey is essential
Lower your tyre pressures for extra grip
Follow other vehicles' tracks closely
questions.explain: Don't drive in icy or snowy weather unless your journey is essential. If it is, take great care, allow more time and drive with care even if the roads have been treated.

questions.q: You have to drive on a road that is icy. Which of these is the safest way to drive?
options: Slowly, in the lowest gear possible
At a steady speed in neutral
Slowly, in as high a gear as possible
Briskly, to spend less time on the ice
questions.explain: When the roads are icy, drive at a slow speed in as high a gear as possible, and accelerate and brake very gently. Avoid sudden actions, as these could cause loss of control.

questions.q: You're approaching a bend on an icy road. When should you do your braking?
options: On the straight before the bend
As you start to steer into the bend
Halfway round the bend
As you leave the bend
questions.explain: Drive particularly slowly on bends, where loss of control is more likely. Brake progressively on the straight before you reach the bend, then steer smoothly round it, avoiding sudden actions.

questions.q: It's a freezing winter night and you notice your tyres are making almost no noise on the road. What could this mean?
options: The road is wet with rain
Your tyres are under-inflated
You're driving on ice
The road has just been gritted
questions.explain: When travelling on ice, tyres make virtually no noise. Steering that feels unresponsive may also mean ice, and that your vehicle is losing its grip on the road.

questions.q: You're planning to overtake a slow-moving vehicle. What does the Highway Code say about your position behind it?
options: Get as close as you can
Straddle the centre line
Drive with your hazards on
Don't get too close to it
questions.explain: Overtake only when it's safe and legal. Don't get too close to the vehicle you intend to overtake; use your mirrors, signal when it's safe and then start to move out.

questions.q: What usually causes a car to skid?
options: Braking early and lightly before bends
Keeping to a steady speed on the straight
Steering smoothly on a dry, level road
Harsh braking, accelerating or steering
questions.explain: Skidding is usually caused by the driver braking, accelerating or steering too harshly, or driving too fast for the road conditions.

questions.q: You're driving on a slippery road and the rear of your car skids to the right. What should you do?
options: Steer to the left
Brake firmly
Steer to the right
Pull the handbrake on
questions.explain: Turn the steering wheel in the direction of the skid. If the rear of the vehicle skids to the right, steer immediately to the right to recover.

questions.q: You brake too harshly on a wet bend and your car starts to skid. What should you do to remove the cause?
options: Press the brake pedal harder
Release the brake pedal fully
Apply the handbrake as well
Switch off the engine
questions.explain: If skidding occurs, remove the cause by releasing the brake pedal fully or easing off the accelerator. Then steer in the direction of the skid.

questions.q: Your car has anti-lock brakes (ABS) and you have to stop in an emergency. How should you use the footbrake?
options: Press firmly and keep the pressure on
Pump it on and off rapidly
Press gently, then use the handbrake
Press firmly, then release it quickly
questions.explain: In an emergency, apply the footbrake firmly and don't release the pressure until the vehicle has slowed to the desired speed. Otherwise, follow the advice in your vehicle handbook.

questions.q: You're driving a car fitted with anti-lock brakes on a wet road. What should you remember?
options: ABS lets you follow more closely
ABS may not shorten your stopping distance
ABS halves stopping distances in the wet
ABS stops the tyres losing grip in water
questions.explain: ABS should help you keep steering control, but don't assume a vehicle with ABS will stop in a shorter distance. On wet roads your gap should be at least doubled.

questions.q: It's an icy morning and you're approaching a zebra crossing where people are waiting to cross. What should you allow for?
options: More time to stop
Less time to stop
No need to slow down
Using your horn to warn them
questions.explain: As you approach a zebra crossing, look out for pedestrians waiting to cross and be ready to slow down or stop. Allow more time for stopping on wet or icy roads.

questions.q: You're driving along a dual carriageway and can see a bank of fog ahead. What should you do before you enter it?
options: Check your mirrors, then slow down
Speed up to get through it quickly
Brake sharply to warn drivers behind
Switch on your hazard warning lights
questions.explain: Before entering fog, check your mirrors, then slow down. Even if fog seems to be clearing, you can suddenly find yourself in thick fog.

questions.q: You see this sign on an exposed stretch of road. What does it warn you of?
options: Low bridge
Side winds
Road works
Ice
questions.explain: This sign warns of side winds. Strong gusts can blow a car, cyclist, motorcyclist or horse rider off course.

questions.q: You're driving on a motorway in fog. What speed should you be driving at?
options: Fast enough to keep up with the traffic around you
Slow enough to stop in the distance you can see
Fast enough to keep the lights ahead in view
Close to the limit so you aren't hit from behind
questions.explain: In fog you should be able to pull up well within the distance you can see clearly. This is particularly important on motorways and dual carriageways, as vehicles are travelling faster.

questions.q: You MUST use headlights when visibility is seriously reduced. What does 'seriously reduced' generally mean?
options: You can't see for more than 200 metres
You can't see for more than 300 metres
You can't see for more than 500 metres
You can't see for more than 100 metres
questions.explain: You MUST use headlights when visibility is seriously reduced, generally when you can't see for more than 100 metres (328 feet). You may also use fog lights, but you MUST switch them off when visibility improves.

questions.q: You've been using your front and rear fog lights in thick fog. The fog has now cleared. What MUST you do?
options: Switch them off
Leave them on until you park
Switch off only the front ones
Leave only the rear ones on
questions.explain: You MUST switch fog lights off when visibility improves. They dazzle other road users and can obscure your brake lights.

questions.q: You're towing a heavily loaded trailer. How could this affect your stopping distance?
options: It will be shorter than usual
It will stay about the same
It may increase significantly
It only changes in wet weather
questions.explain: When towing, be aware that your stopping distance may increase significantly. Leave more space between you and the vehicle in front.

questions.q: You're driving on a windy day. Where are strong gusts most likely to blow you off course?
options: In a sheltered residential street
On an open stretch of road
In a queue of slow-moving traffic
In a multi-storey car park
questions.explain: Strong gusts can blow vehicles off course on open stretches of road exposed to strong crosswinds, or when passing bridges or gaps in hedges.

questions.q: It's very windy. Ahead of you, a motorcyclist is overtaking a high-sided lorry. What should you do?
options: Stay close behind the motorcyclist
Overtake the motorcyclist straight away
Sound your horn to warn the rider
Keep well back from the motorcyclist
questions.explain: In very windy weather, turbulence created by large vehicles can affect other road users. Motorcyclists are particularly affected, so keep well back from them when they're overtaking a high-sided vehicle.

questions.q: You're about to overtake a cyclist on a day with strong winds. How much room should you give them?
options: Less than usual so you pass quickly
More than you would in calm weather
The same as you'd give a parked car
Just enough to clear their handlebars
questions.explain: Take extra care and give more space when overtaking cyclists, motorcyclists and horse riders in bad weather, including high winds, and at night. Gusts can blow them off course.

questions.q: It starts to rain after a long spell of hot, dry weather. What should you be aware of?
options: Your tyres will grip better
Your brakes will work better
The road may become slippery
Your stopping distance will shorten
questions.explain: If it rains after a dry spell, the road surface may become slippery. This could affect your steering and braking.

questions.q: You're on a long drive on a very hot day. Why should you keep your car well ventilated?
options: To avoid becoming drowsy
To stop the tyres overheating
To keep the brakes cool
To stop the engine overheating
questions.explain: In hot weather, keep your vehicle well ventilated to avoid drowsiness. If you're dazzled by bright sunlight, slow down and, if necessary, stop.

questions.q: Your driving instructor warns you not to coast. What does 'coasting' mean?
options: Slowing down by changing to a lower gear
Driving at a steady speed in top gear
Travelling in neutral or with the clutch down
Following close behind another vehicle
questions.explain: Coasting describes a vehicle travelling in neutral or with the clutch pressed down. It can reduce your control because engine braking is eliminated.

questions.q: You're driving down a steep hill. Why is it dangerous to coast in neutral?
options: Your speed will increase quickly
Your engine may overheat
Your fuel use will rise sharply
Your tyres will wear unevenly
questions.explain: Coasting eliminates engine braking, so your speed downhill will increase quickly. It can also affect steering response and make it harder to select the right gear when you need it.

questions.q: You're following a large lorry and would like to overtake it. Why should you drop back?
options: So you can build up speed before pulling out
So the lorry driver can speed up
So you can overtake on the left if needed
So you can see further ahead and be seen
questions.explain: Dropping back increases your ability to see ahead and should allow the driver of the large vehicle to see you in their mirrors. Getting too close will obscure your view of the road ahead.

questions.q: You're making an essential journey in snowy weather. How can you find out about conditions on the roads ahead?
options: Follow the vehicle in front
Watch other cars' brake lights
Phone the police on 101
Listen to travel bulletins
questions.explain: In icy or snowy weather, listen to travel bulletins and take note of variable message signs that may give information about weather, road and traffic conditions ahead.

questions.q: It's raining heavily. Which road users should you take extra care around?
options: Pedestrians, cyclists and horse riders
Cars that have their headlights on
Buses and coaches at bus stops
Lorries using the left-hand lane
questions.explain: In wet weather, take extra care around pedestrians, cyclists, motorcyclists and horse riders. Rain and spray can make it difficult to see and be seen.

questions.q: It's an icy day and you're behind a gritter that's spreading salt. What should you do?
options: Overtake it as soon as you can
Keep back and only overtake with care
Follow closely to use its tracks
Flash your lights so it pulls in
questions.explain: In icy or snowy weather, take care when overtaking vehicles spreading salt or other de-icer, particularly if you're riding a motorcycle or cycle.

questions.q: You're about to overtake a motorcyclist on a single carriageway. How much room should you give them?
options: Less than you'd give a car
Just enough to clear their mirror
Half the width of your lane
At least as much as you'd give a car
questions.explain: Give motorcyclists, cyclists, horse riders and horse-drawn vehicles at least as much room as you would when overtaking a car.

questions.q: It snowed overnight and you have to make an essential journey. What should you check before you set off?
options: That your tyre pressures are reduced
That your fuel tank is almost empty
That your route is clear of delays
That your rear fog lights are on
questions.explain: Before you set off in snowy weather, check your planned route is clear of delays and that no further snowfalls or severe weather are predicted.
