questions.q: You're approaching the start of a contraflow system at road works. Why should you slow down and increase your distance from the vehicle in front?
options: The lanes will be wider than normal
Changes in road camber may affect stability
Speed cameras are only used at the start
The road surface will always be wet
questions.explain: In a contraflow you may be in a narrower lane than normal with no permanent barrier between you and oncoming traffic. At the start and finish, slow down and increase your distance from the vehicle in front, as changes in camber may affect vehicle stability.

questions.q: You're driving through road works where the lanes are narrower than normal. What should you do?
options: Overtake queuing traffic to get through
Keep close to the vehicle in front
Keep a safe distance and watch the lane edges
Straddle the lanes to give yourself room
questions.explain: Narrow lanes at road works are marked by studs or temporary road markings. Keep a safe distance from the vehicle in front and make sure you can clearly see the edges of the lane ahead.

questions.q: You're driving through road works with grit and mud on the road surface. Which road users are most at risk of skidding?
options: Drivers of large lorries
Cyclists and motorcyclists
Drivers of buses and coaches
Drivers of four-wheel-drive cars
questions.explain: Take extra care near cyclists and motorcyclists at road works, as they are vulnerable to skidding on grit, mud or other debris.

questions.q: You're checking your car's tyres before a long journey. What's the minimum legal tread depth for car tyres?
options: 1 mm
2 mm
1.6 mm
3 mm
questions.explain: Cars, light vans and light trailers MUST have a tread depth of at least 1.6 mm across the central three-quarters of the breadth of the tread and around the entire circumference.

questions.q: You're measuring the tread depth on your car's tyres. Over which part of the tyre must the legal minimum depth be met?
options: Central three-quarters of the tread, around the whole tyre
Central half of the tread, around the whole tyre
Outer edges of the tread, around the whole tyre
Central three-quarters of the tread, on one section only
questions.explain: Car tyres MUST have a tread depth of at least 1.6 mm across the central three-quarters of the breadth of the tread and around the entire circumference.

questions.q: You're about to check your tyre pressures at home. When should you do this to get an accurate reading?
options: Straight after a motorway journey
While the engine is running
When the tyres are warm
When the tyres are cold
questions.explain: You should check tyre pressures before your journey, when the tyres are cold. Warm or hot tyres may give a misleading reading.

questions.q: You use your car every day to get to work. How often should you check the tyre pressures?
options: Every week
Once a month
At every service
Only before an MOT
questions.explain: You should check your tyre pressures weekly. Do this before your journey, when the tyres are cold.

questions.q: Your car's tyres are under-inflated. What could this affect?
options: Your windscreen demisters
Your braking and steering
Your engine temperature
Your fuel gauge reading
questions.explain: Your brakes and steering will be adversely affected by under-inflated or over-inflated tyres. You should keep them inflated to the vehicle manufacturer's specification.

questions.q: You notice that your car's tyres are wearing unevenly. What's the most likely cause?
options: Using a different brand of fuel
Checking the pressures when cold
A fault in the brakes or suspension
Driving mainly on motorways
questions.explain: Excessive or uneven tyre wear may be caused by faults in the braking or suspension systems, or wheels that are out of alignment. You should have these faults corrected as soon as possible.

questions.q: You're driving along a dual carriageway when one of your tyres suddenly bursts. What should you do?
options: Brake hard to stop as quickly as possible
Steer sharply onto the verge at once
Switch off the engine straight away
Hold the wheel firmly and roll to a stop
questions.explain: If a tyre bursts while you're driving, try to keep control of your vehicle. Grip the steering wheel firmly and allow the vehicle to roll to a stop at the side of the road.

questions.q: You're stopped by the police and one of your car's tyres is found to be defective. How many penalty points could you get?
options: None
questions.explain: Some vehicle defects can attract penalty points. Using a vehicle with defective tyres carries 3 penalty points.

questions.q: Your car pulls to one side every time you brake. What's the most likely cause?
options: Low engine oil or coolant levels
A brake fault or wrong tyre pressures
Too much fuel in the tank
A weak or flat car battery
questions.explain: If your vehicle pulls to one side when braking, it's most likely to be a brake fault or incorrectly inflated tyres. You should consult a garage or mechanic immediately.

questions.q: You push down on the front of your car and it keeps bouncing up and down. What does this tell you?
options: The tyres are over-inflated
The brake fluid is low
The shock absorbers are worn
The steering lock is on
questions.explain: If your vehicle continues to bounce after you push down on the front or rear, its shock absorbers are worn. Worn shock absorbers can seriously affect the operation of a vehicle and should be replaced.

questions.q: You check under the bonnet and find that the brake fluid level is low. Why is this dangerous?
options: It could result in brake failure
It could flatten the battery
It could cause the engine to overheat
It could make the fuel gauge fail
questions.explain: You should check the fluid levels in your vehicle at least weekly. Low brake fluid may result in brake failure and a crash.

questions.q: You turn the ignition key and several warning lights come on. What should normally happen when the engine starts?
options: They all stay on until you move off
They go out, except the handbrake light
They flash until the engine warms up
They stay on for the first few miles
questions.explain: When you turn the ignition key, warning lights come on but go out when the engine starts (except the handbrake warning light). If they don't, stop and investigate, as you could have a serious fault.

questions.q: You're driving a car with ABS and have to brake hard. What should the ABS help you to do?
options: Always stop in a shorter distance
Keep control of the steering
Brake later on wet roads
Drive closer to the car ahead
questions.explain: ABS should ensure that you keep steering control, but you shouldn't assume that a vehicle with ABS will stop in a shorter distance.

questions.q: Your car is covered in mud after a trip down country lanes. Which of these MUST you keep clean and clear?
options: Lights, reflectors and number plates
The bumpers and the wheel arches
The roof, bonnet and boot lid
The wheels, tyres and door sills
questions.explain: Lights, indicators, reflectors and number plates MUST be kept clean and clear. Windscreens and windows MUST also be kept clean and free from obstructions to vision.

questions.q: You're buying a used car that has tinted glass. On which windows is there no legal limit to how dark the tint can be?
options: The windscreen
The driver's side window
The front passenger window
The rear passenger windows
questions.explain: You MUST NOT use a vehicle with excessively dark tinting on the windscreen or the front windows either side of the driver. There are no limits for rear windscreens or rear passenger windows.

questions.q: You're driving along when a warning light comes on in your instrument panel. What should you do?
options: Ignore it unless the car feels different
Stop and investigate the problem
Wait until the next service to check it
Switch the engine off and on to reset it
questions.explain: You shouldn't ignore warning lights, as they could indicate a dangerous fault developing. If one comes on while you're driving, stop and investigate the problem, as you could have a serious fault.

questions.q: While you're driving, the battery charge warning light comes on. What could this mean?
options: The engine oil needs changing
The tyre pressures are too low
The battery may not be charging
The handbrake is partly on
questions.explain: If the charge warning light comes on while you're driving, it may mean the battery isn't charging. You should have it checked as soon as possible to avoid losing power to the lights and other electrical systems.

questions.q: Your engine has overheated and you've stopped in a safe place. When should you add coolant?
options: Once the engine has cooled naturally
Straight away, while the engine is hot
After pouring cold water over the engine
As soon as the steam has stopped
questions.explain: If your engine overheats, you should wait until it has cooled naturally. Only then remove the coolant filler cap and add water or other coolant.

questions.q: While you're driving, you notice a smell of burning rubber. What should you do?
options: Ignore it unless smoke appears
Wait until your next service
Investigate it straight away
Open the windows and drive on
questions.explain: If your vehicle smells of anything unusual, such as burning rubber, petrol or an electrical fault, investigate immediately. Don't risk a fire.

questions.q: Winter is on its way. What should you make sure of before the cold weather starts?
options: The tyres are over-inflated for extra grip
The battery is well maintained
The screenwash is plain water only
The fuel tank is kept half empty
questions.explain: Before winter, you should make sure the battery is well maintained and that there are appropriate anti-freeze agents in your radiator and windscreen bottle.

questions.q: You notice that diesel has been spilt across the road at a roundabout. Which road users are particularly at risk?
options: Lorry drivers
Tractor drivers
Bus passengers
Motorcyclists
questions.explain: Diesel spillage is dangerous to other road users, particularly motorcyclists, as it significantly reduces the grip between the tyres and the road surface.

questions.q: You've stopped at a petrol station to fill up. What should you never do on the forecourt?
options: Use a mobile phone
Check your tyre pressures
Pay by card at the pump
Clean your windscreen
questions.explain: You should never smoke, or use a mobile phone, on the forecourt of a petrol station. These are major fire risks and could cause an explosion.

questions.q: Your car's exhaust is giving out a lot of smoke. What does the law say about exhaust emissions?
options: They only apply to diesel cars
They MUST NOT exceed prescribed levels
They're only checked when a car is new
They don't matter if the car is taxed
questions.explain: Exhaust emissions MUST NOT exceed prescribed levels. The MOT test checks that your vehicle meets road safety and environmental standards.

questions.q: You're driving with your 10-year-old nephew in the back seat. Who's legally responsible for making sure he's correctly restrained?
options: His parents
You, the driver
The front-seat passenger
Your nephew himself
questions.explain: The driver MUST make sure that all children under 14 years of age wear seat belts or sit in an approved child restraint where required.

questions.q: You're giving a lift to a 15-year-old who refuses to wear a seat belt. Who's legally responsible for them wearing it?
options: You, the driver
The passenger's parents
The car's owner
The passenger
questions.explain: Passengers aged 14 and over are responsible for wearing their own seat belt. The driver is responsible for passengers under 14.

questions.q: You're about to make a manoeuvre in your car. In which situation don't you need to wear a seat belt?
options: When driving below 20 mph
When your car has airbags
When you're reversing
When on a short local journey
questions.explain: You must wear a seat belt if one is fitted, but there are a few exceptions. One is when you're a driver who is reversing, or supervising a learner driver who is reversing.

questions.q: Your passenger is pregnant. What does the law say about her wearing a seat belt?
options: She must, unless her doctor says otherwise
She doesn't need one after six months
She only needs to wear one on motorways
She can choose whether or not to wear one
questions.explain: You must wear a seat belt if you're pregnant, unless your doctor says you don't have to for medical reasons.

questions.q: You own a classic car that was originally made without seat belts. Which passengers aren't you allowed to carry in it?
options: Children under 14 years old
Passengers over 70 years old
Children under 3 years old
Adults in the back seats
questions.explain: If your vehicle was originally made without seat belts, you're not allowed to carry children under 3 years old in it. Children over 3 are only allowed to sit in the back seats.

questions.q: You're driving your young daughter to school. Until when must she normally use a child car seat, whichever comes first?
options: Until 10 years old or 125 cm tall
Until 14 years old or 150 cm tall
Until 8 years old or 120 cm tall
Until 12 years old or 135 cm tall
questions.explain: Children must normally use a child car seat until they're 12 years old or 135 centimetres tall, whichever comes first.

questions.q: You want to fit a rear-facing baby seat in the front passenger seat. What MUST you do first?
options: Deactivate the front airbag
Move the seat fully forward
Put a booster cushion under it
Recline the passenger seat
questions.explain: A rear-facing baby seat MUST NOT be fitted into a seat protected by an active frontal airbag, as in a crash it can cause serious injury or death to the child.

questions.q: You're using a height-based child car seat for your baby. When can your child start using a forward-facing seat?
options: When they're over 6 months old
When they're over 15 months old
When they're over 9 months old
When they're over 3 years old
questions.explain: Height-based seats must be rear facing until your child is over 15 months old. After that, your child can use a forward-facing child car seat.

questions.q: You take a licensed taxi with your 5-year-old son, but the driver doesn't have a child car seat. How should your son travel?
options: On your lap in the back seat
In the front seat with an adult belt
In a rear seat with an adult belt
In a rear seat without a belt
questions.explain: If a taxi driver doesn't provide the correct child car seat, children can travel without one, but only on a rear seat. A child aged 3 or older must wear an adult seat belt.

questions.q: You have to make an unexpected but necessary short journey with a friend's 6-year-old, and you don't have the right child seat. What does the law allow?
options: The child can travel in the front without a belt
The child can use an adult seat belt
The child can share a belt with an adult
The child can sit on an adult's lap
questions.explain: If the correct child car seat isn't available, a child aged 3 or older can use an adult seat belt if the journey is unexpected, necessary and over a short distance.

questions.q: You're carrying young children in the back of your car. What should you do to help keep them safe?
options: Let them get out on the traffic side
Let them sit behind the rear seats
Open the rear windows fully
Use the child safety door locks
questions.explain: You should use the child safety door locks, where fitted, when children are in the vehicle. Children should get in through the door nearest the kerb and shouldn't sit behind the rear seats of an estate or hatchback unless a special child seat is fitted.

questions.q: You're adjusting your driving position before setting off. Why should the head restraint be properly adjusted?
options: To help you see into the blind spots
To keep you alert on long journeys
To help prevent neck and spine injuries
To make it easier to reach the pedals
questions.explain: Head restraints should be properly adjusted to reduce the risk of neck and spine injuries in the event of a collision. You should adjust them, along with your seat, seat belt and mirrors, before you drive.

questions.q: You're driving home in the evening. Between which times MUST your sidelights and rear registration plate lights be lit?
options: Between 7 pm and 7 am
Between sunset and sunrise
Between midnight and 6 am
Only on roads without street lights
questions.explain: You MUST make sure all sidelights and rear registration plate lights are lit between sunset and sunrise.

questions.q: You're planning an evening journey in winter. The Highway Code defines night (the hours of darkness) as which period?
options: From sunset until sunrise
Half an hour after sunset to half an hour before sunrise
One hour after sunset to one hour before sunrise
Two hours after sunset to two hours before sunrise
questions.explain: Night (the hours of darkness) is defined as the period between half an hour after sunset and half an hour before sunrise.

questions.q: You're driving at night on a country road that has no street lighting. Which lights MUST you use?
options: Sidelights only
Hazard warning lights
Front fog lights
Headlights
questions.explain: You MUST use headlights at night, except on a road that has lit street lighting.

questions.q: How often should you check the fluid levels in your car?
options: Only at each service
Once a year at the MOT
When a warning light comes on
At least weekly
questions.explain: Check the fluid levels in your vehicle at least weekly, and make sure you recognise any low fluid warning lights.

questions.q: You know your car is unroadworthy but decide to drive it anyway. What could this do to your insurance?
options: It could make it invalid
It will still cover you in full
It will cover only fire and theft
It will become comprehensive cover
questions.explain: You MUST make sure your vehicle is legal and roadworthy. Driving an unroadworthy motor vehicle may invalidate your insurance.

questions.q: You've just filled up with fuel. What should you check to help prevent fuel leaks?
options: The tank is filled right to the top
The fuel cap is fastened securely
The engine is still running
The fuel gauge shows it's full
questions.explain: Double-check for fuel leaks. Don't overfill your fuel tank, and make sure the fuel cap is fastened securely and its seal isn't torn, perished or missing.

questions.q: You've had new headlight bulbs fitted to your car. Why MUST the headlights be properly adjusted?
options: To stop the bulbs overheating
To prevent dazzling other road users
To reduce your fuel consumption
To make your indicators brighter
questions.explain: Lights MUST be properly adjusted to prevent dazzling other road users. Extra attention needs to be paid to this if the vehicle is heavily loaded.

questions.q: You need to book your car's MOT. How can you recognise an approved MOT test centre?
options: A green sign with a white tick
A red sign with the word 'TEST'
A blue sign with 3 white triangles
A yellow sign showing a black car
questions.explain: You must use an approved MOT test centre. Only centres showing the blue sign with 3 white triangles can carry out your MOT.

questions.q: You've stopped your car on the road for a short time. When may you use your hazard warning lights?
options: To warn you're temporarily obstructing traffic
To let you park on double yellow lines
To let you stop on zig-zag lines
To show you're waiting for a parking space
questions.explain: Hazard warning lights may be used when your vehicle is stationary, to warn that it's temporarily obstructing traffic. Never use them as an excuse for dangerous or illegal parking.

questions.q: It's a warm day and you're leaving your car for a while. Which of these should you never leave in it?
options: The spare wheel
A first aid kit in the boot
A warning triangle in the boot
Children or pets
questions.explain: When you leave your vehicle, never leave children or pets in an unventilated car.

questions.q: You're driving through a built-up area late at night. Between which times MUST you not use your horn, unless another road user poses a danger?
options: 11.00 pm and 6.30 am
Midnight and 6.00 am
11.30 pm and 7.00 am
10.30 pm and 7.30 am
questions.explain: You MUST NOT use your horn when driving in a built-up area between 11.30 pm and 7.00 am, except when another road user poses a danger.

questions.q: You're leaving your car in a town centre. There's a carrier bag of shopping on the back seat. What should you do?
options: Take it with you or lock it in the boot
Leave it there, as it's only shopping
Push it under the seat out of the way
Leave a window open so it can be seen
questions.explain: Take all contents with you, or lock them in the boot. Remember, for all a thief knows a carrier bag may contain valuables.

questions.q: You want to make your car more secure against theft. What could you fit?
options: Wider alloy wheels
An alarm or immobiliser
A larger fuel tank
Brighter headlight bulbs
questions.explain: For extra security, fit an anti-theft device such as an alarm or immobiliser. If you're buying a new car, it's a good idea to check the level of built-in security features.

questions.q: You get a flat tyre while driving on a busy road. What should you do?
options: Keep driving to the nearest garage
Stop at once, wherever you are
Stop when safe and get help if needed
Change it however close the traffic is
questions.explain: If you have a flat tyre, stop as soon as it's safe to do so. Only change the tyre if you can do so without putting yourself or others at risk; otherwise call a breakdown service.

questions.q: Your doctor has given you a certificate exempting you from wearing a seat belt. What must you do with it?
options: Send it to the DVSA
Display it on the windscreen
Give it to your MOT tester
Keep it in your car
questions.explain: If your doctor says you don't have to wear a seat belt for a medical reason, they'll give you a Certificate of Exemption. You must keep it in your vehicle and show it to the police if you're stopped. You'll also need to tell your insurer.

questions.q: You're travelling as a passenger on a coach that has seat belts fitted. What does the law say?
options: You MUST wear one if you're 14 or over
They're only needed on motorways
They're only for children under 14
They're optional for all passengers
questions.explain: Adults, and children aged 14 years and over, MUST use a seat belt or child restraint, where fitted, when seated in minibuses, buses and coaches.

questions.q: You're popping into a shop for just a couple of minutes. What should you do before leaving your car?
options: Leave the engine running to keep it warm
Leave a window open for ventilation
Remove the key and lock the car
Leave the key in so you're quicker
questions.explain: When you leave your vehicle, you should remove the ignition key, engage the steering lock and lock the car, even if you only leave it for a few minutes.

questions.q: You've just received the registration certificate for your car. Where should you keep it?
options: In the glove box, out of sight
Somewhere safe, away from the car
Under the driver's seat
In the boot, with the car locked
questions.explain: You should never leave vehicle documents in the car.

questions.q: You want a cheap way to deter professional thieves from stealing your car. What does the Highway Code suggest?
options: Etch your registration on the windows
Leave the parking lights switched on
Leave the windows open a little way
Leave a coat over the rear seats
questions.explain: You should consider having your registration number etched on all your car windows. This is a cheap and effective deterrent to professional thieves.

questions.q: You've stopped at the side of the road to wait for a friend, who'll be several minutes. What should you do?
options: Keep the engine running to stay warm
Rev the engine now and again
Switch off the engine
Leave the engine idling with the lights on
questions.explain: You MUST NOT leave an engine running unnecessarily while stationary on a public road. If you're likely to be stationary for more than a couple of minutes, apply the parking brake and switch off the engine to reduce emissions and noise pollution.

questions.q: Your car is stationary on a public road with the engine running. In which situation is this acceptable?
options: When you've popped into a shop
When warming up the engine on a cold day
When it's defrosting while you're indoors
When you're stationary in traffic
questions.explain: You MUST NOT leave a parked vehicle unattended with the engine running, or leave the engine running unnecessarily while stationary. It's permissible if the vehicle is stationary in traffic or for diagnosing faults.

questions.q: You're driving in England with your 16-year-old nephew in the car. What does the law say about smoking?
options: You may smoke as he's aged 16
You MUST NOT smoke in the car
You may smoke if he agrees to it
You may smoke if he sits in the back
questions.explain: In England and Wales, the driver MUST NOT smoke or allow anyone to smoke in an enclosed private vehicle carrying someone under 18. Smoking is also a distraction while you're driving.

questions.q: Your car was first registered over 40 years ago and hasn't been substantially changed. What's the MOT requirement?
options: It needs an MOT every year
It needs an MOT every 3 years
It's exempt from the MOT test
It needs an MOT every 6 months
questions.explain: Cars manufactured or first registered over 40 years ago are exempt from the MOT test, unless they've been substantially changed within the previous 30 years.

questions.q: Your car's MOT is due to run out soon. How early can you have the test and keep the same renewal date?
options: Up to a week (minus a day) before
Up to a month (minus a day) before
Up to two weeks (minus a day) before
Up to three months (minus a day) before
questions.explain: You can get an MOT up to a month (minus a day) before it runs out and keep the same renewal date.

questions.q: You're taking your car for its MOT. Which of these does the test NOT cover?
options: The horn and lights
The seat belts
The windscreen wipers
The gearbox
questions.explain: The MOT checks that your vehicle meets road safety and environmental standards. It doesn't cover the condition of the engine, clutch or gearbox.

questions.q: Your car fails its MOT because of a 'dangerous' problem, but your current MOT certificate hasn't run out yet. What should you do?
options: Drive it until the old certificate runs out
Get it repaired before you drive it
Drive it only on roads below 40 mph
Drive it for up to 10 working days
questions.explain: You can only take a failed vehicle away if your current MOT is still valid and no 'dangerous' problems were listed. Otherwise you'll need to get it repaired before you can drive it.

questions.q: You're looking for somewhere to park in an unfamiliar area. Where should you NOT park?
options: Near the brow of a hill
In a marked parking bay
In an off-street car park
Close to the kerb on a straight road
questions.explain: You shouldn't stop or park near the brow of a hill or hump bridge. You MUST NOT leave your vehicle in a dangerous position or where it causes any unnecessary obstruction of the road.

questions.q: You're fitting a sat nav to your windscreen with a mount so you can use it hands-free. What must you make sure of?
options: It doesn't block your view of the road ahead
It's fitted in the middle of the windscreen
It's only switched on while you're parked
It can be held while you're stopped in traffic
questions.explain: You can use a sat nav hands-free, for example in a windscreen mount, but the device must not block your view of the road and traffic ahead. You mustn't hold it while driving, even when you're queuing in traffic.

questions.q: You're using a driver assistance system, such as motorway assist, on a long journey. Who is responsible for the vehicle?
options: You, the driver
The vehicle manufacturer
The system's software provider
Nobody, while it's switched on
questions.explain: As the driver, you're still responsible for the vehicle if you use a driver assistance system like motorway assist. You MUST have full control over these systems at all times.

questions.q: Your new car has a lane departure warning system. What does the Highway Code say about using it while you drive?
options: Use it according to the manufacturer's instructions
Use it only when you start to feel tired
Use it instead of checking your mirrors
Switch it off whenever you drive at night
questions.explain: You may use driver assistance systems while you're driving, but make sure you use any system according to the manufacturer's instructions. Don't rely on them – they're there to assist, and you shouldn't reduce your concentration.

questions.q: Your car can be parked using a hand-held remote control app. What MUST you make sure of when using it?
options: Someone sits in the driver's seat
You use it only in multi-storey car parks
You reply to messages while it parks
You remain in control of the vehicle
questions.explain: When you use a hand-held device to help you park, you MUST remain in control of the vehicle at all times. Don't use the device for anything else while parking, and don't put anyone in danger.

questions.q: You want to check that your eyesight meets the legal standard for driving. In good daylight, from what distance must you be able to read a modern number plate?
options: 10 metres
15 metres
20 metres
25 metres
questions.explain: You MUST be able to read a vehicle number plate, in good daylight, from a distance of 20 metres (or 20.5 metres where an old-style number plate is used).

questions.q: Which of these does the Highway Code recommend you carry for use in an emergency?
options: A spare set of car keys
A full can of petrol
A portable tyre compressor
High-visibility clothing
questions.explain: For emergency use, it's recommended that you have a mobile phone containing emergency contacts (such as breakdown assistance) and high-visibility clothing.

questions.q: Your windscreen is very dirty and covered in smears. What does the law say?
options: It MUST be kept clean and clear
It only matters at night
It only matters before an MOT
It's fine as long as the wipers work
questions.explain: Windscreens and windows MUST be kept clean and free from obstructions to vision. Lights, indicators, reflectors and number plates MUST also be kept clean and clear.

questions.q: You're caught driving without wearing a seat belt. What's the maximum fine you could get?
questions.explain: You can be fined up to £500 if you don't wear a seat belt when you're supposed to. The same applies if a child under 14 isn't in the correct car seat or wearing a seat belt while you're driving.

questions.q: You're driving slowly up a long, steep hill and several vehicles behind want to overtake. There's a climbing lane on your left. What should you do?
options: Use the climbing lane to let them pass
Stay in the main lane and speed up
Stop on the hill so they can get by
Switch on your hazard warning lights
questions.explain: Climbing and crawler lanes are provided on some hills. Use the lane if you're driving a slow-moving vehicle or if there are vehicles behind you wishing to overtake, and watch for signs that it's about to end.

questions.q: You're driving down a long, steep hill. Why shouldn't you rely only on the footbrake to control your speed?
options: It will make your tyres lose pressure
It can cause the engine to overheat
Heavy use can reduce its effectiveness
It will drain the battery quickly
questions.explain: Increased use of the footbrake can reduce its effectiveness. Select a lower gear before you reach a long downhill slope and don't coast, so engine braking helps you control your speed.

questions.q: You're approaching a right-hand bend on a two-way road. Where should you position your car?
options: Well to the left
Close to the centre line
Straddling the centre line
As far right as is safe
questions.explain: Keep well to the left on right-hand bends. This will improve your view of the road and help avoid the risk of colliding with traffic approaching from the opposite direction.

questions.q: You're driving along a winding road. Why should you keep both hands on the steering wheel where possible?
options: To make the steering feel lighter
To stop the airbag from activating
To show other drivers you're alert
To remain in full control of the car
questions.explain: Drive with both hands on the wheel where possible. This will help you to remain in full control of the vehicle at all times.

questions.q: You're in a listed self-driving vehicle with its self-driving function switched on. It prompts you to take back control. What MUST you do?
options: Let it carry on driving itself
Wait until the end of the journey
Ignore it unless the road is busy
Take control when it prompts you
questions.explain: If a self-driving vehicle needs to hand control back to you, it will give you enough warning. You MUST always be able and ready to take control, and do it when the vehicle prompts you, so stay in the driving seat and stay awake.

questions.q: You're coming to a normal stop at traffic lights. What's the safest way to brake?
options: Early and lightly, then more firmly
Late and hard, then release it
Pump the brake pedal on and off
Handbrake first, then footbrake
questions.explain: In normal circumstances, the safest way to brake is early and lightly. Brake more firmly as you begin to stop, then ease the pressure off just before the vehicle comes to rest to avoid a jerky stop.

questions.q: You've just driven through a flooded section of road where the water was deep. What should you do at the first safe opportunity?
options: Check your tyre pressures
Gently test your brakes
Rev the engine to dry it
Check your oil level
questions.explain: If you've driven through deep water your brakes may be less effective. Test them at the first safe opportunity by pushing gently on the brake pedal to make sure that they work.

questions.q: You're driving on a narrow country road with lots of bends. Why should you reduce your speed as you approach each bend?
options: Bends can be sharper than they appear
Country roads have lower speed limits
Your tyres grip less on country roads
Speed cameras are often placed on bends
questions.explain: Take extra care on country roads and reduce your speed at approaches to bends, which can be sharper than they appear. Make sure you can stop within the distance you can see to be clear.

questions.q: You're driving along a country road and approaching a village. What should you do?
options: Keep to the speed you used on the open road
Speed up to get through the village quickly
Use main beam to warn people you're coming
Reduce your speed as you enter the village
questions.explain: You should reduce your speed where country roads enter villages. On country roads, be prepared for pedestrians, horse riders, cyclists, slow-moving farm vehicles or mud on the road.

questions.q: You're on a single-track road and see a car coming towards you. The nearest passing place is on your right. What should you do?
options: Pull into the passing place on your right
Wait opposite the passing place
Flash your headlights and carry on
Drive onto the verge on your left
questions.explain: On single-track roads, if you see a vehicle coming towards you, pull into a passing place on your left, or wait opposite a passing place on your right.

questions.q: Your car doesn't have anti-lock brakes. A child runs out in front of you and you have to stop in an emergency. What should you try to avoid?
options: Braking as soon as you see the hazard
Braking so hard that the wheels lock
Keeping both hands on the steering wheel
Holding the car straight as you stop
questions.explain: In an emergency, brake immediately. Try to avoid braking so harshly that you lock your wheels, as locked wheels can lead to loss of control.

questions.q: You're driving downhill on a narrow single-track road. A vehicle is coming uphill towards you. What should you do?
options: Give way to it whenever you can
Expect it to reverse for you
Flash your headlights to claim priority
Keep going, as downhill has priority
questions.explain: Give way to road users coming uphill whenever you can. If necessary, reverse until you reach a passing place to let the other vehicle pass.

questions.q: You're driving on a single-track road and want to stop for a break. What does the Highway Code say about passing places?
options: You may park in them for up to an hour
You shouldn't park in them
You may park in them in daylight
You may park in ones on your left
questions.explain: Do not park in passing places. They're there so vehicles can pass each other or let following traffic overtake.

questions.q: You're driving along a road with a series of road humps and chicanes. What should you do?
options: Slow down for each hump, then speed up
Drive at the speed limit between features
Swerve around the humps to avoid them
Keep a reduced speed along the whole stretch
questions.explain: Traffic-calming features such as road humps, chicanes and narrowings are intended to slow you down. Reduce your speed as you approach them and maintain a reduced speed along the whole stretch of road.

questions.q: You're driving through a traffic-calmed street with narrowings. A cyclist ahead is riding slowly. What should you do?
options: Overtake before the next narrowing
Stay behind and don't overtake here
Sound your horn so they let you by
Pass them as they ride over a hump
questions.explain: Allow cyclists and motorcyclists room to pass through traffic-calming features. You should not overtake other moving road users while in these areas.

questions.q: You see this sign as you enter a residential street. What does it mean?
options: Hump bridge ahead
Uneven road surface ahead
Road humps for the distance shown
Speed cameras for the distance shown
questions.explain: This sign shows the distance over which road humps extend. Reduce your speed and keep it reduced along the whole stretch of road.

questions.q: You're carrying a tall load on your roof rack in a city with trams. How high above the road are tram overhead wires normally?
options: 4.5 metres
3.5 metres
5.8 metres
6.5 metres
questions.explain: Tramway overhead wires are normally 5.8 metres above the carriageway, but can be lower, in which case height clearance markings are shown. Make sure there's enough clearance for your vehicle and any load before driving under them.

questions.q: You're approaching a low arched bridge and see this sign. What does it show?
options: The bridge is closed to traffic
The road narrows on both sides
There's a weight limit on the bridge
The available width of headroom
questions.explain: This warning sign shows the available width of headroom. Check that your vehicle, including any load, can pass safely.

questions.q: It's a dull, overcast day. Visibility is poor, but you can still see well over 100 metres. Which lights should you use so others can see you?
options: Dipped headlights
Rear fog lights
Front fog lights
Hazard warning lights
questions.explain: Use dipped headlights, or dim-dip if fitted, in dull daytime weather to make sure you can be seen. You MUST NOT use fog lights unless visibility is seriously reduced.

questions.q: You're overtaking another vehicle at night on an unlit road. When should you change from dipped to main beam?
options: Before you pull out to overtake
As soon as you start to pull out
When you're level with the other vehicle
When you're halfway along its side
questions.explain: Keep your headlights dipped when overtaking until you're level with the other vehicle, then change to main beam if necessary, unless this would dazzle oncoming road users.

questions.q: You're stopped in a long queue of traffic at night and the vehicles behind you have also stopped. What should you do to reduce glare for them?
options: Keep pressing firmly on the footbrake
Use the parking brake, not the footbrake
Switch on your rear fog lights
Switch on your hazard warning lights
questions.explain: In stationary queues, apply the parking brake and, once the following traffic has stopped, take your foot off the footbrake to switch off your brake lights. This minimises glare for road users behind.

questions.q: You're thinking about overtaking a slow vehicle on a single carriageway. Which of these should you make sure of first?
options: There's a suitable gap in front of it
The vehicle behind can follow you past
Your hazard warning lights are on
The driver ahead has flashed their lights
questions.explain: Before overtaking, make sure the road is sufficiently clear ahead, road users aren't beginning to overtake you, and there's a suitable gap in front of the road user you plan to overtake.

questions.q: You've parked at the side of the road and are about to leave your car. What MUST you switch off?
options: The engine, headlights and fog lights
Only the engine, as lights don't matter
Only the fog lights, if they're on
Nothing, if you'll be back in minutes
questions.explain: If you stop on the roadside, you MUST switch off the engine, headlights and fog lights, and you MUST apply the handbrake before leaving the vehicle.

questions.q: You see this sign. What should you be prepared for?
options: A hump bridge
A bumpy road surface
Road humps for a set distance
A steep hill downwards
questions.explain: This sign warns of an uneven road. Slow down, and remember that motorcyclists and cyclists may suddenly need to avoid uneven road surfaces.

questions.q: You've started to overtake a car on a single carriageway. What should you do?
options: Move quickly past and don't cut in
Stay alongside until the road widens
Move back in as soon as you're level
Slow down to match the car's speed
questions.explain: Once you've started to overtake, move quickly past the vehicle and allow plenty of room. Move back to the left as soon as you can, but don't cut in.

questions.q: You see this sign on a country road. What does it mean?
options: Two-way traffic straight ahead
Give priority to oncoming traffic
No overtaking
No motor vehicles
questions.explain: This sign means no overtaking. You MUST NOT overtake after it until you pass a sign cancelling the restriction.

questions.q: You're parking a manual car facing uphill next to the kerb. What should you do after applying the handbrake firmly?
options: Reverse gear, wheel turned towards the kerb
Forward gear, wheel turned away from the kerb
Neutral, wheels left straight ahead
Forward gear, wheel turned towards the kerb
questions.explain: When parking facing uphill, park close to the kerb, apply the handbrake firmly, select a forward gear and turn your steering wheel away from the kerb.

questions.q: You're parking a manual car facing downhill next to the kerb. Which gear should you select and which way should you turn the wheel?
options: Reverse gear, wheel towards the kerb
First gear, wheel away from the kerb
Neutral, wheels straight ahead
Reverse gear, wheel away from the kerb
questions.explain: When parking facing downhill, apply the handbrake firmly, select reverse gear and turn your steering wheel towards the kerb. In an automatic, use 'park'.

questions.q: It snowed overnight and your car is covered in snow and ice. Before you set off, what MUST you do?
options: Clear a patch in front of the driver
Clear the windscreen and nothing else
Clear all snow and ice from all windows
Drive slowly until the heater clears it
questions.explain: You MUST be able to see, so clear all snow and ice from all your windows. You MUST also make sure lights are clean and number plates are legible, and you should remove snow that might fall off into the path of others.

questions.q: You have to make an essential journey in snowy weather. Which of these should you take with you?
options: Warm clothing, a torch and a shovel
Your insurance and MOT certificates
A set of spare summer tyres
A full roof box for extra weight
questions.explain: Take an emergency kit of de-icer and ice scraper, torch, warm clothing and boots, first aid kit, jump leads and a shovel, together with a warm drink and emergency food in case you get stuck.

questions.q: You're driving on a road covered in compacted snow and the steering suddenly feels unresponsive. What may this mean?
options: Your power steering fluid is low
There's ice and you're losing grip
Your tyres are over-inflated
The road has just been gritted
questions.explain: If the steering feels unresponsive in snow or ice, this may indicate ice and your vehicle losing its grip on the road. Avoid sudden actions and check your grip by braking gently in a safe place.

questions.q: You're driving in fog and moisture keeps building up on your windscreen. What should you use?
options: Your rear fog lights
Your main beam headlights
Your hazard warning lights
Your wipers and demisters
questions.explain: When driving in fog, use your windscreen wipers and demisters. Also beware of other drivers who are not using headlights.

questions.q: Visibility is good, but another driver has their rear fog lights on. Why MUST fog lights not be used in these conditions?
options: They drain the battery very quickly
They can make the light units overheat
They dazzle others and can hide brake lights
They make indicators harder to see in daylight
questions.explain: You MUST NOT use front or rear fog lights unless visibility is seriously reduced, as they dazzle other road users and can obscure your brake lights.

questions.q: You're waiting to turn out of a junction in thick fog and can't see far in either direction. What should you do?
options: Edge out and wait in the middle of the road
Stop in the correct position and listen
Sound your horn and pull out quickly
Switch on your hazard lights and emerge
questions.explain: Stop in the correct position at a junction with limited visibility and listen for traffic. When you're sure it's safe, emerge positively and don't hesitate in a position that puts you in the path of approaching vehicles.

questions.q: It's foggy and you have no choice but to park on the road. What should you do?
options: Leave your rear fog lights on
Leave your headlights on main beam
Switch off all your lights
Leave your sidelights on
questions.explain: It's especially dangerous to park on the road in fog. If it's unavoidable, leave your parking lights or sidelights on.

questions.q: You see this sign as you approach road works. What does it warn you of?
options: Loose chippings
Falling or fallen rocks
Uneven road
Slippery road
questions.explain: This road works sign warns of loose chippings. Take extra care, especially near cyclists and motorcyclists, as they are vulnerable to skidding on grit and other debris at road works.

questions.q: You see this sign ahead. What should you do before you reach the hill?
options: Select neutral and coast down
Select a lower gear
Speed up to gain momentum
Switch on your fog lights
questions.explain: This sign warns of a steep hill downwards. Select a lower gear before you reach a long downhill slope to help control your speed. Coasting removes engine braking.

questions.q: You see this sign on a narrow country road. What does it warn you of?
options: Falling rocks
A hump bridge
Soft verges
Loose chippings
questions.explain: This warning sign shows that there are soft verges at the side of the road.

questions.q: You come to a level crossing with user-operated gates but no lights. There's a railway telephone beside it. What should you do before crossing?
options: Wait for the gates to open by themselves
Sound your horn and wait for a reply
Cross if you can't hear a train
Phone the signal operator
questions.explain: If there are no lights, stop, look both ways and listen before you cross. If there's a railway telephone, always use it to contact the signal operator to make sure it's safe to cross, and tell them again when you're clear.

questions.q: You come to an open level crossing. It has a 'Give Way' sign but no gates, barriers, attendant or lights. What should you do?
options: Look both ways and listen before crossing
Cross quickly, as trains will give way
Wait for a signal from the operator
Sound your horn and then cross
questions.explain: Open crossings have no gates, barriers, attendant or traffic lights but will have a 'Give Way' sign. Look both ways, listen and make sure there's no train coming before you cross.

questions.q: The half-barriers at a level crossing start to come down, but you can't see a train. What should you do?
options: Drive round the barriers if it's clear
Stop and wait behind the white line
Speed up to cross before they close
Sound your horn and cross slowly
questions.explain: Half-barriers lower automatically because a train is approaching. You MUST obey the flashing red lights and stop behind the white line. Never zig-zag around half-barriers.

questions.q: You see this sign on a country road. What does it warn you of?
options: A single sharp bend ahead
A double bend ahead
A junction on a bend ahead
A road that narrows ahead
questions.explain: This sign warns of a double bend. The first bend may be to the left or the right, as the symbol can be reversed. Reduce your speed before the bends, which can be sharper than they appear.

questions.q: You're driving along a street where trams run in the road. What should you avoid?
options: Driving on top of the rails
Driving in the left-hand lane
Driving close to the kerb
Driving behind a slow bus
questions.explain: Take extra care where trams run along the road. Avoid driving directly on top of the rails, and take care where trams leave the main carriageway so you don't follow them.

questions.q: You need to cross some tram rails on a wet day. What is the safest way to cross them?
options: At a shallow angle
While braking firmly
Along the line of the rails
Directly at right angles
questions.explain: Take extra care when crossing tram tracks, especially if the rails are wet. It's safest to cross the tracks directly at right angles, and cyclists and motorcyclists may need more space to do so.

questions.q: You're driving in a city where trams share the road. How might the width taken up by the trams be shown?
options: By red lines along the edge of the road
By lines of orange cones along the track
By yellow dots or a different road surface
By blue signs placed every 100 metres
questions.explain: The width taken up by trams is often shown by tram lanes marked by white lines, yellow dots or a different type of road surface. You MUST NOT enter a road, lane or route reserved for trams.

questions.q: You want to stop briefly on a road with a tramway. Why must every part of your car be clear of the tram's path?
options: Trams can't steer round obstructions
Tram rails can puncture your tyres
Trams may push vehicles out of the way
Tram wires may touch your car's roof
questions.explain: Don't stop on any part of a tram track except in a designated bay, and make sure all parts of your vehicle are outside the tram path. A tram cannot steer round an obstruction.

questions.q: You're driving along a road with tram tracks. Where should you take extra care?
options: On long straight sections of track
Where the road is at its widest
Where the tracks are furthest from the kerb
Where the tracks cross the road
questions.explain: Take extra care where the track crosses from one side of the road to the other, and where the road narrows and the tracks come close to the kerb.

questions.q: You're driving at night along a street in a built-up area with street lighting. Which lights should you use?
options: Dipped headlights
Sidelights only
Main beam headlights
Front fog lights
questions.explain: You should use dipped headlights, or dim-dip if fitted, at night in built-up areas to make sure you can be seen.

questions.q: You're driving on a very hot day and the road surface has become soft. What could this affect?
options: Your headlight aim
Your speedometer accuracy
Your steering and braking
Your fuel gauge reading
questions.explain: In hot weather the road surface may become soft, or slippery if it rains after a dry spell. These conditions could affect your steering and braking.

questions.q: You come to a level crossing with user-operated gates. The green light is showing. What should you do?
options: Open the gate on your side and drive across
Wait for a railway worker to open the gates
Cross, then leave the gates open for others
Open both gates, check the light, cross quickly
questions.explain: Open the gates or barriers on both sides of the crossing, check the green light is still on and cross quickly. Close the gates or barriers when you're clear of the crossing.

questions.q: You're moving house and carrying some long items in your car. What does the law say about your load?
options: It MUST be secure and not stick out dangerously
It only needs securing on high-speed roads
Passengers can hold it in place by hand
It can overhang 3 metres without markers
questions.explain: You MUST secure your load and it MUST NOT stick out dangerously. Make sure any heavy or sharp objects are secured safely.

questions.q: You've put some heavy tools loose on the back seat of your car. Why is this dangerous?
options: They could set off the car alarm
They could injure someone in a collision
They'll make your tyres wear faster
They'll stop the rear doors locking
questions.explain: You should make sure any heavy or sharp objects are secured safely. If there's a collision, they might hit someone inside the vehicle and cause serious injury.

questions.q: You're setting off on holiday with a fully loaded car. Your handbook gives different tyre pressures for a full load. What should you do?
options: Let some air out for a softer ride
Keep them at the normal setting
Inflate them to the full-load setting
Check them only when you arrive
questions.explain: Tyres MUST be correctly inflated to the vehicle manufacturer's specification for the load being carried. Always refer to the vehicle's handbook or data.

questions.q: Your car is heavily loaded at the back for a long journey. What may you need to adjust?
options: Your speedometer
Your fuel gauge
Your engine idle speed
Your headlights
questions.explain: Carrying a load or pulling a trailer may require you to adjust your headlights. Lights MUST be properly adjusted to prevent dazzling other road users, and extra attention is needed if the vehicle is heavily loaded.

questions.q: You're stopped by the police because your load is insecure and likely to cause danger. How many penalty points could this carry?
questions.explain: You MUST NOT overload your vehicle and you MUST secure your load. Causing, or being likely to cause, danger because of your load or passengers carries 3 penalty points.

questions.q: You're taking your dog with you in the car. How should you carry it?
options: Loose on the back seat
On a passenger's lap in the front
Loose in the front footwell
Restrained in a dog cage or harness
questions.explain: You should make sure dogs or other animals are suitably restrained so they can't distract you or injure you, or themselves, if you stop quickly. A seat belt harness, pet carrier, dog cage or dog guard are ways of restraining animals in cars.

questions.q: You're giving friends a lift and there are more people than seats with seat belts. What does the law say?
options: Two children can share one seat belt
Adults can share a belt on short trips
Only one person may use each belted seat
Extra passengers can sit in the boot
questions.explain: You must wear a seat belt if one is fitted in the seat you're using, and you're only allowed one person in each seat fitted with a seat belt.

questions.q: You're carrying three children under 3, but there's no room for a third child car seat in the back. How must the third child travel?
options: In the back using an adult seat belt
In the front in the correct child seat
On an adult's lap in the back
In the back without any restraint
questions.explain: Children under 3 must be in a child car seat. If there's no room for a third child car seat in the back, the child must travel in the front seat with the correct child car seat.

questions.q: You passed your car driving test in 2015. What's the heaviest trailer you can tow on your licence?
options: 750 kg MAM
3,500 kg MAM
8,250 kg MAM
12,000 kg MAM
questions.explain: If you got your licence from 1 January 1997, you can tow a trailer that weighs up to 3,500 kg maximum authorised mass (MAM). This is known as a 'category BE' vehicle. You MUST NOT tow more than your licence permits.

questions.q: Your grandfather passed his car driving test in 1985. What combined weight of vehicle and trailer can he usually drive?
options: Up to 3,500 kg MAM
Up to 7,500 kg MAM
Up to 8,250 kg MAM
Up to 12,000 kg MAM
questions.explain: If you got your licence before 1 January 1997, you can usually drive a vehicle and trailer with a combined weight of up to 8,250 kg MAM.

questions.q: You're checking whether your car can tow a caravan. What is the 'gross train weight'?
options: The weight of the empty trailer only
The downward weight on the tow ball
The weight of the car with no passengers
The fully loaded car plus fully loaded trailer
questions.explain: The gross train weight is the weight of the fully loaded car plus the fully loaded trailer, and it must not be exceeded. If your VIN plate doesn't list a train weight, you shouldn't use your vehicle for towing.

questions.q: You're loading your caravan for a holiday. Where should you put the heaviest items?
options: Over the caravan's axle(s)
At the very back of the caravan
In the high roof lockers
All on one side of the caravan
questions.explain: You should distribute the weight in your caravan or trailer evenly, with heavy items over the axle(s). This should minimise the possibility of swerving or snaking and loss of control.

questions.q: You're hitching a loaded trailer to your car. How should the load act on the tow ball?
options: It should lift upwards on the tow ball
It should press down, within the maker's limit
It should put no weight on the tow ball
It should be as heavy as you can make it
questions.explain: You should ensure a downward load on the tow ball. The manufacturer's recommended weight and tow ball load should not be exceeded.

questions.q: You're towing a caravan on a dual carriageway when it starts to snake from side to side. What should you do?
options: Brake hard to stop quickly
Accelerate to straighten it up
Ease off and slow down gently
Steer sharply against the swing
questions.explain: If the trailer starts to swerve or snake, ease off the accelerator and reduce speed gently to regain control. Don't brake harshly.

questions.q: You're about to tow a caravan that's wider than the back of your car. What MUST you do?
options: Drive with your hazard lights on
Keep below 30 mph at all times
Have a passenger watch behind for you
Fit suitable towing mirrors
questions.explain: If your trailer or load is wider than your vehicle, or it blocks your view behind, towing mirrors MUST be used. You can be fined and get 3 penalty points for towing without proper towing mirrors.

questions.q: You're buying a trailer to tow with your car. Above what loaded weight must it have a working brake system?
options: 500 kg
750 kg
questions.explain: Your trailer must have a working brake system if it weighs over 750 kg when it's loaded. Any brakes fitted must be in good working order.

questions.q: You're hitching a trailer to your car. Why must you also use a breakaway cable or secondary coupling?
options: In case the trailer becomes detached
To power the trailer's lights
To stop the trailer from snaking
To reduce the load on the tow ball
questions.explain: Your trailer MUST be fitted with a secondary coupling device, such as a safety chain. You must use a breakaway cable or secondary coupling in case the trailer becomes detached from your car.

questions.q: You're towing a trailer behind your car. Which number plate must the trailer display?
options: The trailer's own registration number
No plate is needed on a small trailer
The same number plate as your car
A plate showing your home postcode
questions.explain: You must display the same number plate on your trailer as on your towing car.

questions.q: You're towing a caravan on a single carriageway road where the national speed limit applies. What's your maximum speed?
options: 40 mph
50 mph
60 mph
70 mph
questions.explain: Cars towing caravans or trailers have a speed limit of 50 mph on single carriageways, unless signs show a lower limit. Reduced speed limits apply when you're towing.

questions.q: Your car's maximum authorised mass (MAM) is under 3,500 kg. What's the longest trailer you can tow with it?
options: 5 metres
10 metres
7 metres
12 metres
questions.explain: If your vehicle's maximum authorised mass is 3,500 kg or less, you can't tow a trailer that's longer than 7 metres. This doesn't include the A-frame.

questions.q: Your friend's car has broken down and they ask you to tow it home with a tow rope. What does the Highway Code advise?
options: Use the rope and keep under 40 mph
Use the rope with your hazard lights on
Use the longest rope you can find
Consider professional recovery instead
questions.explain: Towing a vehicle on a tow rope is potentially dangerous. You should consider using a solid tow bar or professional recovery.

questions.q: You're towing a caravan and want to overtake a slow-moving vehicle. What should you bear in mind?
options: You'll be able to accelerate faster
The extra length will affect overtaking
Your stopping distance will be shorter
Other drivers must let you pull in
questions.explain: When towing, remember the extra length will affect overtaking and manoeuvring. The extra weight will also affect braking and acceleration, and your stopping distance may increase significantly.

questions.q: You're having a tow bar fitted to your car, which was first used in 2015. What must the tow bar be?
options: Type-approved for your car
Painted the same colour as the car
Fitted by a DVLA garage
Removable when not in use
questions.explain: If you get a tow bar for your car, it needs to be type-approved, meaning it meets EU regulations and is designed for your car. It will have a label with an approval number and details of the vehicles it's approved for.

questions.q: You've parked your car and trailer at night on a road with a 30 mph speed limit. What does the law say about lights?
options: No lights are needed on a 30 mph road
Only the car needs its sidelights on
The trailer MUST NOT be left without lights
The hazard warning lights must be left on
questions.explain: Cars may be parked without lights on some roads with a 30 mph limit, but other vehicles and trailers, and all vehicles with projecting loads, MUST NOT be left on a road at night without lights.

questions.q: You're choosing a trailer to tow with your car. What's the maximum width allowed for a trailer?
options: 2.00 metres
2.10 metres
2.30 metres
2.55 metres
questions.explain: The maximum trailer width for any towing vehicle is 2.55 metres.

questions.q: You're waiting at a pelican crossing. A bleeping sound starts when the green figure shows for pedestrians. Who is it mainly there to help?
options: Blind or partially sighted people
Drivers waiting at the crossing
Cyclists using the crossing
Children crossing on their own
questions.explain: At some crossings there's a bleeping sound or voice signal to tell blind or partially sighted people when the steady green figure is showing. There may also be a tactile signal to help deafblind people.

questions.q: According to The Highway Code, which road users are most likely to be injured in the event of a collision?
options: Pedestrians, cyclists, horse riders and motorcyclists
Drivers of large goods and passenger vehicles
Car drivers and their front-seat passengers
Van and taxi drivers in busy town centres
questions.explain: The road users most likely to be injured in a collision are pedestrians, cyclists, horse riders and motorcyclists, with children, older adults and disabled people being more at risk. That's why they're placed at the top of the hierarchy of road users.

questions.q: Which of these statements about the hierarchy of road users is correct?
options: It means pedestrians need not consider their own safety
It only applies to drivers of large goods vehicles
Cyclists have a responsibility to reduce danger to pedestrians
It gives cyclists priority over pedestrians on the pavement
questions.explain: Cyclists, horse riders and drivers of horse-drawn vehicles have a responsibility to reduce danger to pedestrians. The hierarchy doesn't remove the responsibility of all road users, including pedestrians, to have regard for their own and others' safety.

questions.q: You're driving slowly along a busy high street. A pedestrian steps off the pavement ahead without looking your way. What should you bear in mind?
options: They've lost their right to use the road
They may have impaired sight or hearing
They should only cross at a marked crossing
You have priority because they didn't look
questions.explain: Always remember that the people you encounter may have impaired sight, hearing or mobility, and that this may not be obvious. Pedestrians may use any part of the road unless signs prohibit them, so be ready to slow down or stop.

questions.q: You're turning left into a side road. A pedestrian is waiting at the kerb to cross the road you're turning into. What should you do?
options: Carry on, as they haven't stepped into the road yet
Sound your horn to let them know you're turning
Give way and let them cross
Speed up to clear the junction before they cross
questions.explain: At a junction you should give way to pedestrians crossing or waiting to cross a road into which or from which you are turning. This applies whether you're turning left or right.

questions.q: The Highway Code says that only pedestrians may use the pavement. Who does this include?
options: Cyclists under the age of 12
Wheelchair and mobility scooter users
Learner motorcyclists on mopeds
Riders of electric scooters
questions.explain: Only pedestrians may use the pavement, and pedestrians include wheelchair and mobility scooter users. Cyclists MUST NOT cycle on a pavement.

questions.q: You're about to turn left into a side road. A cyclist is riding in a cycle lane on your left and is going straight ahead. What should you do?
options: Overtake the cyclist and turn in quickly
Turn in front of them, as they must give way
Sound your horn and then turn left
Stay behind and let them pass the junction
questions.explain: You shouldn't cut across cyclists going ahead when you're turning, whether they're in a cycle lane, a cycle track or on the road. Don't turn if it would cause them to stop or swerve; stay behind and let them pass.

questions.q: You're in a queue of slow-moving traffic, waiting to turn left into a side road. A steady flow of cyclists is moving past the queue on your left. What should you do?
options: Stop and wait for a safe gap in the cyclists
Signal left and turn, as cyclists must give way
Edge across slowly so the cyclists have to stop
Turn quickly before the next cyclist arrives
questions.explain: You should stop and wait for a safe gap in the flow of cyclists if necessary, including when they're moving past or waiting alongside stationary or slow-moving traffic. Don't turn if it would cause a cyclist going ahead to stop or swerve.

questions.q: You've stopped to let an older person cross the road. They're crossing very slowly. What should you do?
options: Rev your engine to hurry them along
Edge forward so they know you're waiting
Be patient and let them take their time
Sound your horn to let them know you're there
questions.explain: Older pedestrians may need more time to cross the road. Be patient and allow them to cross in their own time. Don't hurry them by revving your engine or edging forward.

questions.q: You're driving through a town centre and see a pedestrian carrying a white cane. What does this tell you?
options: They have a hearing impairment
They're blind or partially sighted
They have a learning difficulty
They're recovering from a leg injury
questions.explain: Blind or partially sighted people may carry a white cane or use a guide dog. They may not be able to see you approaching, so take extra care.

questions.q: You see a pedestrian carrying a white cane with a red band on it. What does this mean?
options: They're deafblind
They're partially sighted only
They have a walking difficulty
They're training a guide dog
questions.explain: Deafblind people may carry a white cane with a red band or use a dog with a red and white harness. They may not see or hear instructions or signals, so be patient and give them plenty of time.

questions.q: Children and older pedestrians may not be able to judge your speed and could step out in front of you. At which speed will your vehicle probably kill any pedestrian it hits?
options: 20 mph (32 km/h)
40 mph (64 km/h)
10 mph (16 km/h)
15 mph (24 km/h)
questions.explain: At 40 mph (64 km/h) your vehicle will probably kill any pedestrian it hits. At 20 mph (32 km/h) there's only a 1 in 20 chance of the pedestrian being killed – so kill your speed.

questions.q: You're driving at 20 mph through a residential area. If you hit a pedestrian, what chance is there that they would be killed?
options: 1 in 2
1 in 5
1 in 20
questions.explain: At 20 mph (32 km/h) there's only a 1 in 20 chance of a pedestrian being killed. At 40 mph (64 km/h) your vehicle will probably kill any pedestrian it hits.

questions.q: Why should you take extra care when driving near a pedestrian who has a hearing impairment?
options: They may not hear you approaching
They can't use zebra crossings
They always walk with a guide dog
They'll expect you to sound your horn
questions.explain: People with hearing impairments may not be aware of your vehicle approaching. Always remember that the people you encounter may have impaired sight, hearing or mobility, and that this may not be obvious.

questions.q: You're driving along a residential street lined with parked cars. A group of children is playing on the pavement ahead. What should you do?
options: Speed up to pass them quickly
Keep to the speed limit and carry on
Slow down and be ready to stop
Rely on them staying on the pavement
questions.explain: There's a risk of pedestrians, especially children, stepping unexpectedly into the road. You should drive with the safety of children in mind at a speed suitable for the conditions, and look out for children running out from between parked cars.

questions.q: You're driving at night with your headlights on. How much further away can you see a pedestrian wearing reflective materials?
options: Up to twice as far
Up to three times as far
Up to five times as far
About the same distance
questions.explain: When it's dark, reflective materials such as armbands, sashes and jackets can be seen by drivers using headlights up to three times as far away as non-reflective materials.

questions.q: You're driving along a narrow country road with no pavement. There are walkers in the road ahead. What should you do?
options: Sound your horn and keep to your speed
Flash your headlights so they move aside
Pass them closely to avoid oncoming traffic
Slow down and give them plenty of room
questions.explain: When approaching pedestrians on narrow rural roads without a footway or footpath, always slow down and be prepared to stop if necessary, giving them plenty of room as you drive past.

questions.q: You're about to pass a pedestrian who is walking in the road because there's no pavement. As a guide, how much space should you allow?
options: At least 0.5 metres
At least 1 metre
At least 2 metres
At least 1.5 metres
questions.explain: Allow at least 2 metres of space and keep to a low speed when passing a pedestrian who is walking in the road. If you can't do this safely, wait behind them.

questions.q: You're reversing into a side road. A pedestrian starts to cross the side road behind you. What should you do?
options: Carry on, as they should keep clear
Give way and let them cross
Sound your horn to warn them
Speed up to finish the manoeuvre
questions.explain: When reversing into a side road, look all around the vehicle and give way to any pedestrians who may be crossing the road.

questions.q: You're driving out of a driveway and need to cross the pavement to reach the road. A pedestrian is walking along the pavement towards you. What should you do?
options: Give way to the pedestrian
Sound your horn and drive out
Edge out so they walk round you
Drive out, as you're leaving private land
questions.explain: Drive carefully and slowly when you need to cross a pavement, for example to reach or leave a driveway. Give way to pedestrians on the pavement and to cyclists using a cycle lane or cycle track.

questions.q: You're turning right into a side road. A pedestrian has already started to cross it. Who has priority?
options: You, as you're on the main road
You, as you're signalling to turn
The pedestrian who is crossing
Whoever reaches the junction first
questions.explain: You should give way to pedestrians crossing or waiting to cross a road into which or from which you're turning. If they've started to cross, they have priority, so give way.

questions.q: You're approaching a zebra crossing. A pedestrian has just stepped onto it. What MUST you do?
options: Wave them across
Flash your headlights
Drive on if there's room to pass
Give way to them
questions.explain: You MUST give way when a pedestrian has moved onto a zebra crossing. You should also give way to pedestrians waiting to cross.

questions.q: You're driving at night and catch up with a horse-drawn vehicle. Which lights MUST it have fitted?
options: Amber flashing lights on both sides
Red to the front and white to the rear
White to the front and red to the rear
A single white light on the horse
questions.explain: It's safer not to drive horse-drawn vehicles at night, but if they're used, a light showing white to the front and red to the rear MUST be fitted. They should also have two red rear reflectors.

questions.q: You're approaching a zebra crossing that has a central island. How should you treat it?
options: As two separate crossings
As one single crossing
As a cycle-only crossing
As a crossing with no priority
questions.explain: A zebra crossing with a central island is two separate crossings. Pedestrians wait on the island and treat the second half of the road as a separate crossing.

questions.q: You're waiting at a pelican crossing. The red light changes to flashing amber, but a pedestrian is still on the crossing. What MUST you do?
options: Move off, as the lights have changed
Sound your horn to hurry them
Give way to the pedestrian
Edge forward to show you want to go
questions.explain: At a pelican crossing, flashing amber follows the red 'Stop' light. When the amber light is flashing, you MUST give way to any pedestrians on the crossing. If there are none, you may proceed with caution.

questions.q: You're approaching a pelican crossing where the two halves on each side of the central island aren't in line. How is it treated?
options: As one single crossing
As a zebra crossing
As a toucan crossing
As two separate crossings
questions.explain: When the crossings on each side of the central refuge aren't in line (a 'staggered' crossing), they're two separate crossings. Pelican crossings that go straight across the road are one crossing, even with a central island.

questions.q: How does the light sequence for traffic at a puffin crossing differ from that at a pelican crossing?
options: There's no flashing amber phase
There's a flashing green phase
There's no red light for traffic
There's a longer flashing amber phase
questions.explain: Toucan, puffin and equestrian crossings have no flashing amber phase. The light sequence for traffic at these crossings is the same as at traffic lights.

questions.q: You're approaching a toucan crossing. Who is it designed to be used by?
options: Pedestrians only
Cyclists and pedestrians
Horse riders and cyclists
Cyclists only
questions.explain: Toucan crossings are light-controlled crossings that allow cyclists and pedestrians to share the crossing space and cross at the same time. Cyclists are permitted to ride across.

questions.q: You're approaching a signal-controlled crossing with pavement barriers, extra-wide crossing spaces and a control panel mounted higher than usual. Who is it for?
options: Wheelchair users
Cyclists
School children
Horse riders
questions.explain: Equestrian crossings are for horse riders. They have pavement barriers, wider crossing spaces, horse and rider figures in the light panels and either two sets of controls (one higher) or just one higher control panel.

questions.q: At some signal-controlled junctions, signs and markings tell cyclists to turn right in two stages. What do the cyclists do first when the lights turn green?
options: Go straight ahead and wait at a marked spot
Move to the centre of the road and turn
Ride along the pavement to turn right
Wait at the stop line for the next green
questions.explain: In a two-stage turn, when the lights turn green cyclists go straight ahead to a spot marked by a cycle symbol and turn arrow, then stop and wait there. They complete the turn when the lights facing them turn green.

questions.q: You see this sign. Which road users may use the bus lane ahead as well as buses?
options: Motorcycles only
Cyclists and taxis
Lorries and vans
Cars with passengers
questions.explain: This sign shows a with-flow bus lane ahead which pedal cycles and taxis may also use. Most bus lanes may be used by cyclists, as shown on signs.

questions.q: The lights at a puffin crossing have just changed to green for you, but a pedestrian is still crossing. What should you do?
options: Drive on, as you have priority
Sound your horn to warn them
Drive round behind them
Give way to them
questions.explain: Give way to anyone still crossing after the signal for vehicles has changed to green. This advice applies to all crossings.

questions.q: You're approaching a parallel crossing. A cyclist has moved onto the cycle route part of the crossing. What MUST you do?
options: Carry on, as only pedestrians have priority
Give way to the cyclist
Sound your horn to warn the cyclist
Pass behind the cyclist carefully
questions.explain: Parallel crossings are similar to zebra crossings but include a cycle route alongside the black and white stripes. You MUST give way when a pedestrian or cyclist has moved onto the crossing.

questions.q: A school crossing patrol at the kerb is holding their sign like this. What does it mean?
options: All vehicles must stop now
Children are about to cross the road
They're holding pedestrians back
Drivers must give way to the patrol
questions.explain: School crossing patrols use signals to control the crossing. Holding the sign like a barrier means they're stopping pedestrians from crossing. You MUST obey signals given by school crossing patrols.

questions.q: Why should you treat all horses as a potential hazard, even when they have an experienced rider?
options: They aren't allowed on busy roads
Their riders can't give arm signals
They always move into the middle
They can move very fast if startled
questions.explain: Treat all horses as a potential hazard; they can be unpredictable despite the efforts of their rider. Horses are flight animals and can move incredibly quickly if startled.
