questions.q: You're approaching a stationary bus that's displaying this sign. What should you do?
options: Overtake quickly before it moves off
Sound your horn as you pass
Flash your lights to warn the driver
Drive carefully and slowly
questions.explain: Drive carefully and slowly when passing a stationary bus showing a 'School Bus' sign, as children may be getting on or off.

questions.q: A school crossing patrol gives this signal as you approach. What does it mean?
options: They aren't ready to cross anyone yet
Be prepared to stop for pedestrians
Traffic may carry on with caution
Pedestrians are being held at the kerb
questions.explain: This signal means the school crossing patrol is ready to cross pedestrians and vehicles must be prepared to stop. You MUST obey signals and signs used by school crossing patrols.

questions.q: You're driving at 30 mph and want to overtake a cyclist. As a guide, what's the minimum space you should leave?
options: At least 0.5 metres
At least 0.75 metres
At least 1.5 metres
At least 1 metre
questions.explain: As a guide, leave at least 1.5 metres when overtaking cyclists at speeds of up to 30 mph, and give them more space when overtaking at higher speeds.

questions.q: You're driving on a road with a 50 mph speed limit and are about to overtake a cyclist. How much room should you give them?
options: More than you would at 30 mph
Exactly 1.5 metres, the same as in town
Less, as you'll pass them more quickly
Just enough to avoid touching them
questions.explain: Leave at least 1.5 metres when overtaking cyclists at speeds of up to 30 mph, and give them more space when overtaking at higher speeds.

questions.q: You're following a cyclist along a narrow road. Oncoming traffic means you can't give them enough room to overtake safely. What should you do?
options: Overtake slowly, leaving as much room as you can
Sound your horn so they move closer to the kerb
Flash your headlights to ask them to pull in
Wait behind until it's safe to overtake
questions.explain: You should wait behind the cyclist and not overtake if it's unsafe or not possible to meet the recommended clearances. Be patient until there's a safe opportunity.

questions.q: You're about to leave a roundabout. What should you watch out for at the exit road?
options: Pedestrians who may be crossing it
Traffic joining from the right
Vehicles reversing out of it
Cyclists who must give way to you
questions.explain: At roundabouts, watch out for and give plenty of room to pedestrians who may be crossing the approach and exit roads.

questions.q: You're driving along a road with a cycle lane marked by a broken white line. When should you drive or park in it?
options: Whenever no cyclists are using it
At any time outside rush hour
Only when it's unavoidable
Whenever you need to pass a queue
questions.explain: Don't drive or park in a cycle lane marked by a broken white line unless it's unavoidable. You MUST NOT park in any cycle lane while waiting restrictions apply.

questions.q: You're driving along a road that has a cycle lane. A cyclist is riding on the road just outside the lane rather than in it. What should you do?
options: Accept that they don't have to use it
Sound your horn to tell them to use the lane
Pass them closely, as they should be in the lane
Flash your headlights to warn them
questions.explain: Cyclists are not obliged to use cycle lanes or cycle tracks. Give them at least as much room as you would a car when you overtake.

questions.q: At night, what MUST a bicycle have fitted, as well as front and rear lights?
options: A white rear reflector
A red rear reflector
A flashing amber beacon
A green front lamp
questions.explain: At night a cycle MUST have white front and red rear lights lit. It MUST also be fitted with a red rear reflector, and amber pedal reflectors if it was made after 1 October 1985.

questions.q: You've just crossed the first white line of an advanced stop line when the traffic lights turn red. What should you do?
options: Reverse back behind the first white line
Stop no later than the second white line
Drive on through the red light
Wait with your front wheels over the second line
questions.explain: If your vehicle has crossed the first white line when the signal goes red, you should stop as soon as possible and MUST stop at the second white line. Allow cyclists enough time and space to move off when the green signal shows.

questions.q: You're about to enter a roundabout. A cyclist is in the left-hand lane on the roundabout and is signalling right. What does this mean?
options: They're about to leave at the next exit
They want you to overtake them
They're continuing round the roundabout
They're about to stop at the kerb
questions.explain: Cyclists, horse riders and horse-drawn vehicles may stay in the left-hand lane when they intend to continue across or around the roundabout, and should signal right to show they're not leaving. Take extra care not to cut across them.

questions.q: You're driving on a roundabout behind a cyclist who is in your lane. What should you do?
options: Stay back and give them plenty of room
Overtake them within your lane
Sound your horn so they move left
Drive close behind to hurry them
questions.explain: You should give priority to cyclists on a roundabout, as they'll be travelling more slowly than motorised traffic. Give them plenty of room and don't try to overtake them within their lane.

questions.q: You've parked on the left-hand side of a road and want to open the driver's door, which is on your right. Which hand does The Highway Code suggest you use?
options: Your right hand, nearest the door
Either hand, as long as you're quick
Both hands, to control the door
Your left hand, on the opposite side
questions.explain: Where you can, open the door using the hand on the opposite side to the door, such as your left hand for a door on your right. This makes you turn your head to look over your shoulder, so you're more likely to see cyclists or motorcyclists passing. You MUST make sure you don't hit anyone when you open your door.

questions.q: You're driving along a narrow, quiet road behind a cyclist who is riding in the centre of the lane. What should you do?
options: Sound your horn so they move to the left
Allow them to ride there for their safety
Flash your headlights to ask them to move
Drive close behind to show you want to pass
questions.explain: On narrow sections of road, on quiet roads, at junctions and in slower-moving traffic, cyclists may ride in the centre of the lane. Allow them to do so for their own safety, so they can see and be seen.

questions.q: You're driving behind a group of cyclists who are riding two abreast on a quiet road. Which of these is true?
options: They're breaking the law by riding side by side
They must ride in single file at all times
It can be safer for them to ride two abreast
They must pull over to let you pass
questions.explain: It can be safer for groups of cyclists to ride two abreast, particularly in larger groups or when accompanying children or less experienced riders. Allow them to do so and wait for a safe place to overtake.

questions.q: You're driving behind a cyclist who looks over their shoulder. What could this mean?
options: They're about to pull out or turn right
They want you to overtake them now
They're about to get off their bike
They're checking their rear light
questions.explain: If a rider looks over their shoulder, it could mean they intend to pull out, turn right or change direction. Give them time and space to do so.

questions.q: You're driving behind a cyclist on a road with potholes and drain covers. Why should you give them plenty of room?
options: They might stop to report the potholes
Their lights may not be working
They'll want to speed up past you
They may suddenly change direction
questions.explain: Cyclists and motorcyclists may suddenly need to avoid uneven road surfaces and obstacles such as drain covers or oily, wet or icy patches. Give them plenty of room and be ready for a sudden change of direction.

questions.q: You're waiting to turn right into a side road across a queue of stationary traffic. A driver in the queue leaves a gap for you. What should you look out for before turning?
options: Traffic lights changing ahead of the queue
Motorcyclists coming up on the inside of the queue
Vehicles parked further along the main road
Buses pulling out from stops behind you
questions.explain: When turning right across a line of slow-moving or stationary traffic, look out for and give way to cyclists or motorcyclists on the inside of the traffic you're crossing. Check your mirrors and blind spots carefully.

questions.q: You're waiting to emerge from a side road. Why should you look carefully for motorcyclists before you pull out?
options: They always have priority at junctions
They're not allowed to filter in traffic
They could be approaching faster than you think
They usually ride without headlights
questions.explain: It's often difficult to see motorcyclists and cyclists, especially when they're coming out of or moving off from junctions. Always look out for them before you emerge; they could be approaching faster than you think.

questions.q: What does the law say about lights on a powered mobility scooter being used on the road at night?
options: They're optional
Only a rear light is needed
They MUST be used
They're needed only in fog
questions.explain: Users of powered wheelchairs and mobility scooters MUST follow the same rules about lights as other vehicles if they're fitted, and at night lights MUST be used. Other road users may not see them, so take extra care.

questions.q: You're driving along a country road and see a horse and rider ahead. What's the maximum speed you should slow down to?
options: 15 mph
20 mph
25 mph
10 mph
questions.explain: When you see a horse on a road, you should slow down to a maximum of 10 mph. Be patient, and don't sound your horn or rev your engine.

questions.q: It's safe for you to overtake a horse rider. As a guide, what's the minimum space you should allow?
options: At least 1 metre
At least 2 metres
At least 1.5 metres
At least 0.5 metres
questions.explain: When it's safe to do so, pass horse riders and horse-drawn vehicles wide and slow, at speeds under 10 mph, allowing at least 2 metres of space.

questions.q: You're behind a horse rider on a narrow lane and it isn't safe to overtake. What should you do?
options: Sound your horn to ask them to pull in
Rev your engine so they know you're there
Be patient and stay well back
Drive close behind to encourage them on
questions.explain: Be patient with horse riders and don't sound your horn or rev your engine. Horses are flight animals and can move incredibly quickly if startled.

questions.q: Two horse riders ahead of you are riding side by side. Why might they be doing this?
options: To escort an inexperienced horse or rider
To prevent traffic from overtaking them
Because horses must be ridden in pairs
Because they're about to turn right
questions.explain: Horse riders are often children. Riders may ride in double file when escorting a young or inexperienced horse or rider, so take extra care and be patient.

questions.q: You see this sign while driving through the New Forest. How should you treat any ponies you come across?
options: Sound your horn to move them off the road
Pass them at the speed limit
Flash your lights to scare them away
The same as you would ridden horses
questions.explain: This sign warns of wild horses or ponies. Feral or semi-feral ponies found in areas such as the New Forest, Exmoor and Dartmoor require the same consideration as ridden horses when approaching or passing.

questions.q: You're driving on a country road and a herd of cattle is blocking the road ahead. What should you do?
options: Sound your horn to clear a path
Stop and switch off your engine
Edge forward slowly through the herd
Rev your engine to move them along
questions.explain: If a road is blocked by a herd of animals, stop and switch off your engine until they've left the road. Don't scare animals by sounding your horn, revving your engine or accelerating rapidly once you've passed them.

questions.q: You're following a car that's being driven by an older driver. What should you bear in mind?
options: They're not allowed to drive at night
They must display a special plate
Their reactions may be slower
They're restricted to 40 mph
questions.explain: Older drivers' reactions may be slower than other drivers'. Make allowance for this.

questions.q: According to the Highway Code, about how many new drivers have some kind of collision in their first year of driving?
options: One in fifty
One in a hundred
One in two
One in five
questions.explain: Many newly qualified drivers lack experience. As many as one new driver in five has some kind of collision in their first year of driving, so be patient with new drivers.

questions.q: You're following a car that's displaying a green 'P' plate. What does this tell you?
options: The driver is a qualified instructor
The driver has a medical condition
The car has been specially adapted
The driver has recently passed their test
questions.explain: Drivers who have recently passed their test may display a 'new driver' plate, such as a green 'P' plate. They may lack experience, so be patient with them.

questions.q: You catch up with a powered mobility scooter travelling on the road. What's the maximum speed these vehicles can travel at on the road?
options: 4 mph
8 mph
12 mph
15 mph
questions.explain: Powered wheelchairs and mobility scooters used on the road travel at a maximum speed of 8 mph (12 km/h). Be prepared for them to be moving much more slowly than other traffic.

questions.q: You're driving on a dual carriageway with a 70 mph speed limit. A powered wheelchair is travelling ahead of you. What MUST it display?
options: A flashing blue light
Hazard warning lights
A flashing amber beacon
A 'slow vehicle' sign
questions.explain: On a dual carriageway where the speed limit exceeds 50 mph (80 km/h), powered vehicles used by disabled people MUST have a flashing amber beacon. On other roads you may not have that advance warning.

questions.q: You're driving into a Home Zone. What should you expect?
options: People may be using the whole of the road
Vehicles have priority over pedestrians
Children aren't allowed to play there
The national speed limit applies
questions.explain: In Home Zones and Quiet Lanes, people could be using the whole of the road, for example children playing or a community event. Drive slowly and carefully and be prepared to stop.

questions.q: You see this sign. What does it warn you about?
options: A school crossing patrol ahead
A pedestrian zone with no vehicles
A zebra crossing ahead
Frail pedestrians likely to cross the road
questions.explain: This sign warns that frail (or blind or disabled, if shown) pedestrians are likely to cross the road ahead. Older pedestrians may need more time to cross, so be patient.

questions.q: Which of these is a correct use of your horn?
options: To tell a cyclist to move over
While moving, to warn others you're there
To hurry a pedestrian on a crossing
To tell a learner to move off faster
questions.explain: Use the horn only while your vehicle is moving and you need to warn other road users of your presence. Never sound it aggressively, and be patient with pedestrians at crossings rather than sounding your horn.

questions.q: You're turning left out of a side road and need to cross a cycle track. What should you be aware of?
options: Cyclists must give way to you at the track
Cycle tracks are only used during rush hour
Cyclists may be coming from both directions
Cyclists on the track can only ride one way
questions.explain: You should give way to cyclists approaching or using a cycle track when you're turning into or out of a junction. Be prepared to stop and wait for a safe gap, as the track may be used by cyclists travelling in both directions.
